documents.title: Rev5 questions and discussion on the Consolidated Rules for 2026 (or Legacy)
documents.text:
**VDR/VER December 7 implementation and evidence expectations for existing Rev5 Class C CSPs**

For an existing Rev5 Class C CSP transitioning to VDR/VER by the December 7, 2026 maintain date, could FedRAMP clarify what must be in place for the CSP to be considered as meeting the VDR/VER rules as of that date?

**1. Implementation state:** What VDR and VER capabilities and processes should be operational by December 7 for an existing Rev5 Class C CSP?

**2. Evidence:** What evidence should the CSP retain to demonstrate that VDR/VER was implemented and operating as of the December 7 maintain date? For example, procedures, evaluation/response records, remediation tracking, reporting outputs, or other implementation evidence.

**3. Documentation:** Are updates to SSP/control narratives, ConMon procedures, Security Decision Record content, or other certification artifacts expected by December 7, or may those documentation updates be completed through the normal certification/assessment cycle?

**4. Assessment timing:** Is the expectation that the CSP adopt and operate VDR/VER by December 7, with independent verification/validation occurring later through the normal assessment cycle unless otherwise required?

**5. MUST vs. SHOULD:** For purposes of determining whether a CSP “meets the VDR/VER rules” on December 7, how should CSPs treat applicable SHOULD requirements? If a CSP has a valid, documented justification for deviating from a SHOULD requirement, would that still be considered compliant with the rules, or would the CSP be expected to enter the corrective-action/In Remediation process?

We want to make sure our December 7 readiness activities are aligned with FedRAMP’s expectations and that we understand both the implementation and evidence threshold before the maintain date.

documents.title: Rev5 questions and discussion on the Consolidated Rules for 2026 (or Legacy)
documents.text:
Hello FedRAMP team, 

We're a multi-tenant SaaS provider building our VDR/VER program to Class C timeframes. Our aim is to put engineering effort where risk is highest, avoid noise from routinely replaced images, and keep our reporting transparent. Some questions that we have. 

**Detection time with a continuous scanner (VER-RPT-VDT, FRD-VLD, VER-TFR-EVU, VDR-CSO-DET, VDR-TFR-MVF**).

Our scanner product scans continuously by default, so first-seen dates arrive daily. Its main value is persistently verifying and validating that fixes are in place, since a merged change does not by itself confirm remediation (VDR-CSO-DET, VDR-TFR-MVF). Findings are pulled into our evaluation process on a documented cadence, not daily. VER-RPT-VDT requires the "time and source of the detection," and FRD-VLD describes detection as initial discovery plus determination of affected resources, but neither says which timestamp counts.

1. Can the reported detection time be when the finding enters our evaluation process (the pull), provided the pull cadence is documented, instead of the scanner's first-seen date?
2. If first-seen is expected, is it acceptable during the transition to report the gap between first-seen and evaluation and justify not meeting the 5-day VER-TFR-EVU SHOULD, while we work toward a shorter cadence?

**Drift for machine-based resources (FRD-DET, FRD-MBI, VDR-TFR-PDD, VDR-TFR-PCD).**

Our machine-based resources are defined and deployed through IaC and are routinely replaced rather than modified in place, so each instance matches its code-defined state. Should these resources count as not likely to drift, with changes made through the IaC pipeline treated as updates to the intended state rather than drift?

**Fixes that require a major platform upgrade (FRD-ACV, VER-RPT-AVI, VDR-TFR-PVR).**

Some shared platforms that are core to our infrastructure are on vendor-supported versions, but a fix is only available in a new major version. Because many services depend on these platforms, a major upgrade needs extensive compatibility testing to avoid breaking dependent functionality, which typically can make it months of planned work. Is it appropriate to report these as accepted vulnerabilities with a reviewed category explanation (upgrade and compatibility risk, testing plan, planned upgrade date, compensating controls) plus a per-asset note? We would keep KEVs and internet-reachable likely exploitable findings outside this approach.

**Mitigated KEVs (VDR-TFR-KEV).**

If a KEV is fully mitigated and rated NO but not yet remediated by its CISA due date, should it be reported as overdue? Is a documented mitigation an acceptable justification for the SHOULD, or does BOD 26-04 expect remediation regardless?

Yes.  When you transition to VDR/VER, POA&M requirements go away.  You will transition to FedRAMP Vulnerability Detail Report (VER-RPT-VDT) and a human readable Monthly Activity Report (VER-TFR-MHR).

Your tempo for agency meetings also changes to a quarterly requirement in accordance with Collaborative Continuous Monitoring (CCM-QTR-MTG).

documents.title: Rev5 questions and discussion on the Consolidated Rules for 2026 (or Legacy)
documents.text:
> 1. Implementation state: What VDR and VER capabilities and processes should be operational by December 7 for an existing Rev5 Class C CSP?

All of the applicable VDR and VER rules must be addressed.

> 2. Evidence: What evidence should the CSP retain to demonstrate that VDR/VER was implemented and operating as of the December 7 maintain date? For example, procedures, evaluation/response records, remediation tracking, reporting outputs, or other implementation evidence.

The reports required under the [Reporting](https://www.fedramp.gov/2026/reference/vulnerability-evaluation-and-reporting/#reporting) subset of the VER are sufficient evidence until an SDR is updated. Legacy folks may wish to update the appropriate vulnerability and continuous monitoring controls in their SSP. 

> 3. Documentation: Are updates to SSP/control narratives, ConMon procedures, Security Decision Record content, or other certification artifacts expected by December 7, or may those documentation updates be completed through the normal certification/assessment cycle?

These aren't _required_ by December 7, but it would be a better experience and practice to do so. Trying to work out what the status of a certification package is from significant changes is frustrating for customers. The "annual package maintenance" expectation of Rev5 is one of the biggest problems that 20x addresses.

> 4. Assessment timing: Is the expectation that the CSP adopt and operate VDR/VER by December 7, with independent verification/validation occurring later through the normal assessment cycle unless otherwise required?

Yes.

> 5. MUST vs. SHOULD: For purposes of determining whether a CSP “meets the VDR/VER rules” on December 7, how should CSPs treat applicable SHOULD requirements? If a CSP has a valid, documented justification for deviating from a SHOULD requirement, would that still be considered compliant with the rules, or would the CSP be expected to enter the corrective-action/In Remediation process?

https://www.fedramp.gov/2026/rules/#force-of-the-rule

As long as SHOULD rules are addressed, explained, and the risk posed to agency customers as a result of the decision is identified, then it is "compliant."

It's always important to remember the two sides of FedRAMP rules though - they indicate what the minimum necessary to maintain a FedRAMP Certification, not necessarily what is necessary to keep an agency customer happy for their particular use cases.

You could, for example, not implement any of the SHOULD rules in the VDR/VER and provide good reasons for those (cost, complexity, risk, inapplicability, etc.). FedRAMP will allow you to maintain your FedRAMP Certification in this case. Agency customers, under pressure from CISA to product proof of updated procedures, may feel differently.

documents.text:
Hello, after reviewing the timelines and process involved for adopting VDR/VER for CSPs, I have several questions:

- Is it accurate to say that while there are deadlines of Dec 7th and March 7th involved, there's no external validation or verification that what a CSP claims to be in place, actually is? In other words, a CSP could claim to be meeting the requirements, but won't actually get tested against this until their next annual assessment; is that accurate?
- If CSPs are following the SCR process still, do they need to complete a SCR to adopt VDR/VER processes, considering it's a large change to how vulnerabilities are processed and reported?
- If CSPs are following the SCN process, do they need to complete a SCN? If so, would this be considered a transformative SCN and (likely) trigger an assessment of the change from an independent assessor?

If a SCR isn't required or a transformative SCN assessment isn't required, is there anything in place to validate and verify that a CSP is following VDR/VER before their next annual assessment?

documents.text:
Connect doesnt have a way to mass add folders with our current permission sets. We dont have the bandwidth to create 400+ new folders just for a few months use.  

Transitions to VDR and VER should be done through an SCR/SCN.  The SCN/SCR to transition to VDR/VER should outline the where, this way there is always a paper trail.  Alternatively it can be documented as part of your monthly ConMon brief prior to the transition.  This way if anyone ever questions there is a paper trail indicating all parties were informed, and the rest of the papertrail should exist in the folders chosen.  

This is ultimately why we had our VDR/VER dates pushed right, but when BOD 26-04 came out we adjusted this timeline to have parity with the gov requirement side, but it puts folks who havent transitioned to CDS early in a weird spot.  All that to say I appreciate the questions and thank you for pointing out something I think some folks are probably trying to navigate.

Paul

documents.title: Rev5 questions and discussion on the Consolidated Rules for 2026 (or Legacy)
documents.text:
The core of the December 7 deadline is based on the expectations set by CISA BOD 26-04 - CISA has told all agencies they have until that time to reach Phase III wherein they are ensuring all information systems have adopted a risk-based approach to prioritization and remediation of vulnerabilities. How FedRAMP responds after this deadline will depend on how CISA responds government-wide - CISA might do anything from extending the deadline to mandating that systems not following the updated approach be turned off. 

[Understanding Ruleset Effective Dates](https://www.fedramp.gov/2026/providers/updating/deadlines/?h=%22grace+period%22#understanding-ruleset-effective-dates) in the Important Deadlines section for Cloud Service Providers explains what the Maintain and Grace Ends dates mean:

After December 7, 2026, FedRAMP will request a corrective action plan from cloud services that do not meet the VDR/VER rules. This corrective action plan will be expected to show how the provider will meet the VDR/VER rules. This should not be a burden for any provider because any responsible provider will already be working through a plan to adopt these rules and will just need to share that with us and their agency customers.

Cloud service providers that do not meet FedRAMP's ongoing requirements for FedRAMP Certification are moved into an "In Remediation" status - this will include any provider that does not meet the VDR/VER rules on December 7, 2026. FedRAMP also communicates directly with agencies to ensure they are aware the cloud services they are using have significant gaps like this.

After March 7, 2027, FedRAMP will revoke FedRAMP Certification from cloud services that do not meet the VDR/VER rules.

documents.text:
1. If you are claiming that you are VDR or VER compliant there will be evidence within your repo and within your ConMon optempo and outputs.  Agencies participating in ConMon should be able to easily identify who has changed and identify deficiencies to FedRAMP.  We will work with our agency liaisons and our monthly agency touchpoints to ensure they are prepared.  CSPs should work with them as part of their ConMon processes, to ensure you all are aligned.  Changes to VDR/VER should trigger a Significant Change so there will also be historic change information and impact in your repo and your agency should be engaged during that process.

I'm a little worried about what this question is getting at, but if anyone purposely misrepresents their status to FedRAMP or their Agencies, I will recommend to leadership that we bypass a CAP and go straight to delisting.  

2. Yes.  VDR and VER will most likely affect controls (probably CA-1, CA-5, CA-7) and should be treated as a significant change, regardless if you follow SCR or SCN.  For the control snipers out there... there are probably more controls affected, but its early and I am still on my first coffee.

3.  Yes.  We expect most of these to be adaptive, but the reality is going to be dependent on the changes you need to make to be compliant.  SCN-ADP-NTF contains a section called "Tips on adaptive changes" that has some circumstances listed out as well as a similar section in Transformative section (look at key tests).  Also, if your transition to VDR/VER  is transformative, Independent validation is only required where human validation is needed.

documents.title: Should these five rules carry timeframe_type/timeframe_num?
documents.text:
Sharing a consistency check I ran in a personal capacity while building against the consolidated rules dataset.

I'm planning to maintain an open-source tool that computes VDR and VER response deadlines by reading `fedramp-consolidated-rules.json` rather than embedding the numbers, so that a change to a cadence upstream reaches the tool without a code change. That means every timeframe has to be derivable from the data. I walked all 246 FRR rules at `v2026.07.14.01` to find the ones where it is not.

**What holds, and it holds cleanly.** The dataset encodes timeframes in two shapes and is consistent about both, and `AGENTS.md` documents both placements: it lists simple timeframes among the fields a class-specific variant may carry, and again among the "other useful top-level fields" a requirement may carry. Rules that vary by class put `timeframe_type` and `timeframe_num` inside each `varies_by_class` entry. Flat rules carry the same pair at the top level, and 17 of them do: `AFC-FRP-PNT` (bizdays 10), `CDS-CSO-FRC` (weeks 2), `CDS-UTC-AAD` (bizdays 5), six `REC-IAS-*` rules, five `SCN-*` rules, and `VER-TFR-MHR` (months 1) and `VER-TFR-MAV` (days 192). No rule mixes the two shapes. As a consumer that is genuinely nice to work against.

**The exceptions.** Five flat rules state a numeric timeframe in the statement and encode nothing:

| Rule | Force | Prose timeframe |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `VDR-TFR-NMV` | MUST | at least once every 3 months |
| `CCM-OCR-AVL` | MUST | every 3 months |
| `IVV-CSF-MCA` | MUST | every 3 years |
| `MKT-IIP-DLA` | MUST | within 2 years |
| `MKT-CAS-RFR` | MUST | within 5 business days |

A sixth, `CCM-QTR-SAR`, states a two-sided window ("at least 3 business days after ... AND within 10 business days of such release") that a single `timeframe_type` / `timeframe_num` pair cannot express, so I have left it out rather than counting it as a gap.

To be clear about what this is not: nothing here is a schema violation. `dependentRequired` in `frr_requirement` and `frr_requirement_level` only pairs the two fields when one is present, so the file validates today either way. This is about what a consumer can derive.

**Consumer consequence.** Any tool that builds a compliance calendar from `timeframe_type` / `timeframe_num` silently drops these five cadences, and all five are MUST rules. `VDR-TFR-NMV` is the one that bites me directly: every other timeframe in my VDR and VER calculations comes out of the data, and this one has to be hardcoded, which is exactly the failure the structured fields prevent. `VDR-TFR-PDD` sits one rule below it and its Class A value is `months` / `3`, the same cadence NMV states in prose.

**The question.** Is the omission deliberate on some or all of these? I can see an argument that a verification cadence is a different kind of thing from a response clock and was left unencoded on purpose. If so, I would rather record that as a documented decision than carry a hardcoded exception. If it is simply a gap, each is a two-line addition, and I am happy to open a PR if that is useful.

Also worth linking: @badgerinspace raised `VDR-TFR-NMV` from the interpretation side in [this comment on #146](https://github.com/FedRAMP/community/discussions/146#discussioncomment-17908116) on 2026-08-05, still unanswered. Different question, same rule.

Kyle Versluis (personal capacity)

For existing Rev5 Class C CSP that has not yet implemented CDS/Trust Center capabilities, can FedRAMP clarify the expected interim reporting mechanism for VER?

1. May the CSP continue using its existing USDA Connect Community Portal secure folders for the required at-least-monthly human-readable VER reporting?
2. For VER-TFR-MRH, would placing an updated JSON file in the USDA Connect Community Portal secure folders at least every 14 days satisfy the expectation to make recent historical VDR activity available for automated retrieval, or is an API or similar programmatic retrieval mechanism expected during the interim period?

documents.title: Rev5 questions and discussion on the Consolidated Rules for 2026 (or Legacy)
documents.text:
1. Your FedRAMP Certification is tied to your adherence to FedRAMP rules and requirements. 

2. FedRAMP Authorization Act, (Section 3614 #3) Requires Agencies "to the extent practicable, for any cloud computing product or service the agency seeks to authorize that has received a FedRAMP authorization, **use the existing assessments of security controls and materials** within any FedRAMP authorization package for that cloud computing product or service."   If an agency has unique needs above FedRAMP requirements, they have always been allowed to require those and we regularly see these in Rev5 for some agencies (as noted above).  I would check with your agency contracts for specific terminology and requirements outside of FedRAMP. 

3. For your SSP, the CPO and SDR require a machine and human readable version.  The majority of components in an SSP reside within the CPO and SDR.  They will still receive the same information. 

4. VDR/VER transitions are tied to CISA BOD 26-04.  The entire Agency (not just FedRAMP CSPs) will be required to move to a VDR/VER like process.  Our 12/07 date is explicitly tied to the BOD Phase II timeline so that Federal and FedRAMP CSP requirements and dates aligned.

documents.title: 20x questions and discussion on the Consolidated Rules for 2026
documents.text:
TM...  Sorry Pete is out at an event rubbing elbows with Agencies, 3PAOs, and CSPs....  So you get the third string kicker..

Based on your scenario, you are a Rev5 CSP transitioning to the ruleset...  Something important to call out as 20x processes and Rev5 are different in regards to timelines and reviews.

Transition to Rulesets do not require initial 3rd party validation it just requires you to follow the rules.  Yes, transition to some of the rulesets will change control statements that should be validated during your annual review.  Your VDR/VER example is great as it will affect your CA-5 controls, but you can transition to rulesets anytime before the required dates.

Some Rulesets require notification when transitioning.  For example, the CDS Ruleset, under CDS-CSF-TCM, requires you to "Notify FedRAMP via email: [info@fedramp.gov](mailto:info@fedramp.gov)," when you transition.  

Others, we will request your implementation status at various points through the FSI process.  The evidence of your transition for most of these will be prevalent in you trust center or repo.  The VDR/VER example you provide is an excellent example.  Your March ConMon in your scenario should contain VDR/VER requirements (POA&M should change to Monthly activity report with PAIN thresholds, new timelines, etc).  

When you do your annual assessment we will also ask about status of rulesets and implementation dates.  Your agencies should also be tracking your ruleset adoptions and should identify issues and deficiencies as well.

Hope that helps.

Paul

documents.text:
Addressing FedRAMP Communication (AFC) and Secure Configuration Guide (SCG) are required now. The grace period ended July 1st 2026, but as those requirements were communicated at the beginning of the year, that should not come as a surprise, though some might have only been tracking for existing certifications and not new submissions.

Optional early adoption of CR26 started July 4th. We anticipate receiving packages of many shapes and sizes between now and January 1st. Some will be legacy Rev5 (+ AFC & SCG), others might be 100% CR26, others might be legacy Rev5 + AFC, SCG, VER & VDR, and still others might be some bespoke combination.

Package composition would be a conversation between provider, assessor and agency, but keep the obtain dates top of mind! Remember that agencies have adoption timelines for BOD 26-04, so early adoption of VDR/VER could really benefit them, too.

We recognize some folks are in-flight and have made investments in legacy processes and materials. We can't give business advice or give specific council on how each provider should approach. That is why we built CR26 in the open, provided the flexibility of early adoption, and gave about 6 months of lead time for new submissions.

documents.title: Rev5 questions and discussion on the Consolidated Rules for 2026 (or Legacy)
documents.text:
The VDR/VER requirement dates are tied to CISA BOD 26-04.  It was released on 10 June 2027 and latest implementation requirements were 180  days, which come out to about 7 Dec 2026 so we adjusted our dates for VDR/VER to align.

In general, if you don't meet in your case maintain dates, you should expect a CAP.  The CAP should have a fix NLT than date tied to the grace period and listed as deficient in the MP.  Once the grace period passes, you should expect to be pulled from marketplace and FedRAMP completely.  

First Independent Assessment was meant to cover Initial Rev 5 Assessments and Annual Assessments, not SC support.  Please also note, that the the grace date is tied to you assessment START date, not the DUE date.  There are only a handful of CR26 rules tied to your Independant Assessment start date.  This was done because transitioning to these outside of the AA window doesn't make sense for the most part.       

So if your AA's have started every Nov, the rules explicitly tied to "On the first FedRAMP independent assessment started after 2027-01-01" would be tied to your Nov 2027 Assessment.

documents.title: Rev5 questions and discussion on the Consolidated Rules for 2026 (or Legacy)
documents.text:
For [VDR-CSO-DET](https://www.fedramp.gov/2026/reference/vulnerability-detection-and-response/#vulnerability-detection) (Vulnerability Detection), can FedRAMP clarify a few details around what's expected? Specifically around the following:
- SCA / code scans - are results here expected to be included in VDR and reporting?
- Supply chain monitoring - are SBOM scans expected here or something else?

Traditionally, SCA / code scans have of course been required by FedRAMP to be done, but not required to be reported in ConMon, since ConMon focuses largely on the established inventory. These scans typically create extra noise and can generate thousands of vulnerabilities that are often dependent on upstream codebases. Is this type of data expected in VDR / VER tracking, triaging, and reporting?

Similar question for supply chain monitoring, what would FedRAMP consider a vulnerability here? Is there an expectation of SBOM scans or something else? SBOMs have never been specifically required and would have redundant information with things like container scans, but what is expected here?

documents.title: Rev5 questions and discussion on the Consolidated Rules for 2026 (or Legacy)
documents.text:
The theory with false positive vulnerabilities is that since they're still there and they show up and will presumably always keep showing up, then you'd almost certainly want to track them and persistently evaluate them if there's a change - today's false positive might be tomorrow's PAIN5 after all. That said, we are missing specific guidance on how to report these because we figured there are a few different ways that would make sense in context.

Both VER-RPT-PER and VDR-RPT-VDT would include false positive vulnerabilities by default since they aren't excluded. For VER-RPT-VDT you might simply decide that a number of reporting fields are not applicable if something is a false positive, but it would likely include at least the identifier, detection time/source, and time of evaluation if the vulnerability was first detected and evaluated as a false positive. In the current list of required information for VER-RPT-VDT you could add in item 10 (supplementary information) that it's a false positive, without needing to add it somewhere else. (you're right that there isn't specific instructions here, but there are plenty of ways to approach it)

You can also leverage VER-EVA-GRV (Group Vulnerabilities) to simplify tracking/monitoring/reporting of false positives in a lot of different ways - you could even just have a big False Positives group if you wanted. 

>  Does FedRAMP want to see false positives reported as N0 vulnerabilities?

Not mandatory, but evaluating to N0 would be a reasonable automatic outcome of evaluating to false positive. Agreed that you still also want to flag this as a false positive.

Hope this helps, feel free to follow up with any additional questions!

-Pete @ FedRAMP

documents.title: Rev5 questions and discussion on the Consolidated Rules for 2026 (or Legacy)
documents.text: We build GRC tooling for Rev5 providers. A question we keep getting from providers and their advisors: after a provider adopts VDR/VER and stops producing a POA&M, some agency AOs are expected to keep asking for the legacy POA&M and SSP anyway, at least for a while. AGU-AGC-NAR reads like an agency needs a head-of-agency determination and has to notify FedRAMP before requiring anything beyond the FedRAMP package. In practice, what does FedRAMP expect a provider to do when an agency asks for legacy artifacts after December 7? Point them at the rule, produce both for a transition period, or something else?

documents.title: Rev5 questions and discussion on the Consolidated Rules for 2026 (or Legacy)
documents.text:
> As we work to understand the implementation expectations and plan accordingly, could FedRAMP provide additional context on how it intends to verify that CSPs have implemented VDR by the December 7 deadline?

We simply need to ask you and review your required vulnerability detection and response activity reports to confirm.

> It would also be helpful to understand how FedRAMP is thinking about supporting agencies that may still be establishing the processes needed to receive, process, and evaluate VDR data. 

You should work with your agency customers to supply information in a way that optimizes their experience. The default requirements in the VER are not very different from historical information that cloud service providers were expected to share. Agencies generally manually review spreadsheets and summaries, and they will be able to continue to do this if they do not have tools, expertise, or interest in reviewing more detailed information. 

Remember that agencies are also simultaneously rebuilding all of their own internal processes and tooling to comply with BOD 26-04 and are figuring all of this out on the fly as well.

> Finally, how will FedRAMP evaluate a CSP's progress toward implementation? If a CSP has a documented action plan and is actively taking steps to implement the applicable CR26 requirements by the deadline, would that be sufficient to avoid a corrective action plan, or is full implementation expected by December 7/March 7th?

We are not planning on evaluating progress. Cloud service providers are capable of managing their own progress and don't need to report to us along the way. 

Yes, full implementation is expected by December 7. If full implementation is not completed on that date then the cloud service provider will be expected to supply a corrective action plan to complete the implementation by March 7. This process is explained on the [Rev5 Deadlines](https://www.fedramp.gov/2026/providers/updating/deadlines/rev5/) page.

Please remember that CISA BOD 26-04 requires every single agency to transition to this risk-based approach by December 7. On that date, agencies will need to report their status and the status of the cloud services they use. Historically, there may be a bit of flexibility in a CISA BOD deadline but we have seen circumstances where within a few months of such a deadline agencies have been forced to turn off services that do not comply. The grace period that FedRAMP provided is **only** for FedRAMP Certification itself, it is entirely possible that failure to comply with the VDR/VER will result in agencies turning off your service on that date and considering you in breach of contract (depending on how that's written).

We wrote VDR and VER in a way that would allow any mildly competent cloud service provider to rapidly switch over to it while gaining all of the benefits of the risk-based approach to vulnerability management, at a potential negative cost of needing to massively accelerate response to extremely rare circumstances (like this week's php2shell) _which any secure cloud service was already doing._

documents.title: Rev5 questions and discussion on the Consolidated Rules for 2026 (or Legacy)
documents.text:
These rules are all written intentionally to allow cloud service providers to determine the best and most appropriate approach for their own environment/business/strategy, then to document and share that approach so that customer agencies can determine if it's appropriate for their particular use cases and needs. 

We do strongly recommend that logical groupings be used at scale to reduce noise. The intent of VDR/VER is two-fold:

(1) Provide assurance that vulnerability detection and response is done (detailed overall reports and summaries for reference)
(2) Provide warnings and timely information that explains the risk to customer agency data so customers can make informed risk management decisions, as needed

FedRAMP isn't setting an explicit "this is how you do vulnerability detection and response" technical process because it would immediately be out of date and not apply to many cloud services. Do good security and assure your customers that you do so.

documents.title: Rev5 questions and discussion on the Consolidated Rules for 2026 (or Legacy)
documents.text:
I am completely biased, but I tend to think we are pretty reasonable people — as an example, the lost sponsor / ready conversion pathways were created because some providers got stuck in extenuating circumstances. 

The rules have specific dates so we can get this party started. If you are late to that party, the door might be locked. Lots can happen between now and January. We could be overwhelmed with reviews, a shutdown could halt existing agency reviews, your dog could eat your SSP appendices, etc. 

Stuff happens in this biz and we will do our best to respond as reasonable humans, but if it is Nov and you haven't even looked at VDR / VER, your head is not in the game.

documents.title: Question on VDR Rev5 timeline for CSPs
documents.text:
Hi FedRAMP PMO team — quick clarification question on the Vulnerability Detection and Response (VDR) Rev 5 Open Beta timeline.

In the “Effective Date(s) & Overall Applicability for Rev5” section, VDR is described as optional (Open Beta) starting 2026-02-02, and it also says providers **“MUST plan to address all requirements and recommendations… by the end of the Open Beta on May 22, 2026.”**

Can you confirm whether May 22, 2026 is:

- intended **only for CSPs participating in the VDR Open Beta** (i.e., those that signed up / are accepted into the beta), or

- intended to be a deadline that applies to **all FedRAMP Authorized CSPs**, regardless of beta participation?

If it’s only for beta participants, will there be separate guidance/policy later that establishes expectations and timelines for broader adoption post-beta?  We're road mapping our VDR Rev 5 implementation(s) but will need make some technical changes (likely via SCN 😀) , so we're trying to understand what the timeline looks like.

Thanks in advance!

documents.text: Hey ricmarrey coal - different aspects of the Consolidated Rules for 2026 have different timelines. The applicability and timelines are at the top of each ruleset, and are collected for [Rev5 here](https://www.fedramp.gov/2026/providers/updating/deadlines/rev5/) and [20x here](https://www.fedramp.gov/2026/providers/updating/deadlines/20x/). If you check either the Rev5 CSP section or the reference section for both the VDR and VER you will see that they reflect the timelines from NTC-0014: - [Vulnerability Detection and Response](https://www.fedramp.gov/2026/reference/vulnerability-detection-and-response/) - [Vulnerability Evaluation and Reporting](https://www.fedramp.gov/2026/reference/vulnerability-evaluation-and-reporting/) The key bit is the info box at the top of each policy which includes the deadlines for providers seeking to obtain FedRAMP Certification (2026-12-07) and those seeking to maintain it (2026-12-07). Each document also confirms a grace period ending 2027-03-07.

documents.title: Rev5 questions and discussion on the Consolidated Rules for 2026 (or Legacy)
documents.text:
Follow-up on VER-EVA-EPA: does a vulnerability inherit its component's PAIN?

This builds on the question from @mmaesc1 on 2026-09-10 about shared resources and computing PAIN from the inventory ([link](https://github.com/FedRAMP/community/discussions/146#discussioncomment-18391218)), and @pete-gov's reply beneath it confirming that PAIN is cumulative across agencies, that a rules engine over the inventory is the intended approach, and that ratings can be scoped down where a sub-service is isolated to one customer.

We are building that rules engine and want to confirm how the component and the vulnerability combine before we finish it.

Question 1. Two readings of VER-EVA-EPA seem possible.

(a) Each vulnerability carries the PAIN of the component it sits on, since that is what agencies would feel if the component were fully compromised. A read-only information disclosure in a library on a shared database that serves several agencies would rate N5, the same as a flaw that gives full control of that database.

(b) The component sets a ceiling, and the vulnerability's own achievable effect places it at or below that ceiling. The same read-only disclosure would rate N2 (narrow customer effect) if exploitation cannot expose most federal customer data and cannot interrupt the service, while the full-control flaw on the same database would still rate N5.

Which is intended? Or are both acceptable, provided the method is documented and applied consistently?

Question 2. If reading (b) is acceptable, is a two-stage method acceptable: a rule-based first pass that assigns a provisional PAIN from the component (which agencies it serves, what federal customer data it handles), followed by an adjustment per vulnerability using its technical impact, reachability and exploitability, with both stages recorded in the evaluation?

We understand from the August 5 community update that defaulting high is acceptable. Our question is about the other direction: whether a documented method may rate a vulnerability below its component's ceiling when its achievable effect is narrower, so that the VDR-TFR-PVR windows and the set agencies review under VER-AGM-RVR track the risk to them rather than the component's worst case.

Thanks.

documents.title: Rev5 questions and discussion on the Consolidated Rules for 2026 (or Legacy)
documents.text:
**Do false positives need PAIN, IRV, and LEV? (VER-EVA-EPA / EIR / ELX)**

VER-EVA-EPA, VER-EVA-EIR, and VER-EVA-ELX are MUST rules that apply to all "detected vulnerabilities." FRD-FPV defines a false positive as "a detected vulnerability that is not actually present in an exploitable state," and its note says it applies only if the vulnerability "is not and was not present."

**Why this is unclear to us**

_Reading 1: false positives still require PAIN, IRV, and LEV._
FRD-FPV defines a false positive as a detected vulnerability. VER-EVA-EPA, VER-EVA-EIR, and VER-EVA-ELX apply to all detected vulnerabilities, and none of them exempts false positives. On this reading, a false positive needs a PAIN rating and IRV and LEV determinations, the same as any other finding.

_Reading 2: these evaluations don't apply once a finding is determined to be a false positive._
A false positive is "not actually present in an exploitable state," so estimating the impact of exploiting it, or whether it is reachable or likely exploitable, has little meaning. VER-RPT-VDT also says providers report its fields "(if applicable)," which suggests PAIN, IRV, and LEV may be reported as not applicable for a false positive.

Which is intended?

documents.title: RFC-0030 FedRAMP Rev5 Security Controls Baseline Update for RA, SA, SC, SI, and SR Control Families
documents.text:
### RA-5 (Vulnerability Monitoring and Scanning)

**What works**

- Splitting **traditional monthly scanning + 30/90/180** from VDR-based frequencies and VDR mitigation logic is helpful.

**Suggestions**

- Clarify what “representative samples of similar machine-based information resources” means operationally:
  - minimum sampling rate or statistical approach,
  - how “similar” is determined (e.g., image lineage, config profile, role, exposure),
  - how the CSP proves the sample remains representative as the environment changes.
- “Evaluate ALL vulnerabilities within X days of detection” is strong and useful, but it would help to specify whether “evaluate” means:
  - triage + impact determination,
  - exploitability/reachability determination,
  - assignment of remediation timeline category,
  - and/or documented acceptance/false-positive disposition.
- Confirm how **KEV supersedence** applies under VDR (i.e., does KEV always override VDR timelines, or is it incorporated into VDR’s categorization?).

### SA-4(5) (Config baselines)

**Suggestion**

- Consider requiring documentation to include:
  - rationale for deviations from STIG/CIS,
  - mapping to control objectives,
  - and a repeatable validation method (so 3PAOs can assess consistently).

### SA-5 (System Documentation)

**Concern**

- The proposed parameter “a. (1) in conjunction with the FedRAMP Security Configuration Guidance” is directionally good, but feels incomplete as written (it’s hard to implement or test as a standalone parameter).

**Suggestion**

- Consider explicitly stating what documentation artifacts are required “in conjunction with” SCG (e.g., configuration baseline artifacts, implementation evidence, or update cadence).

### SA-15 (Authorization/Certification wording)

**Suggestion**

- Ensure consistent use across all baselines and templates to avoid mismatched language in SSP/SAR/POA&M narratives.

### SC-7(5) (Deny by default—allow by exception)

**Suggestion**

- Consider explicitly acknowledging typical cloud constructs (“services,” managed control planes, serverless) so CSPs don’t get pushed into artificial “system” mappings.

### SC-7(8) (Authenticated proxy routing) – MAS vs traditional

**Suggestion**

- The bracketed phrase appears to have an unmatched parenthesis in the proposed change; recommend tightening the grammar and explicitly defining what counts as:
  - “outside of assessment scope” under MAS, and
  - “outside the established boundary” under traditional,
     to reduce 3PAO interpretation risk.

### SC-13 (Cryptographic modules in CMVP “historical” status)

**Suggestion**

- Add explicit expectations:
  - what evidence must be provided when a module becomes “historical,”
  - expected timelines or triggers for transition/remediation,
  - how FedRAMP will treat “historical” status during annual assessments vs significant changes.

### SI-2(2), SI-3 (shift to “persistently” for VDR participants)

**Suggestion**

- Define the minimum acceptable evidence of “persistent” (e.g., continuous telemetry + alerting, near-real-time status reporting) so CSPs don’t overbuild and 3PAOs don’t under-test.

### SI-5 (EDs/BODs via FedRAMP Secure Inbox)

**Suggestion**

- Add clarity on:
  - whether timelines are driven by the directive itself or FSI guidance (or both),
  - whether CSPs must maintain a standing ED/BOD tracker artifact and where it lives (SSP appendix vs ConMon deliverable).

### SI-8 (DMARC link update)

**Suggestion**

- Consider a short note about scope:
  - applies when sending email “on behalf of the government,”
  - and whether subdomains / third-party senders used by the CSO must also meet policy=reject + reporting requirements.

documents.title: Rev5 questions and discussion on the Consolidated Rules for 2026 (or Legacy)
documents.text:
> 1. If a CSO currently has only one agency customer, would N5 never apply since there are not multiple federal agencies to be impacted?

Correct.

> 2. If a CSO is still seeking its first federal customer, how should N ratings be evaluated since they all require impact to at least one agency.

There is no PAIN without agency impact, however if a cloud service offering has no data to provide about their historical handling of vulnerabilities then it may be difficult to assess the quality of their vulnerability detection and response program. We don't have hard requirements here but would expect folks who take this seriously to simulate PAIN or apply it to their commercial customers/etc.

> 3. For a CSO that is not directly used by agencies but is leveraged by other CSOs that may or may not have agency customers, how should you evaluate the number of impacted agencies?

The VER is focused entirely on requirements for reporting to likely or certainly impacted federal customers. It does not weigh in on requirements for reporting to commercial customers because that would be outside the scope of FedRAMP's authority.

There is no direct PAIN in this case, same as #2, so it is up to the cloud service offering to demonstrate their commitment to their commercial customers. Cloud service offerings that use other cloud services should address risks in their MAS.

> It feels like the conservative, simpler, and more correct security-wise approach for most CSOs would be to evaluate all vulnerabilities as if they impact multiple agencies.

Yes. The VDR/VER are designed to allowed both qualitative and quantitative assessment of how effective a cloud service offering's vulnerability detection and response is, and how seriously they take such activities. Cloud service offerings that prioritize responding to any potentially serious vulnerability, regardless of potential agency impact, are more likely to score higher when evaluated for their performance and capabilities in this area...  especially compared to cloud service offerings that barely meet deadlines and rarely respond to vulnerabilities as a priority.

documents.title: Balancing FedRAMP Rev5 against improvements to FedRAMP 20x
documents.text:
Posting our VDR BiR feedback to the FedRAMP PMO here in a public form per the suggestion of the FedRAMP PMO.  


Overall, the VDR standard is a significant leap forward for vulnerability management within FedRAMP and we are very supportive of this direction. We already operate a mature vulnerability automation that aligns well with the principles behind VDR but fitting that output to the standard as written was harder than expected. For smaller CSPs without comparable tooling or engineering resources, this could be a significant lift, particularly for providers running most or all their production workloads in containers, where vulnerability volume scales quickly.

**Feedback**
**Focus**: VDR-RPT-VDT (Vulnerability Details) and VDR-RPT-AVI (Accepted Vulnerability Info)
 
**BLUF** - The reporting requirements under VDR-RPT-VDT and VDR-RPT-AVI prescribe an excessive level of structured detail per vulnerability, most of which requires narrative human input and review. This conflicts with the BIR's stated intent of streamlining vulnerability response and enabling automated, machine-readable reporting. Two simplifications would significantly reduce provider burden, improve consistency of the resulting data, and make agency review more efficient.

**1. Consolidate VDR-RPT-VDT elements 6–11 into a single "justification" field and maybe add category designation field**

Elements 1-5 (tracking ID, detection time/source, evaluation time, internet-reachability, exploitability) are objective, machine-derivable attributes that fit cleanly into structured fields. Elements 6–11, by contrast, require narrative human judgment and overlap with one another. Breaking these out into discrete fields drives redundant content and incentivizes box-checking over substantive risk explanation. Also it isn't something that scales well, well at least not in a way where you are going to get good quality data at large scale (aka container CVEs)

A single "justification" field would efficiently capture most of the same information:

- Element 6 historically and currently estimated potential adverse impact - documented in the justification narrative.
- Element 7 time and level of each completed and evaluated reduction in adverse impact - documented in the justification, including any mitigating controls applied and their effective dates.
- Element 8 estimated time and target level of next reduction - documented in the justification, including planned remediation milestones and any suppression expiration date.
- Element 9 overdue or likely to become overdue, with explanation - addressed in the justification when the vulnerability is at risk of exceeding SLAs.
- Element 10 supplementary information for agencies - any additional context relevant to agency risk decisions is included in the justification.
- Element 11 final disposition – documented in the justification narrative.

**1b** [this next part starts to spill over into my 2nd bit of feedback]. Then maybe add a disposition/category designation field with the following options (open to more options as needed).  

- False Positive 
- Vendor Dependency 
- Planned Fix 
- Accepted Risk 

This collapses six discrete fields into one structured narrative tied to a categorical disposition. It is easier for providers to maintain accurately, easier for agency reviewers to consume in a single pass.

**2. Eliminate the difference in reporting between "accepted" and other reported vulnerabilities**

VDR-RPT-VDT and VDR-RPT-AVI define two near-identical reporting schemas that diverge only modestly, VDR-RPT-AVI drops elements 7, 8, 9, and 11 from VDR-RPT-VDT and adds an acceptance explanation. Maintaining two parallel structures introduces large process complexity for limited analytic benefit.  Acceptance explanation can be the same as justification.  

More fundamentally: a vulnerability that has been "accepted" is still a risk to agency data. The acceptance label does not change the underlying risk posture; it only signals how the provider intends to track it going forward.  The current bifurcation arguably understates risk by indicating to agencies (per the VDR-AGM-RVR note) that accepted vulnerabilities warrant less ongoing review.

**Recommendation**: Collapse VDR-RPT-VDT and VDR-RPT-AVI into a single reporting schema covering all vulnerabilities, with the disposition field carrying the categorical signal (e.g. False Positive, Vendor Dependency, Planned Fix, and/or Accepted Risk). Agencies retain the full ability to filter and prioritize on disposition.

documents.title: Rev5 questions and discussion on the Consolidated Rules for 2026 (or Legacy)
documents.text:
> Which is intended? Or are both acceptable, provided the method is documented and applied consistently?

This would vary depending on the vulnerability. In that example:

(a) A vulnerability that allows complete exposure of all data, or the ability to change and manipulate all data, might have a minimum PAIN equal to the PAIN of the component.

(b) A vulnerability that might allow the existence of certain types of data to be exposed without directly impacting the CIA of that data could be much lower than the PAIN of the component. 

(c) A vulnerability where perhaps a single non-critical column could be manipulated such that a certain type of document wouldn't be available would be much lower than the PAIN of the component.

(d) A vulnerability where all data could be exposed but it requires ritual sacrifice of a still-functioning PS1 on Halloween on the front lawn of the datacenter facility would have a very PAIN but would not likely be exploitable.

etc.

The goal of evaluation is to sorta start by assuming the worst, then understand the mitigating circumstances that would make it less bad. There are a TON of ways that a centralized database could be exploited while having minimal customer effects on the agencies using the related service.

> Question 2. If reading (b) is acceptable, is a two-stage method acceptable: a rule-based first pass that assigns a provisional PAIN from the component (which agencies it serves, what federal customer data it handles), followed by an adjustment per vulnerability using its technical impact, reachability and exploitability, with both stages recorded in the evaluation?

Yes and no - adjustment using its technical impact: yes. That would be adjustments made similar to my examples above - there's a big difference between pwning a database and stealing a single tenant's internal document hashes. Technical impact absolutely matters for PAIN. **It should be incredibly rare for a PAIN5 vulnerability to hit even core components that are used by every customer.**

Adjustment using reachability and exploitability: no. PAIN is intended to be part of a tripod:

(1) Is it likely exploitable? (VER-EVA-ELX)
(2) Is it internet-reachable? (VER-EVA-EIR)
(3) What is the PAIN if it it _is_ exploited?

All 3 of those should be answered. A PAIN5 that is not internet reachable or likely exploitable (such as example (d) in my response above) should still be mitigated, but it's far less urgent. Goal here is to mitigate quickly.

> Our question is about the other direction: whether a documented method may rate a vulnerability below its component's ceiling when its achievable effect is narrower, so that the VDR-TFR-PVR windows and the set agencies review under VER-AGM-RVR track the risk to them rather than the component's worst case.

Yes, this is STRONGLY ENCOURAGED. It is the intent of the rules. :)

documents.title: Rev5 questions and discussion on the Consolidated Rules for 2026 (or Legacy)
documents.text:
VER-EVA-EFP requires that false positives are identified but does not state a specific way that they should be reported.  Neither VER-RPT-VDT nor VER-RPT-AVI include a section for false positive reporting.  Is it up to each CSP to decide how they want to report false positives (with input from agency customers)?  Does FedRAMP want to see false positives reported as N0 vulnerabilities?  While this is an option, not all N0 vulnerabilities will be false positives, so using this label without further clarification seems like it could introduce confusion.  

I apologize if this has been addressed elsewhere.  I looked around for a while before posting.

documents.title: Balancing FedRAMP Rev5 against improvements to FedRAMP 20x
documents.text:
**Focusing on the grouping of vulnerabilities**
Thanks, the grouping framing helps, but I want to push on the mechanics a bit because I don't think I fully understand how it reconciles with [VDR-RPT-VDT](https://preview.fedramp.gov/2026/providers/rev5/rules/vulnerability-detection-and-response/#vulnerability-details) and [VDR-RPT-AVI](https://preview.fedramp.gov/2026/providers/rev5/rules/vulnerability-detection-and-response/#accepted-vulnerability-info). Hopefully my lack of clarity also highlights areas where the standard could be improved. As I read VDR-RPT-VDT and and VDR-RPT-AVI, each CVE essentially needs its own row, or close to it. Scanners do sometimes pick up 3-4 related CVEs at the same time, but that still doesn't get anywhere near the final report row count suggested above. 

On grouping itself: [VDR-EVA-GRV ](https://preview.fedramp.gov/2026/providers/rev5/rules/vulnerability-detection-and-response/#group-vulnerabilities)makes sense in principle, but VDR-RPT-VDT and VDR-RPT-AVI then requires per-vuln "time and source of the detection" (# 2) and "time of completed evaluation" (# 3) as reporting elements, in addition to other requirements. If I group ~300 distinct container CVEs into a handful of logical groupings, those ~300 CVEs will have hit at different timestamps across different scan cycles, and evaluations will have completed at different points as different teams worked through their respective contexts. 

How is grouping supposed to reconcile with those time fields? Some explicit guidance, or an example of what a "grouped" row actually looks like at the schema level, would help. I know the PMO is generally reluctant to publish examples, but it isn't clear to me what you're looking for here and examples would be extremely helpful. 

**To the direct question:** do you genuinely expect ~300 distinct container CVEs to compress to fewer than 10 reporting rows under the VDR? That seems aggressive given that base-image vulns are only one of several CVE source categories; language-specific dependencies, OS packages, and application-layer issues generally don't share evaluation context across products. I want to make sure I'm not under-grouping out of habit, but I also don't want to over-group in a way that obscures real per-context risk.

documents.title: RFC-0026 Clarifying CA-7 Continuous Monitoring Expectations for Rev5 Providers
documents.text:
CSP-AB submits the following comment to RFC-0026:

**Requirement RV5-CA07-VLN (Vulnerability Reporting)** - Sharing Operating System, Database, Web Application, Container, and Service Configuration Scans, at least monthly; AND sharing updated Plans of Action and Milestones (POA&Ms), at least monthly; AND sharing all scans performed by an Independent Assessor, at least annually.

- This reads as the traditional path under RV5-CA07-VLN requiring CSPs to share raw Operating System, Database, Web Application, Container, and Service Configuration scans monthly with all agency customers. This creates a significant and unexplained asymmetry with the VDR BIR, which explicitly prohibits irresponsible disclosure of sensitive vulnerability details that would likely lead to exploitation (VDR-RPT-NID), and instead requires only structured, risk-contextualized reporting. If VDR is considered an acceptable — and arguably superior — alternative to traditional ConMon, the traditional path should not impose a more expansive and security-degrading disclosure burden by default.

We recommend the following changes to RV5-CA07-VLN:

1. Raw scan sharing should not be a baseline requirement. Unprocessed scan output provides limited value to most agency customers, who generally lack the tooling and expertise to interpret it. Validation of scan results by a 3PAO during annual assessments is the appropriate mechanism for independent verification. Monthly raw scan distribution to all agencies does not meaningfully improve risk awareness and may increase attack surface by broadly distributing detailed exploitability information. FedRAMP should remove the requirement to share raw scans with all agency customers and treat scan artifacts as 3PAO review materials, not agency deliverables. Sharing with agency customers beyond the lead agency should be governed by individual agency contracts, not mandated uniformly.

2. Scan results shared with any party — including 3PAOs and lead agencies — should explicitly be permitted to be redacted. CSPs should be permitted to redact specific details from scan results (including plugin IDs, CVE identifiers, and exploit path details) when disclosure of those details would likely facilitate exploitation of an unmitigated vulnerability. Redacted findings must retain a CSP-assigned unique tracking identifier, affected component classification, and risk level sufficient to support risk-based decision-making. This aligns with the responsible disclosure principle already established in VDR-RPT-NID and VDR-FRP-ADV. Full unredacted details should be available for correlation by the CSP in the event of a CISA-directed response, legal hold, or FedRAMP corrective action — consistent with the existing FedRAMP authority to require additional sensitive information under those circumstances — but should not be required for routine distribution.

3. FedRAMP should clarify the disclosure asymmetry between the traditional path and VDR explicitly. As currently written, CSPs on the traditional path face a stricter and less security-conscious disclosure posture than those adopting VDR. If the intent is for VDR to represent a modernization and improvement, the traditional path should be updated to match VDR's responsible disclosure principles, not left in a state that inadvertently penalizes CSPs who have not yet adopted VDR.

documents.text: > @pete-gov Related to PAIN ratings, if a CSP only uses the tripod you mention above (exploitability, reachability, and PAIN/impact) to evaluate vulnerabilities and didn't include all 8 evaluation factors, would that be seen as not fulfilling the evaluation criteria for VER? The evaluation factors in [VER-EVA-EFA (Evaluation Factors)](https://www.fedramp.gov/2026/reference/vulnerability-evaluation-and-reporting/?h=VER-EVA-ELX#evaluation-factors) _help you do the evaluation required by the other rules._ It's not an either or thing, you will not be able to accurate determine if something is likely exploitable under [VER-EVA-ELX Evaluate Exploitability](https://www.fedramp.gov/2026/reference/vulnerability-evaluation-and-reporting/?h=VER-EVA-ELX#evaluate-exploitability) if you don't consider the relevant Evaluation Factors. Also, a reminder that [It's Not a Trap!](https://www.fedramp.gov/2026/rules/#its-not-a-trap). Do the right thing that matters for your business and is supported by your security and engineering team, especially for SHOULD rules. Demonstrate why it's the right technical approach. Consider how you want to respond to a potential customer that doesn't like the way you do it or disagrees with your technical reasons. As long as you do that for the rules, FedRAMP isn't going to nit pick you. > On a side note, would it make sense to add PAIN (agency impact) as a 9th evaluation factor for VER-EVA-EFA? Since you already have reachability and exploitability included? Reachability is an evaluation factor/input, "internet reachable" is an evaluation outcome that is based partially on reachability. Exploitability is also an evaluation factor/input, whereas "likely exploitable" is an evaluation outcome that is based partially on exploitability. PAIN is also an evaluation outcome, not a factor/input. ## Example A playful example that is exactly the type of situation we all dream of when we're imagining compliance: Your cloud service stores master break-glass codes in a safe in the CEO's office. You find during a red team exercise that the CEO regularly leaves the safe unlocked while he is in the office and watching Tik Tok with headphones on and his back to the safe and the door. The red team suggests that anyone could walk into his office and grab the codes to own the entire business. - Criticality: Pretty critical, these could take over everything. - Reachability: Not internet-reachable. Turns out the CEO has a high grade office door that is always locked when he watches Tik Tok. He's got 6 armed guards outside because the business is a bit sketchy. It's probably not very reachable at all, internet or not. - Exploitability: Not really exploitable, and definitely not _likely_ exploitable. Maybe if all 6 guards were in on it, or John Wick got involved? This is probably not a vulnerability to worry about being exploited though. - Detectability: Fairly unlikely a threat actor would find out about this unless they visit the CEO's office on business. Monitor info on the dark web and make sure no one is talking about it and you're probably fine? - Prevalence: Full, master codes, takes over the whole cloud service offering. Bad stuff. Based on these factors you'd probably say it's not remotely likely to be exploitable and the whole thing is so unlikely that it's basically PAIN0. No one is going to waste time fighting through those six guys and rob the safe. But... you ignored two factors in your evaluation. Let's say you add those in, and the evaluation shows: - Proximate Vulnerabilities: Oh guess what it turns out that amazing secure door is internet connected with some known vulnerabilities so that anyone within 30 feet can unlock it with their phone. And 3 of those armed guards are brand new, just stated last week, because the previous 3 got sick all at once! - Known Threats: The CEO's son just stole John Wick's car and killed his dog. The cloud service offering just stood up a new crypto exchange with $10 billion in private keys. Okay, now you got a PAIN5 and then some. 😉 Doesn't matter if that vuln isn't internet-accessible or likely-exploitable, you are gonna get got if you don't respond appropriately.

documents.title: RFC-0030 FedRAMP Rev5 Security Controls Baseline Update for RA, SA, SC, SI, and SR Control Families
documents.text:
This is the most substantive RFC in the March batch, and the VDR integration work in RA-05 is well-structured. The impact-tiered cadences correctly reflect the VDR philosophy, and the evaluation windows are operationally tight but appropriate for Class D commitments. Several specific comments follow.

On RA-05(a) container scanning. The proposed parameter text references operating system/infrastructure, web applications (including APIs), and databases. It does not reference containers. Current FedRAMP guidance in the Continuous Monitoring Playbook requires container scanning, and leaving the RA-05(a) parameter silent about containers while being explicit about other resource types creates an asymmetric reading that invites CSPs to deprioritize container scans.

From agency-side authorization experience, I directed Agency Authorization lifecycle work for 60+ enterprise cloud deployments at the VA, including systems with heavy container usage. Container-native architectures do not have their vulnerabilities surfaced by OS and infrastructure scanning. The community discussion captured this correctly: for CSPs doing container scans, a majority of identified vulnerabilities come from that scanner type, and there is no substitute pathway for containerized workload findings.

Recommend one of two fixes. Either explicitly include containers in the RA-05(a) parameter text for the traditional pathway (preserving status quo and eliminating the asymmetric reading), or explicitly confirm in the VDR pathway language that containers are machine-based resources subject to the representative sampling approach. The latter is the stronger long-term answer because it treats containers as first-class machine-based resources under VDR’s philosophy. Either way, the silence in the current proposed text should be closed.

On SI-05 security alerts, advisories, and directives. Support for FSI process integration for Emergency Directive and Binding Operational Directive responses. Consistent with the IR-07 FSI alignment in RFC-0028. Recommend that specific response timelines be referenced from the FSI guidance, with the guidance itself carrying those definitions. That keeps the baseline durable as FSI guidance evolves with operational experience.

On SI-02(2) and SI-03 persistent language for VDR participants. Correct use of the existing FRMR definition of persistent. This aligns with how the VDR BIR describes continuous monitoring and avoids introducing a second definition.

On SA-15 Authorization/Certification terminology. Useful transition marker consistent with RFC-0023’s Initial Outcome. Consider a note that the terminology will remain “Authorization/Certification” through the CR26 transition so CSPs understand the durable shape of the language.

On SC-13 Cryptographic Modules historical status. The referenced page is a 2022 archive. Recommend the PMO confirm whether that archive remains the authoritative guidance or whether it should be refreshed into a current Rev. 5/20x document.

On SC-07 and SA-04(5). Supportive. The MAS BIR accommodation in SC-07(8) and the documentation/validation requirement for custom baselines in SA-04(5) are both appropriate alignments.

General note - The VDR pathway integration across SI-02(2), SI-03, and RA-05 is good work and the right direction. Closing the container scanning gap in RA-05 makes the pathway coherent for traditional and VDR-track providers alike.

One structural concern remains across the VDR framework that this RFC surfaces but does not resolve. The Phase 2 VDR design gives CSPs significant latitude to classify and contextualize their own vulnerability risk. Public comments on the 20x requirements have recommended that independent assessors be given more formal oversight authority here: assessors embedded in KSI validation are well-positioned to provide input on the severity of KSI failures, and that role has not been formalized in the published requirements. The control updates in this RFC extend VDR's reach further into Rev5 without addressing that gap. As CR26 finalizes the VDR pathway, formalizing IA oversight of CSP risk classification decisions would meaningfully strengthen the pathway's integrity.

Michael Schroeder

It's both, but reading 2 in effect.

If you identify a vulnerability following [VER-EVA-EFP Evaluate False Positives](https://www.google.com/url?q=https://github.com/FedRAMP/community/discussions/146&source=chat&ust=1791028483675000&usg=AOvVaw2A_lKdilbcCGeAxGfzhOJ_) and determine it is a false positive vulnerability then you have also immediately completed the remaining required evaluations.

The exploitability of a false positive vulnerability is null. The internet-reachability of a false positive vulnerability is null. The PAIN of a false positive vulnerability is null. The factors under VER-EVA-EFA Evaluation Factors are all null. This evaluation applies automatically. Therefore, as you said, these evaluations may be reported as not applicable, null, irrelevant, or whatever you think best communicates the lack of risk from a false positive vulnerability.

If it were me, I'd probably report false positives as Accepted Vulnerabilities in a specific "false positive" grouping ([VER-EVA-GRV Group Vulnerabilities](https://www.fedramp.gov/2026/reference/vulnerability-evaluation-and-reporting/#group-vulnerabilities)). There may be other ways to best present this information to customers though!

I've also taken a note to clarify [VER-EVA-EPA Estimate Potential Agency Impact](url) with the ability to assign PAIN 0 or N/A.

I completely support CSP-AB’s position. This comment correctly identifies an asymmetry where the "traditional path" inadvertently forces a less secure disclosure posture than the modernized VDR approach.
For example, an IaaS provider has a responsibility is to maintain the security of the shared environment. Mandating the broad distribution of raw, unredacted scans to every agency customer creates unnecessary  systemic risk. If an IaaS provider’s foundational layer is exposed through over-sharing, every SaaS provider and government agency sitting on top of that infrastructure also inherits that risk.  Aligning these requirements with VDR’s risk-contextualized reporting ensures that agencies receive actionable intelligence without forcing the CSP to affect security--which is prohibited in VDR.
