documents.text:
To add, FedRAMP is not in a business relationship with any cloud service providers. Cloud service providers and agencies enter into contracts about what the cloud service provider will do, and the agency should be expected as a customer to have additional expectations. If a customer using a product asks a business for something that customer wants, what should the business do? 

The only time when FedRAMP would chime in on anything like that is if a customer is asking for something that would jeopardize the FedRAMP Certification of that business. In that case, FedRAMP would expect the business to navigate this by finding a way to meet FedRAMP requirements while addressing their customer needs regardless.

> In practice, what does FedRAMP expect a provider to do when an agency asks for legacy artifacts after December 7? 

FedRAMP expects providers to work with their customers to ensure they have a positive customer experience with the product they are offering.

In the particular case of requesting additional materials such as an OG POA&M, that is a trivial request that has no relation whatsoever to the FedRAMP Certification and is not even an additional security requirement. It's an agency customer asking for some custom information in a custom spreadsheet. This has no negative impact on a FedRAMP Certification or a businesses ability to deliver required materials to other agency customers. 

And for any business that is adopting modern tooling to manage the VDR/VER requirements, it should be a trivially automatable output to provide to customers that want it.

documents.title: Balancing FedRAMP Rev5 against improvements to FedRAMP 20x
documents.text:
Overall, I think maybe you're considering this as if you're going to manually create a bunch of artisanal vulnerability reports for FR - but the purpose of these rules are to ensure that providers are using a proper vulnerability management workflow. As part of that workflow, there will be automated and/or human decisions that are made. Those decisions should be tracked. Then all you need to do in the report is output that information from your tracking system. The reporting data itself should be a trivial data export, not the location where decisions are made and tracked.

Please don't track vulnerability detection and response in a spreadsheet. 🙈 

> BLUF - The reporting requirements under VDR-RPT-VDT and VDR-RPT-AVI prescribe an excessive level of structured detail per vulnerability, most of which requires narrative human input and review. 

Everything necessary for this report should exist in a vulnerability tracking system and be outputted based on the information a cloud service provider has already determined. There shouldn't be anything new created for this report if the VDR rules are being followed.

The narratives for VDR-RPT-VDT would include an explanation if the vulnerability is likely to become overdue, which should only ever be true after human review and consideration and the explanation should already exist in any vulnerability tracking system. And, of course, any supplemental information the provider wants to provide. These only would be included **if applicable.**

For VDR-RPT-AVI, there should be no world in which a vulnerability is accepted without reasons and documentation created by a human in a vulnerability tracking system.

In general the entire point of these requirements are to remove narratives and simply provide information that has already been tracked in a cloud service provider's vulnerability tracking system.

> A single "justification" field would efficiently capture most of the same information

We expect agencies, CISA, and FedRAMP itself to care mightily about being able to effectively parse this information. Having these fields buried in a narrative justification would make doing so inefficient.

> Recommendation: Collapse VDR-RPT-VDT and VDR-RPT-AVI into a single reporting schema covering all vulnerabilities...

This is already the case in effect. You can use a single schema to cover all vulnerabilities by leaving some fields blank for vulnerabilities that are being responded to vs vulnerabilities that have been accepted.

documents.title: RFC-0033 FedRAMP 20x Phase 4 Development Tracks for 20x Class D
documents.text:
**Comments on RFC-0033: FedRAMP 20x Phase 4**
Date: October 8, 2026
To: FedRAMP Program Management Office
Submitted via: RFC-0033 comment thread on GitHub
Comment period: September 9, 2026 through October 9, 2026
From: Excentium, Inc.

Excentium, Inc. is a FedRAMP Recognized Independent Assessment Service and a Service-Disabled Veteran-Owned Small Business headquartered in Reston, Virginia. We have held A2LA accreditation for FedRAMP assessment work continuously since 2015 and served as the independent assessor for one of the cloud services certified through the FedRAMP 20x Low pilot. We partner with government and commercial industry to strengthen our nation's cyber infrastructure.

These comments draw on two bodies of work. The 20x Low pilot gave us direct experience with a compressed schedule and requirements still being developed. Four years as the Independent Assessment Service for a federal agency's multi-bureau shared cloud service offerings, assessed under Rev5 at the Moderate and High baselines, gave us sustained exposure to agency assurance expectations for consequential workloads. The recommendations below address specific terms, dates, and assessment mechanisms so providers and assessors can reach a common reading.

Excentium supports the direction of RFC-0033. Extending FedRAMP 20x to Class D completes the Certification Class range for the 20x Type, while extending it to self-hosted and hybrid-hosted services opens the pathway to providers responsible for their physical infrastructure. Developing these requirements through three simultaneous tracks and public RFCs gives providers, assessors, and agencies an opportunity to resolve implementation questions together.

References to CR26 use the Consolidated Rules for 2026, version 2026.10.08.01, published and verified on October 8, 2026. We use Independent Assessment Service following FRD-ASR. Proposed RFC requirements are identified as proposals; they do not establish current obligations.

### R1. Classification Test for Mixed Hosting Footprints

**Ref:** New FedRAMP Definitions for Cloud-Hosted, Self-Hosted, and Hybrid-Hosted; MAS-CSO-IIR

The proposed Cloud-Hosted and Self-Hosted definitions use where machine-based information resources primarily run and who takes responsibility for the physical infrastructure. Hybrid-Hosted applies where some resources are cloud-hosted and others are self-hosted. Please clarify how the two uses of primarily interact with the Hybrid-Hosted definition and whether a materiality threshold applies.

This classification determines which requirements attach. Anticipated item 2 applies to cloud-hosted and hybrid-hosted Class D services, while Track 2 eligibility includes primarily self-hosted or hybrid-hosted services. An offering that runs almost entirely on certified cloud infrastructure and includes a small component for which the provider takes physical-infrastructure responsibility appears to fit the Hybrid-Hosted definition. Providers need to know whether that component always determines the classification or whether its function and significance affect the result.

The test should account for the resources identified under MAS-CSO-IIR, including resources that can affect the confidentiality, integrity, or availability of federal customer data through security functions. Equipment ownership alone does not establish responsibility for physical infrastructure. A test based only on direct handling of federal customer data would also omit applicable resources with indirect security effects.

**Recommendation:** Publish the classification test and explain how primarily and Hybrid-Hosted apply to a mixed offering. State whether any materiality threshold applies, how physical-infrastructure responsibility is established, and how the result affects item 2 and Track 2 eligibility. Use the MAS-CSO-IIR applicability condition so providers and assessors can reach a consistent classification.

### R2. The Six Month Period Without Corrective Action

**Ref:** Anticipated Requirements item 1; AFC-FRP-COR; SCN-FRP-CAP; VER-FRP-ARP; IEC-FRP-ORV; FRC-CCL-UCC

Item 1 proposes that an offering obtain and maintain a 20x Class C Certification without corrective action for six months before becoming eligible for 20x Class D after the Phase 4 pilot. The proposal leaves open which corrective-action events interrupt that period.

AFC-FRP-COR describes consequences that can range from negative Marketplace ratings to suspension of Certification, depending on severity. SCN-FRP-CAP and VER-FRP-ARP refer to a formal provider Corrective Action Plan. Individual rules also publish corrective actions: IEC-FRP-ORV provides for a Corrective Action Plan and a three-month grace period to implement proper procedures in specified circumstances. These mechanisms can produce different eligibility results. An assessor organizational plan under REC-IAS-CAP addresses a separate subject and should be distinguished from corrective action affecting the provider or offering.

Adoption milestones may fall within the first six-month eligibility windows. Current 20x deadline guidance identifies January 1, 2027 as the Maintaining Ongoing Certification date for many rulesets, with the grace period ending at the first independent assessment started after that date. For existing Certifications, the guidance says providers should adopt by the maintaining date and requires a plan to adopt by the end of the grace period if they have not done so. VDR and VER have a maintaining date of December 7, 2026 and a grace period ending March 7, 2027. Providers need to know how an adoption-related plan affects Class D eligibility.

FRC-CCL-UCC requires a new application to upgrade Certification Class, with applicable requirements met in advance. The six-month condition therefore needs a defined start date and a clear point at which it must be satisfied. A material change to architecture, hosting, a relied-upon security function, or a validation method can also change whether earlier operating history represents the offering that seeks Class D. An assessor should be able to examine a dated record of the change, its affected assurance, and the disposition of the earlier evidence.

**Recommendation:** Identify the corrective-action events that affect the six-month period, who determines their effect, and whether each preserves, pauses, or restarts the clock. Confirm whether the period begins with Class C Certification and must be complete at the Class D application. Explain the treatment of adoption-related Corrective Action Plans and how a Class D Pilot Certification relates to the post-pilot six-month condition. Define when material changes require a recorded determination that the prior operating history remains representative, and the evidence for that determination.

### R3. Certification Profile in Items 2 and 3

**Ref:** Anticipated Requirements items 2 and 3; FRD-CPF; FRD-TPR; MAS-CSO-IIR; MAS-CSO-TPR

We understand from FedRAMP's September 23 response in General Discussion 172 that a reference to Certified, without a specified Type, includes both Rev5 and 20x at the stated Class. That answer resolves the initial Type question. Incorporating the interpretation into the pilot requirements will give providers and assessors a common reference. FRD-CPF also includes Certification Path, so any Path restrictions should be stated.

The same response explains that Rev5 end dates and transition requirements will be finalized during Phase 5. Current guidance closes applications for new Rev5 Certifications on June 11, 2027 and provides that existing Rev5 Certifications remain active until at least December 31, 2028 unless FedRAMP is otherwise directed. Please explain how dependency eligibility will be handled as Phase 5 establishes the transition, including whether reliance continues while an upstream Certification remains valid or ends on a separately announced date.

Item 3 also needs a scope clarification. FRD-TPR defines a Third-Party Information Resource by its incomplete inclusion in the offering's Minimum Assessment Scope. MAS-CSO-TPR addresses third-party information resources used by the offering, subject to MAS-CSO-IIR applicability. That construction covers relevant indirect security functions as well as applicable resources that handle federal customer data.

MAS-CSO-TPR requires documentation of usage and configuration, justification for use, mitigation measures, and compensating controls. Providers need to understand how those provisions relate to the proposed Class B minimum when an applicable resource relies on an offering Certified below Class B or without FedRAMP Certification. For any permitted exception, an assessor could examine the resource's function, relevant data and control flows, privileged access, potential effect on security functions and availability, and the provider's retained responsibilities. The decision should record the relied-upon assurance, compensating measures, and events that require reassessment.

**Recommendation:** Incorporate FedRAMP's existing interpretation that the Class references include Rev5 and 20x, and identify any Path restrictions. Explain the treatment of valid Rev5 dependencies during the transition and the notice associated with any separate eligibility cutoff. Align item 3 with FRD-TPR and MAS-CSO-TPR while preserving MAS-CSO-IIR applicability. State whether the Class B minimum is absolute. If exceptions are permitted, require a documented impact determination, specific compensating measures and evidence of their effectiveness, an approval authority, and conditions for continuing review.

### R4. Assurance Engineering Resources and Agency GRC Integration

**Ref:** Anticipated Requirements item 4; FRC-CSO-JSN; CDS-CSO-PUB; CDS-CSO-CBF; CDS-CSO-HAD; CDS-CSO-PSM; CDS-TRC-PAC; FRD-PFA

Item 4 combines support for agency review of the Certification Package with ongoing integration of assurance data into agency GRC systems. Each commitment needs a stated assessment criterion so providers know what to demonstrate and assessors know what to validate.

The integration commitment can build on existing CR26 interfaces. CDS-CSO-PUB requires public information in human-readable and JSON formats; CDS-CSO-CBF requires automation to keep them consistent. CDS-TRC-PAC requires documented programmatic access to all FedRAMP Certification Data. CDS-CSO-HAD requires snapshots aligned to Ongoing Certification Reports, and CDS-CSO-PSM requires per-service materials at Class D. The October 5 clarification to FRC-CSO-JSN also addresses standard web consumption of public JSON, including appropriate CORS behavior and response headers. These rules provide a concrete basis for describing the additional integration support expected at Class D.

A practical demonstration would have an agency consumer retrieve applicable public JSON through a standard browser, validate it against the corresponding FedRAMP schema, associate the results with the correct offering, service, rule, and reporting period, and retrieve the relevant historical snapshot. The assessor could examine the recorded ingestion result, human-readable and JSON consistency, CORS and response headers, and the documented interface. Access to protected Certification Data should be exercised under the appropriate authorization, separately from public JSON access.

Active support for agency package review also involves people and availability. FRD-PFA describes a Persistent FedRAMP Assessment as focused on Key Security Indicators. A support commitment needs evidence of the agency-facing outcome and the provider's ability to sustain it. Documented support routes, escalation arrangements, and measurable response commitments would let an Independent Assessment Service examine that capability.

**Recommendation:** State whether item 4 will be expressed as a Certification rule, a KSI with a defined validation method, or a documented commitment in Certification Data. For Class D, require a demonstrated agency GRC ingestion exercise using the applicable CDS and FRC-CSO-JSN interfaces, with results an assessor can reproduce or inspect. Define the measurable evidence for agency package review support, including escalation and response arrangements, and identify the additional Class D outcome to validate.

### R5. FOCI and Automated Validation Indicators

**Ref:** Anticipated Requirements item 5; REC-IAS-AFI; REC-IAS-CFI; KSI-CED-RAT; KSI-CNA-OFA; KSI-RPL-RRO; KSI-RPL-TRC; CDS-CSO-AVR; FRC-CSX-VVK; SDR-CSX-KSI; IVV-CSO-SEE; IVV-IAS-VEF

CR26 already addresses foreign interest, influence, and control for assessors. REC-IAS-AFI requires annual reporting, and REC-IAS-CFI requires updated information within 48 hours of a change in foreign ownership or control. These recognition obligations offer a useful reporting model for a provider construct, with its own defined scope and acceptance criteria.

Placing FOCI within the Key Security Indicators also raises a measurement question. Ownership and control information describes an organizational condition. A KSI needs a security outcome that can be persistently validated. The Cybersecurity Education theme shows that organizational matters can be expressed as indicators, so the proposal should explain the provider outcome and the evidence that will establish it over time.

Availability already has anchors in CR26. KSI-CNA-OFA addresses optimization for high availability and rapid recovery. KSI-RPL-RRO addresses recovery objectives, and KSI-RPL-TRC addresses testing recovery capability. CDS-CSO-AVR requires Class B, C, and D providers to maintain a web service showing current and historical availability of core services over at least the past 30 days. Class D can extend these measures with clearly stated assurance expectations.

A provider FOCI indicator should also show whether measures addressing identified risks remain effective as ownership, personnel access, governance, or relevant dependencies change. Existing federal determinations could supply evidence where their organization and offering scope applies; an assessor would still need a mapping of coverage, exclusions, and any additional mitigations.

FRC-CSX-VVK requires at least four automated methods per Key Security Indicator for 20x Class D. Santoshkumarpuppala's September 20 comment in the formal RFC thread recommends an observed failing run to show that a method can detect the condition it claims to detect. We support that test and add an assessment of shared dependencies. For each method, evidence could identify the controlled failing condition, expected and observed result, method version, and evidence source. The assessor should examine whether methods depend on the same upstream signal or processing path, and whether their combined coverage remains useful if one dependency fails. A representative test environment, replay, or other justified technique can demonstrate detection without disrupting production.

**Recommendation:** Publish the intended scope of the provider FOCI theme, including whether it reaches ownership, personnel, supply chain, or a combination. Define the mitigation outcome to be validated over time and how annual and change-triggered reporting supports it. Consider accepting applicable federal FOCI determinations, including those under 32 CFR 117.11, with a scope mapping and gap analysis for the offering. Build new availability indicators on KSI-CNA-OFA, the Recovery Planning theme, and CDS-CSO-AVR. For automated validation, require evidence that methods detect representative failing conditions and identify shared sources or dependencies, leaving the test technique to the provider.

### R6. Class C Review Timing Against the December 1 Deadline

**Ref:** Phase 4 Track 1; FedRAMP response in General Discussion 172 on September 18, 2026

Track 1 requires a CR26-compliant FedRAMP 20x Class C Certification received before December 1, 2026. Providers applying for Class C before November 13 and intending to participate are asked to send a notice of intent after submitting the application. The dates are eighteen days apart, and eligibility depends on completed Certification.

FedRAMP's September 18 response confirms the completed Class C prerequisite and explains that late applications cannot be promised priority review. The notice-of-intent date therefore provides a coordination step; it does not establish a completion window. Providers would benefit from indicative review assumptions when deciding whether their readiness and schedule support Phase 4 participation.

**Recommendation:** Publish indicative Class C review timing and the readiness assumptions that affect it, subject to package completeness and available review capacity. Provide practical guidance on the remaining opportunity to qualify before December 1 and explain how notices of intent are used. Preserve the distinction between submitting an application and receiving Certification.

### R7. The Independent Assessment Service Role in the Phase 4 Pilot

**Ref:** Phase 4 Track 1 items 4 and 5; REC-IAS-ADA; REC-IAS-RQU; REC-IAS-SEP

Track 1 expects participants to engage a FedRAMP Recognized Independent Assessment Service. Providers planning a Class D engagement need to understand the personnel competence and technical capabilities expected of the assessor, as well as how independent assessment will be maintained during pilot collaboration.

Excentium is a FedRAMP Recognized Independent Assessment Service and could be engaged by a Phase 4 participant. We disclose that interest here. These questions apply to the assessors and providers participating across the pilot.

REC-IAS-ADA establishes an ongoing recognition experience floor of at least two initial or ongoing assessments for Class B, C, or D Certifications every two years, without specifying a Certification Type. REC-IAS-RQU separately requires the roles and personnel qualifications prescribed by A2LA R311, subject to a specifically published exception for a limited pilot or other explicitly scoped process. Meeting the recognition experience floor does not by itself describe the competence needed for every Class D engagement. Please state any additional Class D experience or capabilities expected for evaluating automated assurance.

REC-IAS-SEP bars an assessor from independently assessing the same offering within two years after supplying advisory or consulting services, subject to a specifically published scoped exception. Participation in developing or interpreting program requirements and offering-specific advisory or consulting work need clear treatment during the pilot. The collaboration described in Track 1 makes this boundary worth publishing early so providers and assessors can plan their roles.

**Recommendation:** Publish the competence expectations for assessors supporting Phase 4, including any additional Class D experience or technical capabilities. Clarify which pilot activities constitute offering-specific advisory or consulting services under REC-IAS-SEP and which constitute participation in developing or interpreting program requirements. If a pilot exception is needed, publish its scope, permitted activities, independence safeguards, and retained assessment duties. Confirm the direct technical channel to the PMO for assessors supporting participants.

### R8. Publishing Themes From the Direct Engagement Rounds

**Ref:** Phase 4 Tracks 2 and 3

Tracks 2 and 3 pair targeted direct engagement with public RFCs so other parties can participate. The direct tracks will help shape the drafts on which the broader community comments.

Provider Round 1 runs November 4 through November 20, 2026, and Round 2 runs January 4 through January 15, 2027. The proposed self-hosted and hybrid-hosted rules publish for comment on February 10, after both rounds. Publishing the themes discussed would help parties outside the direct tracks understand the basis for that draft.

**Recommendation:** Publish a short summary of the themes from each direct engagement round as it concludes, protecting information that cannot be disclosed. Make those summaries available with the related public RFCs so all commenters can address the issues informing the Consolidated Rules for 2027.

### R9. Question Timing for Assessment Services

**Ref:** Phase 4 Track 3

Track 3 states that assessment services will receive the same general questions and information as providers and respond from their assessment perspective. The first assessor round runs October 19 through October 23, 2026. The RFC carrying the general questions publishes November 4, when provider Round 1 begins.

Sending the questions with the October 12 assessor notification would allow participants to review them against their engagement history and bring specific examples to the first round.

**Recommendation:** Send the general questions to qualifying assessment services with the October 12 notification, including any background material needed to prepare for the October 19 through October 23 meetings.

### R10. Confirming Eligibility for the Assessment Service Track

**Ref:** Phase 4 Track 3

Track 3 publishes its eligibility criterion: a recognized assessment service must be the current assessor of record or have been the primary assessor within the last three years for a provider qualifying for Track 2. FedRAMP will identify qualifying services using the information available to it and the Marketplace, then notify them at the public email address in their Marketplace listing.

Notifications are targeted for October 12, 2026, with an October 16 opt-in deadline. A service that believes it meets the published criterion needs a timely route to resolve a missing invitation or a disputed eligibility determination during that short window.

**Recommendation:** Provide a contact route for assessment services that believe they meet the published Track 3 criterion and have not received an invitation by October 13. Identify the supporting evidence needed, such as the qualifying provider and offering, the assessor relationship, and the relevant dates. Explain how a missing invitation or disputed eligibility determination can be resolved before the October 16 opt-in deadline.

### R11. Aligning Guidance on Class D Availability

**Ref:** CR26 guidance on Choosing a Certification Type; Phase 4 Track 1 target dates

Current CR26 guidance anticipates piloting 20x Class D in late 2026 and making it available as a formal option in early 2027. RFC-0033 places the pilot in FY27 Q1 and Q2, with final review extending into the beginning of Q3. The March 23, 2027 FedRAMP Day is tentative, and the final Phase 4 rules will be incorporated into the Consolidated Rules for 2027.

These statements serve different planning purposes. Providers need an indicative target for general availability outside the pilot, together with the dependencies that could affect it. That information is particularly useful before June 11, 2027, the final date to apply for a new Rev5 Certification.

**Recommendation:** Align the Certification Type guidance with the Phase 4 planning schedule and state an indicative target for general availability of 20x Class D outside the pilot. Distinguish that target from pilot package deadlines and the tentative FedRAMP Day, and identify the review and rule-publication dependencies that could affect it. Keep the guidance current so providers can plan against the June 11 Rev5 application deadline.

### R12. Reusing Physical Infrastructure Assurance in Tracks 2 and 3

**Ref:** Phase 4 Tracks 2 and 3; MAS-CSO-IIR; IVV-CSO-SEE; IVV-IAS-VEF

Tracks 2 and 3 ask which existing certifications and classifications can support self-hosted or hybrid-hosted offerings and what remains to be assessed for FedRAMP. An assessor-reviewed mapping would let FedRAMP reuse applicable infrastructure assurance while making the coverage of that assurance visible to agencies.

The mapping should identify the issuing body, standard and edition, current certificate or assessment report, covered facilities and services, validity period, exclusions, relevant findings, and shared responsibilities. It should connect each relied-upon assessment result to the actual deployed environment and the FedRAMP requirement or security outcome it supports. For example, evidence about a facility's physical access, power, environmental protections, or recovery arrangements has value when the facility and services covered match the offering and the provider's retained responsibilities are clear.

An Independent Assessment Service could examine that mapping, identify residual gaps, and perform targeted verification and validation of the remaining work. A certificate title alone does not establish that a specific offering, facility, or configuration is covered. This record would let the provider, assessor, FedRAMP, and relying agencies understand exactly which assurance can be reused.

**Recommendation:** Use Tracks 2 and 3 to develop an assessor-reviewed mapping for physical-infrastructure assurance. Specify the evidence of coverage and applicability, exclusions and retained responsibilities, relevant findings, and the gap analysis. Reuse covered results with targeted independent verification of residual FedRAMP requirements and security outcomes.

Excentium appreciates the opportunity to comment on RFC-0033 and welcomes further discussion of these recommendations with the FedRAMP PMO.

Class D addresses workloads where threats to the confidentiality, integrity, or availability of federal customer data may lead to catastrophic harm, including loss of life. Clear requirements and assessable evidence will help agencies place confidence in the resulting Certification. We support developing that assurance in the open and resolving the practical questions while the requirements are being written. This work supports our shared mission to reduce the vulnerabilities of our Nation.

Respectfully submitted,

Colin Corlett  
President and Chief Executive Officer  
Excentium, Inc.
1768 Business Center Drive, Suite 220  
Reston, VA 20190

# RFC-0030 FedRAMP Rev5 Security Controls Baseline Update for RA, SA, SC, SI, and SR Control Families

❓   **Please note that FedRAMP will not answer questions in this thread as it is reserved for public comment. If you would like to ask a question or generally discuss this RFC informally, please use the [General discussion and Q&A for RFCs related to Rev5 Updates (RFCs 0026, 0027, 0028, 0029, & 0030) thread](https://github.com/FedRAMP/community/discussions/129). Thank you!**

**Status:** Closed
**Start Date:** March 19, 2026
**Closing Date:** April 22, 2026
---

## **Summary**

This is a technical RFC that proposes updates to the Additional FedRAMP Security Technical Controls Requirements and Guidance for FedRAMP Rev5 baselines.

To save space and to limit the breadth of a single RFC, this technical document shows only the proposed changes to the current baseline document and is restricted to a few control families.  If verbiage is being updated, only the specific wording that is to be changed is identified in the old verbiage section.  If the verbiage to be added is not replacing previous verbiage, but being added, it will be identified as “NEW” in the old verbiage section.  

Since this spreadsheet covers hundreds of controls across multiple tabs and sections, only those specific controls, sections, and tabs identified are being proposed for updates. If it is not mentioned below, changes are **not** being proposed.  

**Commenters are advised to please mention specific controls in their comments!**

This RFC addresses controls in the following families:

* Risk Assessment (RA)  
* System and Service Acquisition (SA)  
* System and Communications Protection (SC)  
* System and Information Integrity (SI)  
* Supply Chain Risk Management (SR)

## **Motivation**

Many Rev5 FedRAMP Requirements and Guidance statements are based on outdated approaches that predated the release of the FedRAMP Authorization Act and M-24-15. This set of Requirements and Guidance needs a refresh to match FedRAMP’s current rules and approach.

The updates formalized after this RFC will be included in the FedRAMP Consolidated Rules for 2026. That set of rules will be valid until December 31, 2028. FedRAMP will provide a transition plan for adopting any new guidance that will enable cloud service providers to update their approach as part of their annual assessment as appropriate.

These changes are designed to lower the burden for cloud service providers and eliminate previous pain points.

Additionally, NIST released 800-53 Rev 5.2.0 in August of 2025. While this update was minor, control updates from NIST will require updates to FedRAMP Security Control Baseline in order to reflect this update. These changes will happen without public comment through FedRAMP since these are direct reflections of NIST changes.  As subsequent iterations of the FedRAMP Security Control Baseline are published, it is FedRAMP’s intent only to carry over the following information from NIST 800-53: Control Family, Control Name, and Control ID. Following this will be FedRAMP-Defined Assignment / Selection Parameters and additional FedRAMP Requirements and Guidance.

## **Proposed Changes to Risk Assessment Family**

This section contains proposed changes to the FedRAMP Requirements and Guidance section for each of these controls.

### **RA-05: Vulnerability Monitoring and Scanning**

**Tabs Affected:** High Baseline, Moderate Baseline, Low Baseline  
**Sections Affected:** FedRAMP-Defined Assignment / Selection Parameters  
**Current Verbiage:** RA-5 (a) [monthly operating system/infrastructure; monthly web applications (including APIs) and databases]  
RA-5 (d) [high-risk vulnerabilities mitigated within thirty (30) days from date of discovery; moderate-risk vulnerabilities mitigated within ninety (90) days from date of discovery; low-risk vulnerabilities mitigated within one hundred and eighty (180) days from date of discovery]  
**Proposed Change**: RA-5 (a) [monthly operating system/infrastructure; monthly web applications (including APIs) and databases for traditional Rev 5 processes] [For those opting into the Vulnerability Detection and Response:

Low Systems  
Providers SHOULD persistently perform vulnerability detection on representative samples of similar machine-based information resources, at least once every 7 days.   
Providers SHOULD persistently perform vulnerability detection on all information resources that are likely to drift, at least once every month.  
Providers SHOULD evaluate ALL vulnerabilities as required by VDR-TFR-EVU (Evaluation) within 7 days of detection.

Moderate   
Providers SHOULD persistently perform vulnerability detection on representative samples of similar machine-based information resources, at least once every 3 days.  
Providers SHOULD persistently perform vulnerability detection on all information resources that are likely to drift, at least once every 14 days.  
Providers SHOULD evaluate ALL vulnerabilities as required by VDR-TFR-EVU (Evaluation) within 5 days of detection.

High  
Providers SHOULD persistently perform vulnerability detection on representative samples of similar machine-based information resources, at least once per day.  
Providers SHOULD persistently perform vulnerability detection on all information resources that are likely to drift, at least once every 7 days.  
Providers SHOULD evaluate ALL vulnerabilities as required by VDR-TFR-EVU (Evaluation) within 2 days of detection.]

RA-5 (d) [high-risk vulnerabilities mitigated within thirty (30) days from date of discovery; moderate-risk vulnerabilities mitigated within ninety (90) days from date of discovery; low-risk vulnerabilities mitigated within one hundred and eighty (180) days from date of discovery for traditional Rev 5 processes] [For those opting into the Vulnerability Detection and Response mitigation timelines requirements are laid out in section VDR-TFR-PVR and are based on a combination of impact categorization, potential for impact, internet reachability, and likely exploitability].  
**Rationale:** Updated based on BIRs.

### **RA-05: Vulnerability Monitoring and Scanning**

**Tabs Affected:** High Baseline, Moderate Baseline, Low Baseline  
**Sections Affected:** Additional FedRAMP Requirements and Guidance  
**Current Verbiage:** RA-5 Guidance: See the vulnerability scanning requirements defined in the FedRAMP Continuous Monitoring Playbook.   
 RA-5 (a) Requirement: an accredited independent assessor scans operating systems/infrastructure, web applications, and databases once annually.  
 RA-5 (d) Requirement: If a vulnerability is listed among the CISA Known Exploited Vulnerability (KEV) Catalog (https://www.cisa.gov/known-exploited-vulnerabilities-catalog) the KEV remediation date supersedes the FedRAMP parameter requirement.  
 RA-5 (e) Requirement: to include all Authorizing Officials.  
 RA-5 Guidance: Informational findings from a scanner are detailed as a returned result that holds no vulnerability risk or severity, and for FedRAMP, does not require an entry onto the POA&M or entry onto the RET during any assessment phase.  
Warning findings, on the other hand, are given a risk rating (low, moderate, high or critical) by the scanning solution and should be treated like any other finding with a risk or severity rating for tracking purposes onto either the POA&M or RET depending on when the findings originated (during assessments or during monthly continuous monitoring). If a warning is received during scanning, but further validation turns up no actual issue then this item should be categorized as a false positive. If this situation presents itself during an assessment phase (initial assessment, annual assessment or any Significant Change Request or SCR), follow guidance on how to report false positives in the Security Assessment Report (SAR). If this situation happens during monthly continuous monitoring, the false positive is captured as a deviation request in the POA&M.  
Warnings are commonly associated with scanning solutions that also perform compliance scans, and if the scanner reports a “warning” as part of the compliance scanning of a CSO, follow guidance surrounding the tracking of compliance findings during either the assessment phases (initial assessment, annual assessment or any SCR) or monthly continuous monitoring as it applies. Guidance on compliance scan findings can be found by searching on “Tracking of Compliance Scans” in FAQs.  
**Proposed Change:** RA-5 Guidance: See the vulnerability scanning requirements defined in the FedRAMP Continuous Monitoring Playbook for traditional Rev5 pathway. For those who have opted into the Vulnerability Detection and Response BIR, please see Vulnerability Detection and Response Guidance.  Evaluation criteria is drastically different for Service Providers who opted into the BIR and should pay close attention to evaluation factors listed in section VDR-EVA-EFA of the Vulnerability Detection and Response Guidance.   
RA-5 (a) Requirement: an accredited independent assessor scans operating systems/infrastructure, web applications, and databases once annually.  
RA-5 (d) Requirement: If a vulnerability is listed among the CISA Known Exploited Vulnerability (KEV) Catalog (https://www.cisa.gov/known-exploited-vulnerabilities-catalog) the KEV remediation date supersedes the FedRAMP parameter requirement.  
RA-5 (e) Requirement: to include all Authorizing Officials.  
RA-5 Guidance: Informational findings from a scanner are detailed as a returned result that holds no vulnerability risk or severity and for FedRAMP does not require an entry onto the POA&M or entry onto the RET during any assessment phase.  
Warning findings, on the other hand, are given a risk rating (low, moderate, high or critical) by the scanning solution and should be treated like any other finding with a risk or severity rating for tracking purposes onto either the POA&M or RET depending on when the findings originated (during assessments or during monthly continuous monitoring). If a warning is received during scanning, but further validation turns up no actual issue then this item should be categorized as a false positive. If this situation presents itself during an assessment phase (initial assessment, annual assessment or any SCR), follow guidance on how to report false positives in the Security Assessment Report (SAR). If this situation happens during monthly continuous monitoring, the false positive is captured as a deviation request in the POA&M.  
Warnings are commonly associated with scanning solutions that also perform compliance scans, and if the scanner reports a “warning” as part of the compliance scanning of a CSO, follow guidance surrounding the tracking of compliance findings during either the assessment phases (initial assessment, annual assessment or any SCR) or monthly continuous monitoring as it applies. Guidance on compliance scan findings can be found by searching on “Tracking of Compliance Scans” in FAQs.  
**Rationale:** Updated based on BIRs.

### **RA-05: Vulnerability Monitoring and Scanning**

**Tabs Affected:** High Baseline, Moderate Baseline, Low Baseline  
**Sections Affected:** Continuous Monitoring Periodicity  
**Current Verbiage:** RA-5 (a) [monthly operating system/infrastructure; monthly web applications (including APIs) and databases]  
 RA-5 (d) [high-risk vulnerabilities mitigated within thirty (30) days from date of discovery; moderate-risk vulnerabilities mitigated within ninety (90) days from date of discovery; low-risk vulnerabilities mitigated within one hundred and eighty (180) days from date of discovery].  
**Proposed Change**: RA-5 (a) [monthly operating system/infrastructure; monthly web applications (including APIs) and databases for traditional Rev 5 processes] [For those opting into the Vulnerability Detection and Response:

Low Systems  
Providers SHOULD persistently perform vulnerability detection on representative samples of similar machine-based information resources, at least once every 7 days.   
Providers SHOULD persistently perform vulnerability detection on all information resources that are likely to drift, at least once every month.  
Providers SHOULD evaluate ALL vulnerabilities as required by VDR-TFR-EVU (Evaluation) within 7 days of detection.

Moderate Systems   
Providers SHOULD persistently perform vulnerability detection on representative samples of similar machine-based information resources, at least once every 3 days.  
Providers SHOULD persistently perform vulnerability detection on all information resources that are likely to drift, at least once every 14 days.  
Providers SHOULD evaluate ALL vulnerabilities as required by VDR-TFR-EVU (Evaluation) within 5 days of detection.

High Systems  
Providers SHOULD persistently perform vulnerability detection on representative samples of similar machine-based information resources, at least once per day.  
Providers SHOULD persistently perform vulnerability detection on all information resources that are likely to drift, at least once every 7 days.  
Providers SHOULD evaluate ALL vulnerabilities as required by VDR-TFR-EVU (Evaluation) within 2 days of detection.]

RA-5 (d) [high-risk vulnerabilities mitigated within thirty (30) days from date of discovery; moderate-risk vulnerabilities mitigated within ninety (90) days from date of discovery; low risk vulnerabilities mitigated within one hundred and eighty (180) days from date of discovery for traditional Rev 5 processes] [For those opting into the Vulnerability Detection and Response mitigation timelines requirements are laid out in section VDR-TFR-PVR and are based on a combination of impact categorization, potential for impact, internet reachability, and likely exploitability].  
**Rationale:** Updated based on BIRs.

## **Proposed Changes to Systems and Services Acquisition Family**

This section contains proposed changes to the FedRAMP Requirements and Guidance section for each of these controls.

### **SA-04(5): Acquisition Process | System, Component, and Service Configurations**

**Tabs Affected:** High Baseline  
**Sections Affected:** FedRAMP-Defined Assignment / Selection Parameters  
**Current Verbiage:** SA-4 (5) (a) The service provider shall use the DoD STIGs to establish configuration settings; Center for Internet Security up to Level 2 (CIS Level 2) guidelines shall be used if STIGs are not available; Custom baselines shall be used if CIS is not available.  
**Proposed Change:** SA-4 (5) (a) The service provider shall use the DoD STIGs to establish configuration settings; Center for Internet Security up to Level 2 (CIS Level 2) guidelines shall be used if STIGs are not available; Custom baselines shall be used if CIS is not available and must be documented and validated during independent assessment.  
**Rationale:** Updated to ensure custom baselines are documented and reviewed.

### **SA-05: System Documentation**

**Tabs Affected:** High Baseline, Moderate Baseline, Low Baseline  
**Sections Affected:** FedRAMP-Defined Assignment / Selection Parameters  
**Current Verbiage:** NEW  
**Proposed Change:** a. (1) in conjunction with the FedRAMP Security Configuration Guidance  
**Rationale:** Updated based on SCG requirements.

### **SA-15: Development Process, Standards, and Tools** 

**Tabs Affected:** High Baseline, Moderate Baseline  
**Sections Affected:** High Baseline, Moderate Baseline  
**Current Verbiage:** SA-15 (b)-2 [FedRAMP Security Authorization requirements]  
**Proposed Change:** SA-15 (b)-2 [FedRAMP Security Authorization/Certification requirements]  
**Rationale:** Updated to reflection transition to a certification authority.

## **Proposed Changes to Systems and Communications Protection Family**

This section contains proposed changes to the FedRAMP Requirements and Guidance section for each of these controls.

### **SC-07(5): Boundary Protection | Deny by Default — Allow by Exception**

**Tabs Affected:** High Baseline, Moderate Baseline  
**Sections Affected:** Additional FedRAMP Requirements and Guidance  
**Current Verbiage:** SC-7 (5) [any systems]  
**Proposed Change:** SC-7 (5) [all systems/services]  
**Rationale:** More inclusive of cloud design.

### **SC-07(8): Boundary Protection | Route Traffic to Authenticated Proxy Servers**

**Tabs Affected:** High Baseline, Moderate Baseline  
**Sections Affected:** FedRAMP-Defined Assignment / Selection Parameters  
**Current Verbiage:** SC-7 (8)-2 [any network outside of organizational control and any network outside the authorization boundary].  
**Proposed Change:** SC-7 (8)-2 [any network outside of organizational control and any network outside of assessment scope (for those following MAS BIR), or established boundary (for those following traditional Rev 5).  
**Rationale:** Take into account MAS.

### **SC-13: Cryptographic Protections**

**Tabs Affected:** High Baseline, Moderate Baseline, Low Baseline  
**Sections Affected:** Additional FedRAMP Requirements and Guidance  
**Current Verbiage:** New  
**Proposed Change:** For Cryptographic Modules list as "historical" in the CMVP database, please ensure Service Providers follow FedRAMP instructions here: https://www.fedramp.gov/archive/2022-12-22-crypto-modules-historical-status/  
**Rationale:** This update was added to address a common issue seen during the authorization/certification process.  

## **Proposed Changes to Systems and Information Integrity Family**

This section contains proposed changes to the FedRAMP Requirements and Guidance section for each of these controls.

### **SI-02(2): Flaw Remediation | Automated Flaw Remediation Status**

**Tabs Affected:** High Baseline, Moderate Baseline  
**Sections Affected:** FedRAMP-Defined Assignment / Selection Parameters  
**Current Verbiage:** SI-2 (2)-2 [at least monthly]   
**Proposed Change:** SI-2 (2)-2 [at least monthly for those CSPs following traditional Rev 5 processes]  [persistently for those CSPs participating in VDR BIR].    
**Rationale:** Updated based on VDR requirements.

### **SI-03: Malicious Code Protection**

**Tabs Affected:** High Baseline, Moderate Baseline, Low Baseline  
**Sections Affected:** FedRAMP-Defined Assignment / Selection Parameters  
**Current Verbiage:** SI-3 (c) (1)-1 [at least weekly]   
**Proposed Change:** SI-3 (c) (1)-1 [at least weekly for those CSPs following traditional Rev 5 processes]  [persistently for those CSPs participating in VDR BIR].    
**Rationale:** Updated based on VDR requirements.

### **SI-05: Security Alerts, Advisories, and Directives**

**Tabs Affected:** Low Baseline, Moderate Baseline, High Baseline  
**Sections Affected:** Additional FedRAMP Requirements and Guidance  
**Current Verbiage:** SI-5 Requirement: Service Providers must address the CISA Emergency and Binding Operational Directives applicable to their cloud service offering per FedRAMP guidance.This includes listing the applicable directives and stating compliance status.  
**Proposed Change:** SI-5 Requirement: Service Providers must address the CISA Emergency Directives (EDs) and Binding Operational Directives (BODs) applicable to their cloud service offering per FedRAMP guidance. This includes listing the applicable directives and stating compliance status. EDs and BODs can be found here:  https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/directives  
EDs and BODs responses will be coordinated through the FedRAMP Secure Inbox (FSI) process.  Service Providers are required to follow all response timelines in accordance with FSI guidance.  
**Rationale:** Updated to reflect FSI process.

### **SI-08: Spam Protection**

**Tabs Affected:** Moderate Baseline, High Baseline  
**Sections Affected:** Additional FedRAMP Requirements and Guidance  
**Current Verbiage:** SI-8 Guidance:   
When CSO sends email on behalf of the government as part of the business offering, Control Description should include implementation of Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting & Conformance (DMARC) on the sending domain for outgoing messages as described in DHS Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 18-01.  
https://cyber.dhs.gov/bod/18-01/   
SI-8 Guidance: CSPs should confirm DMARC configuration (where appropriate) to ensure that policy=reject and the rua parameter includes reports@dmarc.cyber.dhs.gov. DMARC compliance should be documented in the SI-08 control implementation solution description, and list the FROM: domain(s) that will be seen by email recipients.  
**Proposed Change:** SI-8 Guidance:

Independent assessors will have to do more than just reviewing scan results (if applicable) to validate that cloud services are meeting the requirements for vulnerability detection and response following the VDR process, but that would certainly be part of it. Cloud services are expected to provide whatever information an independent assessor needs to validate the service and contracts should be structured appropriately or independent assessors should note what areas they were unable to validate due to lack of evidence/access. Nothing changes with the VDR on this other than the nuance of what the independent assessor is validating.

For [VDR-CSO-SIR](https://www.fedramp.gov/2026/reference/vulnerability-detection-and-response/#sampling), the following is written: "_Providers MAY sample effectively identical information resources..._". This points to sampling being a optional rule, but not strictly necessary.

However, a later VDR rule, [VDR-TFR-PSD](https://www.fedramp.gov/2026/reference/vulnerability-detection-and-response/#persistent-sample-detection), states the following: "_Providers with Class C Certifications SHOULD persistently perform vulnerability detection on representative samples of similar machine-based information resources, at least once every 3 days._"

Understanding that technically SHOULD rules have some wiggle room, does the combination of these two rules read as:
- A) Sampling is optional and if you do sampling, you should perform scans at least once every 3 days or
- B) Sampling is not optional and you should perform scans at least once every 3 days or
- C) Is something else intended?

documents.text:
Apologies for the delayed response:

> "CSPs must verify and validate documentation, personnel, and budgets every 3 months"
>
>    Where verification effectively means: "collecting some sort of evidence that documentation, personnel records, and budgets are actually being followed" and
>    Where validation effectively means: "checking that the collected evidence shows documentation personnel records and budgets are being followed correctly"
>
> Is this an accurate interpretation of the requirements involved?

Yes! This is exactly what's intended and is a perfect of example of drawing all the reusable definitions/etc. into a more human-approachable phrasing. 

> Instead of reviewing them every 1/3 years, now they'd need to be verified and validated every 3 months. 

Yes.

> And then finally, if all of the above is true, would it make sense to notate this on the "Rev5 Control Guidance" page, given there's no direct mention that a VDR rule is impacting documentation?

The SP 800-53 Rev5 -01 controls don't require verification and validation in the same way the VDR does. Reviewing and updating policies is not the same as verifying the policies are in place and validating that they are working. You can do the latter frequently without needing to do the former - though in a situation where a verification or validation fails, you'd probably want to consider updating the policy. Same thing if a law or rule changes which might trigger the need to develop/document/disseminate updated policies - but if there's no law/rules changes then no trigger to develop/document/disseminate. 

I guess we could require an ODP for the typical (-01 c.2) enhancements including "failing a check in the VDR" for the organization-defined events but that seems unnecessary since it's built into the VDR?

Does that make sense? 

> Same question from the tooling angle. If VDR-TFR-NMV means documentation, personnel and budgets get verified and validated every 3 months, should those show up in the MAS inventory (MAS-CSO-IIR) with a last verified date, the same way machine resources are tracked under VDR-TFR-MVF? Trying to decide whether they are inventory rows or live somewhere else.

It makes sense to track last verified dates in the MAS, but you'd also summarize this verification and validation in your vulnerability detection and response activity reports.

documents.title: Balancing FedRAMP Rev5 against improvements to FedRAMP 20x
documents.text:
Posting our VDR beta feedback here per the PMOs suggestion:
 
### Summary
Participation in the FedRAMP Vulnerability Disclosure Report (VDR) beta provided valuable insight into the program's direction and surfaced both meaningful improvements over legacy processes and areas that would benefit from additional clarification before broad adoption. 
Overall, the shift toward a numerically-tiered vulnerability framework is a positive step, and the tight response timelines appropriately push organizations toward automation. At the same time, guidance on artifact expectations, partial remediation definitions, and the practical implications of SHOULD versus MUST requirements will be important to resolve.
 
### Successes and Improvements
Improved triage through the N# severity scale. The N# vulnerability severity scale represents a meaningful improvement over the previous Deviation Request heavy Plan of Action and Milestones (POA&M) process. This was accomplished by shifting the evaluation to earlier in the process. This allows teams to concentrate attention and remediation resources on the most urgent, high-severity findings rather than spending equal effort managing a large volume of lower-priority items that had previously required individual deviation requests. 

Focus on automation. The tight response windows prescribed by the VDR framework make manual, ad hoc vulnerability management untenable at scale. This creates a clear incentive to invest in automated scanning and alerting workflows. Organizations that embrace this push toward automation will be better positioned for success.

### Areas for Clarification and Guidance
Artifact requirements are vague The beta guidance did not clearly specify which artifacts should be submitted, or  in what format. This creates risk, organizations may need to produce different artifact sets tailored to individual auditor preferences or those of their Authorizing Official (AO). Where an auditor's expectations and an AO's expectations diverge, there is currently no clear mechanism to resolve that conflict, potentially resulting in duplicative or inconsistent documentation.

Suggestions include having an example of a Vulnerability Index for tracking the vulnerabilities in both a machine and human readable version. While we understand that VDR offers freedom for CSPs to deliver what AOs want to see for VDR; having an example of what meets FedRAMPs expectations would help guide organizations. 

Additional guidance on partial remediation would reduce ambiguity. The current framework does not clearly define what constitutes a valid partial remediation. For example, whether applying a compensating control, isolating an affected component, or reducing the attack surface qualifies as progress toward closure. Explicit criteria or worked examples for partial remediation scenarios would significantly reduce this ambiguity.
 
Further clarify SHOULD versus MUST requirements. The distinction between SHOULD and MUST requirements in the VDR framework deserves greater emphasis. In practice, stakeholders often focus on the most visible data point, such as the 4-hour response window for N5 (critical) vulnerabilities. Without fully understanding that many requirements are aspirational rather than mandatory. Clear visual or structural differentiation between MUST and SHOULD language would reduce misinterpretation and help organizations prioritize their compliance efforts accurately.

documents.title: Rev5 questions and discussion on the Consolidated Rules for 2026 (or Legacy)
documents.text:
> If an IA is starting an assessment in October and ending end of December, is the IA required to provide IV&V statements/write-ups for the Rulesets that are in place (ie: AFC, SCG, MKT, VDR/VER), if so, how does the CSP answer those if the SDR isn't required until 2027? 

The CSP and IAS should split the difference here on implementing as much as they can within scope so that they don't have to do it again a bit later. It's flexible though. Roll your own supplement. For SCG, for example, we just asked folks to link us to it.

December/January is going to be a weird time, make the right choice based on the CSPs needs, and the CSP should demonstrate they're aware of the upcoming changes and working towards them, and it'll probably be all right.

> Also, should this Annual Assessment Submission packet that is finalized in December be packaged as a CR26 assessment or should the IA deliver the assessment results with the traditional SAP/SAR since not all the rulesets are required?

All the CR26 rules are available for early adoption, so it's up to the CSP how they want to deliver if it's happening in December. As a reminder, there's a grace period for **everything** in Rev5. For some of those (like the SDR), the grace period is based on when the first FedRAMP independent assessment (aka annual assessment) starts, not when it ends. So someone completing an annual assessment in December can early adopt everything or make a choice to push off a whole bunch of stuff until their next assessment starts in Sep 2027.

> Will FedRAMP require Product Vulnerability Disclosure Reports (VDR) in a machine readable format from cloud providers - see OpenSSF proposal for a detailed description why a machine readable product VDR standard format is needed today,

FedRAMP _recommends_ reporting in a machine-readable format unless there is a valid reason not to. It is not an explicit mandatory requirement because sometimes there are valid reasons not to.

FedRAMP's requirements and recommendations for reporting are detailed in the [Vulnerability Detection & Response](https://www.fedramp.gov/docs/20x/vulnerability-detection-and-response/) process.

documents.title: RFC-0026 Clarifying CA-7 Continuous Monitoring Expectations for Rev5 Providers
documents.text:
We strongly support the CSP Advisory Board's comment on RV5-CA07-VLN, and echo concerns raised by other commenters in this thread.
The traditional path as written inadvertently forces a less secure disclosure posture than the modernized VDR approach. VDR explicitly prohibits disclosure of details likely to facilitate exploitation (VDR-RPT-NID) — the traditional path should not impose a stricter and less security-conscious standard than the path FedRAMP is actively promoting.

It is worth noting that in practice, this requirement was historically associated only with JAB-authorized systems. Codifying it now as a uniform requirement for all CSPs to provide to all agency customers would represent a significant and operationally unsafe expansion of existing expectations.

Several practical realities reinforce why this requirement is unsafe as written:

- Raw scans are impractical and dangerous to distribute broadly. 3PAOs with dedicated tooling already struggle to process them, and the FedRAMP ConMon team previously struggled to parse them for the JAB — agencies cannot reasonably be expected to do the same, and there is no assurance they can adequately protect this data once obtained.
- Raw scans provide no actionable value to agencies. Risk-contextualized summaries are what agencies can actually act on. Unprocessed output identifying specific vulnerabilities on specific systems increases attack surface without improving agency decision-making.
- Systemic risk compounds for IaaS providers. Over-sharing at the foundational layer exposes every SaaS provider and agency tenant sitting on top of that infrastructure.

We support the CSP-AB's recommendations that raw scans be treated as 3PAO review materials, that CSPs be permitted to redact sensitive exploitability details while preserving risk-level information, and that the traditional path be aligned with VDR's responsible disclosure principles.  If FedRAMP determines that raw scan access must remain available outside of VDR, we strongly recommend it be limited to a single designated lead agency that has demonstrated the capability and controls to responsibly manage this data — and that even then, sharing be governed by agency contract rather than uniform mandate.

documents.title: General discussion / Q&A on Rev5 improvements and changes in 2026
documents.text:
I strongly support FedRAMP's strategic direction with the new Vulnerability Detection and Response framework. Given the current threat environment, including the increasing speed and automation of exploitation activity, a more risk-based and responsive approach to vulnerability management is clearly needed.

That said, I wanted to raise a practical implementation concern that may affect CSPs' ability to meet the required timelines, particularly where agency approval processes do not yet align with the newer Significant Change Notification approach.

The current timeline for CSP adoption, including the December 7 implementation date and the subsequent 90-day grace period, appears to assume that agencies will broadly accept the SCN process for VDR-related system changes. In practice, CSPs may still encounter agency-specific expectations that require use of the more traditional Significant Change Request process (we are seeing this with many agencies on other less significant changes). This creates a potential disconnect between FedRAMP's intended modernization path and how implementation may actually occur across different agency authorization environments.

There are three areas where additional PMO guidance or engagement could materially reduce implementation risk.

### 1. Agency Alignment on SCN Usage

FedRAMP's updated approach to significant changes provides an important opportunity to move from pre-approval-heavy processes toward more continuous, notification-based governance. However, some Agency Authorizing Officials and security teams may continue to require SCRs for changes that CSPs believe are appropriate for SCN handling.

For CSPs working with agencies that take a more conservative approach, the challenge is not unwillingness to comply with VDR expectations. Rather, it is that agency-specific change management expectations may materially extend implementation timelines.

Additional PMO clarification on when VDR-related changes should be handled through SCN, and perhaps even direct engagement with agencies to encourage consistent adoption of that approach, would be very helpful.

### 2. 3PAO Capacity and Cost Considerations

If VDR-related changes are treated as SCRs by many agencies, CSPs may be required to obtain additional 3PAO assessment support. This could create two practical challenges.

First, the cost of additional 3PAO assessment activity can be significant, especially for small and mid-sized SaaS providers that may not have budgeted for a major assessment cycle on this timeline.

Second, the 3PAO ecosystem has finite capacity. If a large number of CSPs are simultaneously directed into SCR-driven assessment activities, there is a real possibility of scheduling backlogs that could delay implementation even for CSPs acting in good faith.

This does not reduce the importance of the VDR requirement, but it does suggest that the success of the rollout may depend on ensuring that the change process is scaled appropriately.

### 3. Avoiding Unintended Marketplace Impact

A rigid enforcement posture, without accounting for agency-level process dependencies or 3PAO capacity constraints, could have unintended consequences for the FedRAMP marketplace.

Some specialized or smaller CSPs may face delays that are outside their direct control. Larger providers may also view repeated high-friction compliance changes as a factor in evaluating the cost and predictability of continued participation in the FedRAMP ecosystem.

The concern is not that enforcement should be weakened. Rather, enforcement should distinguish between CSPs that are not engaging and CSPs that are actively implementing VDR but are delayed by agency process requirements, assessment scheduling, or other documented dependencies.

### Suggested PMO Actions

To support successful adoption while preserving the security intent of the VDR framework, I would respectfully suggest the following:

1. **Provide additional agency-facing guidance on SCN applicability.**
   Clarify that VDR-related implementation changes should generally be handled through SCN where the nature of the change supports that path, unless there is a specific risk-based reason to require an SCR.

2. **Engage directly with Agency AOs and security teams.**
   Help ensure agencies are aligned with FedRAMP's modernization goals and are not unintentionally creating implementation barriers through inconsistent change management expectations.

3. **Establish a conditional safe harbor for good-faith implementation.**
   Consider allowing CSPs that have documented implementation plans, active milestones, and evidence of progress to remain in good standing where delays are caused by agency-directed SCR requirements, 3PAO scheduling constraints, or similar dependencies.

4. **Clarify enforcement expectations.**
   Distinguish between CSPs that are not taking action and CSPs that are actively working toward compliance but require additional time due to factors outside their direct control.

5. **Consider phased enforcement where appropriate.**
   A phased or risk-based enforcement model could help preserve the urgency of VDR adoption while avoiding unnecessary disruption to agencies and the CSP marketplace.

Overall, I fully support the goal of improving vulnerability detection and response across FedRAMP-authorized systems. My concern is that the implementation path needs to account for how agency change management and 3PAO assessment capacity work in practice. With additional PMO guidance and agency alignment, FedRAMP can maintain the urgency of the VDR transition while reducing the risk of avoidable delays, unnecessary costs, or unintended marketplace disruption.

documents.title: The Sprint to 20x Phase Two
documents.text:
To get the ball rolling, I'm releasing the following summary of changes from RFC-0012 that will be released in the upcoming Vulnerability Detection and Response Standard tomorrow.

# 20x Vulnerability Detection and Response Standard Changes

The purpose of FedRAMP, as defined in modern law and policy, is not to simply to determine if cloud services are sufficiently secure for government use; FedRAMP exists to provide a standardized and reusable approach to security assessment and authorization that enables agencies to make informed risk-based decisions when integrating cloud services into agency information systems. Cloud service providers who wish to sell their services to agencies must report on the ongoing security decisions they make and agencies will review that information to determine if they wish to use these cloud services.

An early version of this standard was released as RFC-0012 Continuous Vulnerability Management (CVM) Standard, with aspects of the problems related to Plans of Action & Milestones discussed with the Federal Secure Cloud Advisory Committee. FedRAMP received a significant amount of both formal and informal public comment on the proposed CVM and has made considerable changes to this Vulnerability Detection and Response (VDR) Standard as a result.

The VDR Standard includes the following significant changes for initial release:

- Credibly Exploitable Vulnerabilities have been renamed to Likely Exploitable Vulnerabilities to reinforce the importance of assessing how likely something is, to reuse the term likely that is becoming a critical aspect of FedRAMP assessment, and to default to simpler plain language. As a bonus, the spoken acronym for LEV is clearly distinct from KEV. 
- The historical concept of Plans of Action & Milestones (POA&Ms) has been completely eliminated and replaced with simply labeling a weakness that the cloud service does not plan to fix as an accepted weakness. Agencies are expected to integrate these into their formal Plans of Action & Milestones for any federal information systems that rely on the cloud service offering based on their own policies.
- Providers are more strictly urged to avoid sharing sensitive information that would likely lead to exploitation and are no longer required to even report specifics of the underlying vulnerability itself (and agencies are more strictly urged not to request it). Instead, providers should share sufficient information so that agencies can understand the risk to their information. In practice, this should lead to less noise shared with agencies and allow them to focus on real underlying risks, but it is a significant shift for both providers and agency customers from today’s default.
- FedRAMP has defined impact effects based on commercial service impact that a provider can understand without having knowledge of the agency use cases for their service. The potential adverse impact calculation has been changed to consider impact to the entire population (N) of agency customers. Both changes enable providers to create more quantitative assessments of the overall potential adverse impact that applies for FedRAMP.
- Maximum recommended timeframes for many aspects of vulnerability detection and response have been separated by FedRAMP authorization impact level to focus the most aggressive expectations on the highest impact services.
- This policy now encourages representative sampling of resources on a more aggressive schedule than polling all resources, urges providers to automatically assess newly deployed resources, and focuses recurring assessments on resources that are most likely to change. 
- Leveraging authority in the FedRAMP Authorization Act and M-24-15, this updated policy includes agency specific requirements and recommendations.
- Many other minor changes have been made to order, wording, recommendations, and other items based on feedback. For example, many commenters were confused about partial mitigation vs full mitigation so this update clarifies that partial mitigation is encouraged in steps until full mitigation is achieved. Another example is the definition and use of “persistently” to mitigate quite a lot of confusion around the different uses of “continuous” in different contexts.

This standard will be revised and reopened for public comment based on feedback from the FedRAMP 20x Pilot Phase Two/Three and the Rev5 VDR Closed Beta; the next revision is anticipated in Jan/Feb, 2026.

Thank you for clarifying the intent, this wasn't immediately apparent to me or, it seems, to other commenters.

**Recommendation: Establish a Dedicated KSI for Penetration Testing**
I strongly recommend creating a standalone KSI specifically for penetration testing activities. Given that penetration testing represents one of the most critical components of application security assessment, it warrants its own dedicated KSI rather than being embedded within broader standards.

**Benefits of a Dedicated KSI:**
- Enhanced visibility for agency customers: A dedicated KSI would streamline review processes through agency GRC tooling, making it easier to locate and assess penetration testing documentation
- Addresses customer priorities: Penetration test reports consistently rank as the most requested documentation from agency customers during security reviews
- Reduces ambiguity: The current structure lacks clarity regarding requirements for human-led penetration testing and red teaming activities

**Current Gaps:** The existing framework creates confusion in several ways:
- The Vulnerability Detection and Response standard doesn't explicitly mandate human-led penetration testing and red teaming
- KSI-MLA-03 notably excludes mapping to CA-8 and CA-8(2)
- The [VDR](https://github.com/FedRAMP/docs/blob/main/pdf/FRMR.VDR.vulnerability-detection-and-response.pdf) standard's language is non-prescriptive, using "SHOULD" rather than mandatory language in the one small mention about penetration testing. 

> FRR-VDR-RP-02: Providers SHOULD include high-level overviews of ALL vulnerability detection and response activities conducted during this period for the cloud service offering; this includes vulnerability disclosure programs, bug bounty programs, penetration testing, assessments, etc.

documents.title: RFC-0014 Phase Two Security Indicators
documents.text:
@pete-gov thank you for the clarification. While I appreciate that penetration testing and red teaming falls under the FedRAMP VDR standard's "vulnerability detection" definition, the current framework lacks the specificity needed to ensure agencies receive meaningful security assurance.

**Key concerns**
1.	**Lack of Specificity**: The VDR standard treats penetration testing as one example among many vulnerability detection methods, without establishing minimum requirements for human-led security testing.
2.	**No Quality Standards:** There are no defined criteria for what constitutes an acceptable penetration test or red team exercise, leaving significant room for interpretation
3.	**Market Confusion:** We're seeing vendors market simple external, unauthenticated scans as "penetration tests" or "red team exercises" - practices that provide minimal security value but technically satisfy the broad current language.
4.	**Lack of Actionable Requirements:** No specific methodology, frequency, or tester qualification standards for human-led security testing.

**Recommendations**

FedRAMP should establish explicit penetration testing requirements including:
- Clear definitions distinguishing pen testing and red teaming from automated scanning
- Minimum scope and methodology standards (similar to what exists for Rev5)
- Tester qualification requirements
- Specific frequency expectations

Without clearer standards, it can be difficult for agencies to distinguish between CSPs conducting rigorous, human-led security validation and those relying on more limited scanning activities presented as comprehensive testing. This lack of clarity around how penetration testing and red teaming are interpreted within the current KSIs and VDR standard may reduce the level of assurance that FedRAMP authorizations are intended to provide.
