# RFC-0028 FedRAMP Rev5 Security Controls Baseline Update for CP, IA, IR, MA, and MP Control Families

❓   **Please note that FedRAMP will not answer questions in this thread as it is reserved for public comment. If you would like to ask a question or generally discuss this RFC informally, please use the [General discussion and Q&A for RFCs related to Rev5 Updates (RFCs 0026, 0027, 0028, 0029, & 0030) thread](https://github.com/FedRAMP/community/discussions/129). Thank you!**

**Status:** Closed
**Start Date:** March 19, 2026
**Closing Date:** April 22, 2026
---

# FedRAMP Rev5 Security Controls Baseline Update for CP, IA, IR, MA, and MP Control Families

---

## **Summary**

This is a technical RFC that proposes updates to the Additional FedRAMP Security Technical Controls Requirements and Guidance for FedRAMP Rev5 baselines.

To save space and to limit the breadth of a single RFC, this technical document shows only the proposed changes to the current baseline document and is restricted to a few control families. If verbiage is being updated, only the specific wording that is to be changed is identified in the old verbiage section. If the verbiage to be added is not replacing previous verbiage, but being added, it will be identified as “NEW” in the old verbiage section.  

Since this spreadsheet covers hundreds of controls across multiple tabs and sections, only those specific controls, sections, and tabs identified are being proposed for updates. If it is not mentioned below, changes are **not** being proposed.  

**Commenters are advised to please mention specific controls in their comments!**

This RFC addresses controls in the following families:

* Contingency Planning (CP)  
* Identification and Authentication (IA)  
* Incident Response (IR)  
* Maintenance (MA)  
* Media Protection (MP)

## **Motivation**

Many Rev5 FedRAMP Requirements and Guidance statements are based on outdated approaches that predated the release of the FedRAMP Authorization Act and M-24-15. This set of Requirements and Guidance needs a refresh to match FedRAMP’s current rules and approach.

The updates formalized after this RFC will be included in the FedRAMP Consolidated Rules for 2026. That set of rules will be valid until December 31, 2028. FedRAMP will provide a transition plan for adopting any new guidance that will enable cloud service providers to update their approach as part of their annual assessment as appropriate.

These changes are designed to lower the burden for cloud service providers and eliminate previous pain points.

Additionally, NIST released 800-53 Rev 5.2.0 in August of 2025.  While this update was minor, control updates from NIST will require updates to FedRAMP Security Control Baseline in order to reflect this update.  These changes will happen without public comment through FedRAMP since these are direct reflections of NIST changes.  As subsequent iterations of the FedRAMP Security Control Baseline are published, it is FedRAMP’s intent only to carry over the following information from NIST 800-53; Control Family, Control Name, and Control ID. Following this will be FedRAMP-Defined Assignment / Selection Parameters and additional FedRAMP Requirements and Guidance.

## **Proposed Changes to Contingency Planning Family**

This section contains proposed changes to the FedRAMP Requirements and Guidance section for each of these controls.

### **CP-02: Contingency Plan**

**Tabs Affected:** High Baseline, Moderate Baseline, Low Baseline  
**Sections Affected:** Additional FedRAMP Requirements and Guidance  
**Current Verbiage:** CP-2 Requirement: CSPs must use the FedRAMP Information System Contingency Plan (ISCP) Template (available at: https://www.fedramp.gov/assets/resources/templates/SSP-A06-FedRAMP-ISCP-Template.docx).   
**Proposed Change**: CP-2 Requirement: CSPs must use the FedRAMP Information System Contingency Plan (ISCP) Template (available at:   
https://www.fedramp.gov/resources/templates/SSP-Appendix-G-Information-System-Contingency-Plan-(ISCP)-Template.docx).  
**Rationale:** Update existing link to active link.

### **CP-02(8): Contingency Plan | Identify Critical Assets**

**Tabs Affected:** High Baseline, Moderate Baseline   
**Sections Affected:** FedRAMP-Defined Assignment / Selection Parameters  
**Current Verbiage:** NEW  
**Proposed Change:** CP-2 (8) - [essential]  
**Rationale:** Parameter previously undefined.

### **CP-03: Contingency Training**

**Tabs Affected:** High Baseline, Moderate Baseline, Low Baseline  
**Sections Affected:** Additional FedRAMP Requirements and Guidance  
**Current Verbiage:** CP-3 (a) Requirement: Privileged admins and engineers must take the basic contingency training within 10 days. Consideration must be given for those privileged admins and engineers with critical contingency-related roles, to gain enough system context and situational awareness to understand the full impact of contingency training as it applies to their respective level. Newly hired critical contingency personnel must take this more in-depth training within 60 days of hire date when the training will have more impact.  
**Proposed Change**: CP-3 (a) Requirement: Privileged admins (to include TLAs) and engineers must take the basic contingency training within 10 days. Consideration must be given for those privileged admins and engineers with critical contingency-related roles, to gain enough system context and situational awareness to understand the full impact of contingency training as it applies to their respective level. Newly hired critical contingency personnel must take this more in-depth training within 60 days of hire date when the training will have more impact.  
**Rationale:** Adjustment due to verbiage updates within SCG.

## **Proposed Changes to Identification and Authentication Family**

This section contains proposed changes to the FedRAMP Requirements and Guidance section for each of these controls.

### **IA-02: Identification and Authentication**

**Tabs Affected:** High Baseline, Moderate Baseline, Low Baseline  
**Sections Affected:** Additional FedRAMP Requirements and Guidance  
**Current Verbiage:** IA-2 Requirement: For all control enhancements that specify multifactor authentication, the implementation must adhere to the Digital Identity Guidelines specified in NIST Special Publication 800-63B.  
IA-2 Requirement: Multi-factor authentication must be phishing-resistant.  
IA-2 Requirement: All uses of encrypted virtual private networks must meet all applicable Federal requirements and architecture, dataflow, and security and privacy controls must be documented, assessed, and authorized to operate.  
IA-2 Guidance: “Phishing-resistant" authentication refers to authentication processes designed to detect and prevent disclosure of authentication secrets and outputs to a website or application masquerading as a legitimate system.   
**Proposed Change:** IA-2 Requirement: For all control enhancements that specify multifactor authentication, the implementation must adhere to the Digital Identity Guidelines specified in NIST Special Publication 800-63B.  
Multi-factor authentication must be phishing-resistant. Per CISA, One-time password (OTP), Mobile push notification with number matching and Token-based OTP are NOT phishing resistant.  
https://www.cisa.gov/sites/default/files/publications/fact-sheet-implementing-phishing-resistant-mfa-508c.pdf  
IA-2 Requirement: Authentication Factors and their applicable protocols must be explicitly identified within applicable control documentation to include the System Security Plan. When following traditional Rev 5 processes, the Architecture Boundary Diagram must show every instance of MFA to include protocol, where applicable. This should, at a minimum, be at every ingress point  into the boundary.    
IA-2 Requirement: All uses of encrypted virtual private networks must meet all applicable Federal requirements and architecture, dataflow, and security and privacy controls must be documented, assessed, and authorized to operate.  
**Rationale:** This update was added to address a common issue seen during the authorization/certification process.

### **IA-02(1): Identification and Authentication (organizational Users) | Multi-factor Authentication to Privileged Accounts**

**Tabs Affected:** High Baseline, Moderate Baseline, Low Baseline  
**Sections Affected:** Additional FedRAMP Requirements and Guidance  
**Current Verbiage:** Multi-factor authentication must be phishing-resistant.  
**Proposed Change:** Multi-factor authentication must be phishing-resistant. Per CISA, One-time password (OTP), Mobile push notification with number matching  
and Token-based OTP are NOT phishing resistant.  
https://www.cisa.gov/sites/default/files/publications/fact-sheet-implementing-phishing-resistant-mfa-508c.pdf  
**Rationale:** This update was added to address a common issue seen during the authorization/certification process.

### **IA-02(2): Identification and Authentication (organizational Users) | Multi-factor Authentication to Non-privileged Accounts**

**Tabs Affected:** High Baseline, Moderate Baseline, Low Baseline  
**Sections Affected:** Additional FedRAMP Requirements and Guidance  
**Current Verbiage:** Multi-factor authentication must be phishing-resistant.  
**Proposed Change:** Multi-factor authentication must be phishing-resistant. Per CISA, One-time password (OTP), Mobile push notification with number matching  
and Token-based OTP are NOT phishing resistant.  
https://www.cisa.gov/sites/default/files/publications/fact-sheet-implementing-phishing-resistant-mfa-508c.pdf  
**Rationale:** This update was added to address a common issue seen during the authorization/certification process.

### **IA-11: Reauthentication**

**Tabs Affected:** High Baseline, Moderate Baseline, Low Baseline  
**Sections Affected:** Additional FedRAMP Requirements and Guidance  
**Current Verbiage:** The fixed time period cannot exceed the limits set in SP 800-63.  
**Proposed Change:** The fixed time period cannot exceed the limits set in SP 800-63B.  
**Rationale:** Updated to accurately reflect the correct Publication.

## **Proposed Changes to Incident Response Family**

This section contains proposed changes to the FedRAMP Requirements and Guidance section for each of these controls.

### **IR-02: Incident Response Training**

**Tabs Affected:** High Baseline, Moderate Baseline, Low Baseline  
**Sections Affected:** FedRAMP-Defined Assignment / Selection Parameters  
**Current Verbiage:** IR-2 (a) (1) [ten (10) days for privileged users, thirty (30) days for Incident Response roles]  
**Proposed Change:** IR-2 (a) (1) [ten (10) days for privileged users (to include TLA), thirty (30) days for Incident Response roles]  
**Rationale:** Alignment with the FedRAMP Secure Configuration Guidance (SCG).

### **IR-06: Incident Reporting**

**Tabs Affected:** High Baseline, Moderate Baseline, Low Baseline  
**Sections Affected:** Additional FedRAMP Requirements and Guidance  
**Current Verbiage:** IR-6 Requirement: Reports security incident information according to the guidance in the FedRAMP Continuous Monitoring Playbook.  
**Proposed Change:** IR-6 Requirement: Reports security incident information according to the guidance in the FedRAMP Continuous Monitoring Playbook or Vulnerability Detection and Response (VDR) guidance (as applicable).  
**Rationale:** Alignment with the FedRAMP Vulnerability Detection and Response (VDR) guidance.

### **IR-07: Incident Response Assistance**

**Tabs Affected:** High Baseline, Moderate Baseline, Low Baseline  
**Sections Affected:** Additional FedRAMP Requirements and Guidance  
**Current Verbiage:** NEW  
**Proposed Change:** CSPs must maintain a centralized point of contact and appropriate response rates to FedRAMP incidents as identified within FedRAMP Secure Inbox Guidance.  
**Rationale:** Alignment with the FedRAMP Secure Inbox (FSI) guidance.

## **Proposed Changes to Maintenance Family**

This section contains proposed changes to the FedRAMP Requirements and Guidance section for each of these controls.

### **MA-05: Maintenance Personnel**

**Tabs Affected:** Low Baseline, Moderate Baseline, High Baseline  
**Sections Affected:** Additional FedRAMP Requirements and Guidance  
**Current Verbiage:** NEW  
**Proposed Change:** CSPs should clearly document nationality requirements for maintenance personnel, where applicable.  
**Rationale:** Added due to recent events

## **Proposed Changes to Media Protection Family**

This section contains proposed changes to the FedRAMP Requirements and Guidance section for each of these controls.

### **MP-06(1): Media Sanitization | Review, Approve, Track, Document, and Verify**

**Tabs Affected:** High Baseline  
**Sections Affected:** Additional FedRAMP Requirements and Guidance  
**Current Verbiage:** MP-6 (1)  Requirement: Must comply with NIST SP 800-88  
**Proposed Change:** MP-6 (1)  Requirement: Must comply with NIST SP 800-88 Rev 2  
**Rationale:** Administrative update.

### **MP-06(3): Media Sanitization | Nondestructive Techniques**

**Tabs Affected:** High Baseline  
**Sections Affected:** Additional FedRAMP Requirements and Guidance  
**Current Verbiage:** MP-6 (3)  Requirement: Must comply with NIST SP 800-88  
**Proposed Change:** MP-6 (3)  Requirement: Must comply with NIST SP 800-88 Rev 2  
**Rationale:** Administrative update.

documents.title: RFC-0036 FedRAMP 20x Class D Cloud-Hosted Pilot Requirements
documents.text:
# RFC-0036 FedRAMP 20x Class D Cloud-Hosted Pilot Requirements

- Status: Open
- Start Date: October 15, 2026
- Closing Date: November 19, 2026

**Note:** You can discuss this RFC without making formal comment in discussion #181 .

## **Summary & Motivation**

The FedRAMP 20x Cloud-Hosted Class D Pilot will explore the impact and implementation of the highest assurance level of FedRAMP Certification for cloud-hosted services. This RFC proposes specific changes to a variety of rulesets and key security indicators to test during the Phase 4 pilot.

This RFC includes the following:

- 2 new definitions
- Miscellaneous updates to 6 different rulesets
- 10 new Key Security Indicators

Additional rules and Key Security Indicators may be added during or after the Phase 4 pilot, and the existing rules and indicators are likely to change based on direct feedback during the pilot. FedRAMP understands that it would be convenient to know exactly what the rules are likely to be a year in advance, but that is not a realistic approach to developing a new process that is responsive to real world impacts.

**The addition of Foreign Ownership, Control or Influence (FOCI) information:**

FedRAMP seeks to drive a balance between the amount of assurance related to FOCI that agencies might expect and the varying amounts of assurance related to FOCI that different cloud service providers may invest in. The goal is to provide basis rules and indicators that a cloud service provider can follow to provide an appropriate level of assurance, based on their own business strategy, in a fashion that can be shared with all potential agency customers. FedRAMP FOCI practices do not replace agency-specific needs or determinations, but should allow cloud service providers that implement them to save time and effort during an agency review.

FedRAMP will make no determinations on FOCI itself, only confirm whether cloud service providers adequately demonstrate that they persistently review the necessary indicators to understand FOCI and their business.

## **Feedback Requested**

This RFC is intended specifically for the Phase 4 Cloud-Hosted pilot. FedRAMP is looking for feedback on the clarity, applicability, reasonability, and achievability of the proposed rules and Key Security Indicators for companies who wish to meet the highest levels of assurance for federal customers.

This RFC does not address Self-Hosted or Hybrid-Hosted rules or requirements as those are not part of the Phase 4 pilot.

## **New Definitions**

**FRD-FOR:** Foreign Ownership, Control, Or Influence (FOCI)

> A condition that occurs when a foreign entity has the power to direct or influence the management or operations of a cloud service offering used or relied upon by agencies. The full extent of the definition of FOCI includes any federal definition or regulation that defines the extent of possible foreign ownership, control, or influence as it might apply to a cloud service offering.

**FRD-FPS:** Foreign Person

> Has the meaning given in 31 CFR 800.224, that is: “(1) Any foreign national, foreign government, or foreign entity; or (2) Any entity over which control is exercised or exercisable by a foreign national, foreign government, or foreign entity.”
>
> _Note: [Reference URL](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-31/subtitle-B/chapter-VIII/part-800/subpart-B/section-800.224)_

## **Miscellaneous Requirements**

Please note that this RFC does not reproduce existing Class D rules that will apply to FedRAMP 20x in the Consolidated Rules for 2026; only new or modified rules are added. Participants are encouraged to review all existing Class D rules, of which there are many, for context while reviewing these updated requirements for FedRAMP 20x.

This section contains individual rules that are new or modified from existing rulesets.

### Vulnerability Detection and Response

**VDR-TFR-MVX** Persistent Machine Verification and Validation for 20x

> Providers with 20x Class D Certification MUST verify and validate the status of machine-based information resources at least once every 3 days.
>
> _Note: This matches the current Class C expectation for this rule._

### Vulnerability Evaluation and Reporting

**VER-EVA-IOC** Indicators of Compromise

> Providers with 20x Class D Certifications SHOULD evaluate detected vulnerabilities, considering the context of the cloud service offering, to determine when the likelihood of exploitation is high enough to initiate forensic activities such as searching for indicators of compromise; then do so.
>
> _Note: This is an entirely new rule. It may also be ported to Rev5 in CR27._

**VER-TFR-MRH** Historical Activity

> Providers with Class 20x D Certifications MUST make all recent historical vulnerability detection and response activity available in JSON format for automated retrieval by all necessary parties (e.g. using an API service or similar); this information SHOULD be updated persistently, at least once every 7 days.
>
> _Note: This proposes a change from SHOULD to a MUST for 20x Class D._

### Security Decision Record

**SDR-CSX-KMT** Key Security Indicator Metrics

> Providers with 20x Class D Certifications MUST also include historical metrics in their Security Decision Record, supplying at least the following information for each applicable Key Security Indicator:
>
> 1. Summary of each metric over the past 30 days
> 2. Summary of metric up to the past year (where available)
> 3. Metric data (including status of persistent validation) every 4 hours up to the past year (where available)
>
> _Note: This should be supplied as a supplemental to the main Security Decision Record via API \- see CDS-CSX-API (API Certification Date)._

### Certification Data Sharing

**CDS-CSX-API** API Certification Data

> Providers with 20x Class D Certifications MUST responsibly supply all machine-readable parts of the FedRAMP Certification Package via web-compatible Application Programming Interface (API).
>
> _Note: This is a NEW rule for 20x Class D to increase the quality of assurance commensurate with the expectations for Class D._

### Cryptographic Module Use

**CMU-CSO-PQS** Post-Quantum Cryptography Status

> Providers with 20x Class D Certifications MUST document the post-quantum cryptography status of digital key establishment and digital signatures used to protect federal customer data, also adding at least the following information:
>
> 1. Whether each algorithm is Post-Quantum Cryptography, part of a hybrid implementation with post-quantum cryptography, or neither
> 2. The target date to transition it to post-quantum cryptography or a hybrid implementation (if available and applicable)
>
> _Note: This is a NEW rule for the Phase 4 pilot and the Consolidated Rules for 2027 and is therefore not included in RFC-0035 Cryptographic Module Use Rules Updates._

### FedRAMP Certification for 20x Class D

_(Note: This section includes proposed formal language for some rules that were mentioned in RFC-0033, and the proposed language was adjusted based on feedback from that RFC)_

**FRC-FRA-FOD** FOCI Determinations are Agency Specific

> FedRAMP MUST NOT request details of the foreign ownership, control, or influence of providers and will not make determinations about whether a provider's foreign ownership, control, or influence is acceptable.
>
> _Note: Agencies determine whether a provider's foreign ownership, control, or influence is acceptable for their use. FedRAMP verifies only that providers know and track foreign ownership, control, or influence. This rule makes it clear that FedRAMP does not intend to collect sensitive business information but does expect cloud service providers to be able to supply that information when required by their customers per a contract with them._

**FRC-CLD-PCD** Progressive Certification to Class D

> Providers seeking a FedRAMP 20x Class D Certification MUST maintain a 20x Class C Certification without corrective action for at least 6 months OR receive a special exemption from FedRAMP to apply directly for a 20x Class D Certification due to an urgent critical need; such exemptions may include cloud services prioritized by the FedRAMP Board and limited pilots.
>
> _Notes:_
>
> - _For the purposes of the FedRAMP 20x Phase 4 Pilot, a full non-pilot 20x Class C Certification is necessary to qualify for participation but six months without corrective action is not required._
> - _FedRAMP is a government program that is not funded by fees or services. Program certification for Class D is very complicated and requires considerable investment and commitment from FedRAMP \- traditional sponsorship for Class D (High) often took many years. This breaks up investment and review by expecting a cloud service to demonstrate a progressive level of assurance over time instead of starting at the highest level. Any cloud service provider seeking a 20x Class D Certification can start at 20x Class C, then once this review is completed and they have demonstrated clear understanding of the requirements they can apply for a 20x Class D with additional support from the government with less risk to the taxpayer._
> - _No one with a Rev5 Class D will be expected to give up their Class D Certification, but transitions from Rev5 Class D will still be expected to move through 20x Class C first (we anticipate most Rev5 Class D offerings will seek to maintain their Rev5 Class D even after obtaining a 20x Class D)._

**FRC-CLD-CCH** Certified Cloud Hosting

> Providers seeking a FedRAMP 20x Class D Certification MUST be deployed on a FedRAMP Class C or FedRAMP Class D Certified Infrastructure-as-a-Service/Platform-as-a-Service offering; OR meet all applicable FedRAMP 20x Class D Self-Hosted or Hybrid-Hosted rules.
>
> _Note: This is a NEW rule that clarifies a gap in the current rules. Self-Hosted and Hybrid-Hosted rules do not exist yet; they will be developed during Phase 4 separately._

**FRC-CLD-CTP** Certified Third-Party Services

> Providers seeking a FedRAMP 20x Class D Certification SHOULD limit the likely handling of federal customer data within the cloud service offering to third-party information resources that are included in a FedRAMP Class B, Class C, Class D, or Class G Certified offering.
>
> _Note: This is a NEW rule intended to ensure that the full lifecycle of federal customer data can be assessed for risk by agencies._

## **Key Security Indicators**

FedRAMP has many rules that include specific assurance expectations for 20x (and Rev5) Class D compared to other FedRAMP Certification Classes. Key Security Indicators go beyond assurance to demonstrate that the cloud service provider is maintaining and tracking critical security information over time. FedRAMP 20x Class D providers will need to use at least 4 different automated methods to track Key Security Indicator status and are encouraged to go well beyond this. FedRAMP 20x Class D is intended to be competitive, such that providers who invest in additional automation, greater assurance, and high speed response and communication will consistently outperform providers that only seek to meet the minimal bar \- though efficient providers at the minimum bar may compete on price or specific use cases.

In addition to all existing Key Security Indicators, FedRAMP proposes adding the following new Key Security Indicators specifically for FedRAMP 20x Class D based on the additional security capabilities expected from a High baseline (note that many automation capabilities are already addressed):

**KSI-CMT-TNP** Testing in Non-Production Environments

> Planned changes are persistently verified and validated in simulated or non-production environments before production environments.
>
> _Related Controls: CM-4(1)_

**KSI-IAM-MST** Monitoring Suitability

> Privileged and high risk information resources have their access, privileges, suitability, and activities persistently reviewed and evaluated.
>
> _Note: This includes personnel, funds, and tech such as AI agents/etc. where access, privileges, suitability, and activity review is appropriate._
>
> _Related Controls: SI-4(19), SI-4(20)_

**KSI-IAM-MPI** Managing Personnel Identities

> The background and identity of personnel is persistently verified and validated, based on their privileges and assigned roles.
>
> _Related Controls: IA-12(4), SI-4(19)_

**KSI-RPL-MCA** Maintaining Cryptographic Access

> The ability to make critical information available in the event of cryptographic key loss or failure is persistently reviewed.
>
> _Related Controls: SC-12(1)_

**KSI-SVC-IED** Inspecting Encrypted Data

> Encrypted data is appropriately and responsibly inspected during transmission for malicious content and compliance with organizational data policies.
>
> _Related Controls: SI-4(10)_

**KSI-SVC-UAS** Using Automated Security

> Processes critical to the security of the system are supported by automated tools to ensure compliance and consistency.
>
> _Related Controls: AU-6(1), AU-7(1), CM-3(1), CM-5(1), CM-6(1), CM-8(2), IR-2(2), IR-5(1), PS-4(2), SI-2(2), SI-4(12), SI-5(1), SI-7(2), SI-7(5)_

**KSI-PIY-DFC** Detecting FOCI Changes

> Changes in foreign ownership, control, or influence are detected and appropriate actions are taken.
>
> _Note: Sensitive details of such changes or actions should not be included in Key Security Indicator metrics._

**KSI-PIY-RFP** Reviewing Foreign Persons

> Foreign persons able to direct or decide matters affecting the cloud service offering are persistently reviewed.
>
> _Note: Sensitive details of such persons should not be included in Key Security Indicator metrics._

**KSI-PIY-RFB** Reviewing Foreign Businesses

> Foreign business relationships that support the cloud service offering are persistently reviewed for ongoing risks.
>
> _Note: Sensitive details of such businesses should not be included in Key Security Indicator metrics._

**KSI-PIY-MFD** Maintaining FOCI Determinations or Mitigations

> Foreign ownership, control, or influence determinations and/or mitigation agreements, issued by U.S. government agencies covering the entity that operates the cloud service offering, are persistently reviewed and maintained.
>
> _Note: Sensitive details of such determinations or agreements should not be included in Key Security Indicator metrics._

documents.title: RFC-0030 FedRAMP Rev5 Security Controls Baseline Update for RA, SA, SC, SI, and SR Control Families
documents.text:
Public comment from Raj P sent to pete@fedramp.gov:

Please find my public comments below on RFC-0030 FedRAMP Rev5 Security Controls Baseline Update for RA, SA, SC, SI, and SR Control Families.

Comment 1: RA-05: Vulnerability Monitoring and Scanning

Meeting both tracks of Rev 5 baselines while also allowing for VDR opt-in baselines is a sound idea. However each requirement for VDR opt-in whether scanning frequency, drift detection, or evaluation window for all three baselines use SHOULD instead of must. This means there is no actual requirement for a system designed for High baseline to actually scan daily and evaluate vulnerabilities within 2 days of detection. When comparing both tracks while looking at the self-assessment customers, CSPs, and assessors will see them as offering the same capabilities when this language clearly cannot be enforced. I believe this to be unintentional.

Comment 2: SA-04(5) and SI-02(2) / SI-03

The addition to SA-04(5) that requires custom baselines to be documented and validated as part of the independent assessment activity is an excellent (and extremely long needed) band-aid for High baseline systems.

The language used in SI-02(2) and SI-03 are very different from RA-05 because it simply states participants for VDR BIR must persistently review security alerts. There is no definition given for persistent or reference to a special number. RA-05 clearly defines what will be reviewed and how frequently (every 3 days, every 7 days, etc.). By not locking down these two controls CSPs who choose VDR leave participants with nothing they can actually document and assessors with nothing they can actually test.

Comment 3: SC-13 and SI-05

Including SC-13 for historic CMVP modules closes a long time authorization gap. Updating SI-05 to specifically state EDs and BODs, adding the CISA link and requiring all responses to flow through FSI are improvements. The proposed language falls short by not defining what qualifies as an adequate FSI response as well as what the repercussion is for missing FSI timelines. Will most likely lead to wild variance from CSP to CSP.

Thank you for the opportunity to comment on this RFC.

documents.title: Rev5 questions and discussion on the Consolidated Rules for 2026 (or Legacy)
documents.text:
> I believe this was mentioned on a community update discussion but I'd like to confirm. There seems to be some confusion about when an annual assessment needs to start producing CR26 package materials (CPO, SDR, OCR) instead of a legacy Rev5 package (SAP, RET, SAR). Is it expected that all FedRAMP Annual Assessments that kickoff in 2027 should be against all CR26 requirements (all rules and controls/KSIs)? Is there a switch over date when the PMO will no longer accept Legacy FedRAMP Rev5 packages (SAP, RET, SAR etc) and the CSP can ensure their packages are what the PMO is expecting to maintain their certification(s)?
>
> If this is spelled out in the CR26 material, please let me know. I haven't found it.

Each ruleset has Maintaining Ongoing Certification and Grace Period Ends dates (previously "Maintain" and "Grace Ends"). These are all summarized and explained here for Rev5: https://www.fedramp.gov/2026/providers/updating/deadlines/rev5/

They land in a few different ways at a few different times because we expected some folks to invest in them differently. Some of them have explicit maintain dates and grace period end dates that are mandatory regardless of the FedRAMP independent assessment timing - cloud service providers will be expected to make significant changes to implement those. That includes the CCM rules for the OCR, which will be mandatory for everyone on April 2, 2027.

So if you start an assessment on July 31, 2027:

- Grace period has ended for AFC, SCG, MKT, VDR, VER, CMU, IEC, and SCN
- Grace period extends through the FedRAMP independent assessment (so it has to be implemented and included in it) for FRC, IVV, MAS, and CPO
- You can still hold off a bit longer before implementing CCM, CDS, and SDR. 

Those details shift a bit as the date shifts throughout the year. 

By the end of 2027 everything will be switched over for everyone no matter what except for CDS. 

(edit: removed incorrect statement confusing 2027-07-01 with 2027-01-01 for CPO)

documents.title: RFC-0030 FedRAMP Rev5 Security Controls Baseline Update for RA, SA, SC, SI, and SR Control Families
documents.text:
This RFC carries the most operational weight in the batch. The VDR pathway and cryptographic module guidance in particular will reshape how CSPs run their vulnerability and compliance programs.
RA-05 (Vulnerability Monitoring and Scanning), VDR Pathway:
The VDR pathway is the headline change across the entire RFC batch, and I support the direction. Moving from calendar based scanning to detection and response cadences reflects how mature security programs actually operate. A few concerns about the specifics:
The detection frequency ranges (every 7 days at Low to daily at High) with evaluation timelines compressed from 7 to 2 days are aggressive but achievable for CSPs with modern tooling. The question is what happens at the boundary. If a CSP detects a vulnerability on day 1 and evaluates it by day 2, the remediation timeline then varies by impact, exploitability, and internet reachability. That’s three variables producing a matrix of possible deadlines. Is FedRAMP publishing that matrix, or is the CSP expected to define its own remediation SLAs within guardrails? If the latter, the acceptable range of those guardrails needs to be specified; otherwise 3PAOs will interpret “reasonable” differently across engagements.
For CSPs not on the VDR pathway, the traditional monthly scanning cadence is maintained. But the RFC doesn’t address what happens when a CSP wants to transition from traditional to VDR midcycle. Is that a decision that takes effect at the next annual assessment? Can a CSP adopt VDR for specific system components while maintaining traditional scanning for others? Or is it all or nothing at the authorization boundary level?
SC-13 (Cryptographic Protections), Historical CMVP Modules:
Adding guidance for modules listed as “historical” in the CMVP database addresses a real pain point. CSPs have been caught in a bind where modules they deployed in good faith transition to historical status due to certificate expiration or algorithm deprecation, and the previous guidance was effectively “replace it,” which for embedded crypto modules in production infrastructure is a multiquarter effort, not a patch.
What’s the expected posture? If a module goes historical, is there a grace period to transition, or does the CSP need to document it as a POA&M immediately? And does the guidance distinguish between modules that went historical due to administrative expiration (vendor didn’t renew) versus algorithmic deprecation (the underlying crypto is actually weaker)? Those are very different risk profiles and should warrant different response timelines.
SI-05 (Security Alerts), CISA EDs and BODs:
Aligning with CISA Emergency Directives and Binding Operational Directives through the FSI process makes sense. One clarification: CISA directives are binding on federal agencies, not on commercial entities. When FedRAMP requires CSPs to comply with EDs and BODs via FSI response timelines, that’s FedRAMP extending CISA’s authority to CSPs through the authorization relationship. That’s a legitimate policy choice, but the RFC should be explicit about it rather than implying that EDs and BODs directly apply to CSPs. The legal basis matters for CSP counsel evaluating compliance obligations, and clarity here avoids unnecessary exchanges during assessments.
SR (Supply Chain Risk Management), No Changes:
Noted. Given the current emphasis on supply chain security across the federal government (EO 14028, CISA SBOM guidance, the C-SCRM requirements in NIST 800-161 Rev 1) the absence of any SR updates is surprising. Is FedRAMP planning a dedicated SR focused RFC, or is the assessment that the existing SR controls are adequate as is? Not requesting changes for the sake of changes, but the gap between federal supply chain policy momentum and the “no changes” here is worth acknowledging.

documents.title: General discussion and Q&A for RFCs related to Rev5 Updates (RFCs 0026, 0027, 0028, 0029, & 0030)
documents.text:
"Providers MUST share vulnerability information with all agency customers and FedRAMP using one of the following two processes:

Implementing the Vulnerability Detection and Response Balance Improvement Release for Rev5 (either in Beta or Wide Release); or

Sharing Operating System, Database, Web Application, Container, and Service Configuration Scans, at least monthly; AND sharing updated Plans of Action and Milestones (POA&Ms), at least monthly; AND sharing all scans performed by an Independent Assessor, at least annually."


I read the non-VDR path as explicitly requiring raw scan results. To be clear, right now we don't typically have to share raw scan results with all agencies. Just lead agencies. Most agencies lack the capabilities to parse all of our raw scan results anyways, to the point where even the lead agency doesn't do it. Personally, I think parsing by 3PAOs during assessments is validation enough, given that agencies are not equipped to handle such information. Can you clarify if the intent with these lines is to require raw scans be shared in rev5 with all agencies, and NOT in VDR? If so, it sounds like VDR is actually a step backwards for transparency, though an improvement in disclosure safety. I'd rather see the requirement for providing monthly or continuous raw vuln scans removed entirely, and they be artifacts of 3PAO review only, and disclaimers made that csps may redact necessary information from scan results to protect the system as well (even with 3PAOs), so long as level of risk is understood well enough for assessment.

documents.title: RFC-0027 FedRAMP Rev5 Security Controls Baseline Update for AC, AT, AU, CA, and CM Control Families
documents.text:
A few specific observations at the control level.
AC-10 (Concurrent Session Control): Limiting top level administrative accounts to one concurrent session at the High baseline makes sense as a security measure. The operational question is how this interacts with break glass procedures. If a critical incident requires two administrators to access the same service account simultaneously (one performing remediation while another monitors) does this control require denying the second session? If so, the incident response playbook and the access control policy are in direct tension. Consider adding language that addresses emergency access scenarios, or explicitly state whether break glass accounts are subject to this limit.
CA-05 (Plan of Action and Milestones): The differentiated timelines for BIR participants versus traditional processes are a good idea in principle. But the RFC introduces multiple acronyms (BIR, CCM, VDR, SCN) without a single place that maps them to concrete CSP obligations. A CSP reading CA-05 needs to cross reference RFC-0026, the BIR guidance, the VDR framework, and the CCM playbook just to understand what frequency applies to them. This isn’t a comment about the policy; it’s about navigability. Consider a decision tree or lookup table: “If you are [pathway], your CA-05 cadence is [X].”
CM-06 and CM-07 (Configuration Settings / Least Functionality): Both now reference the Security Configuration Guidelines (SCG). This is the third RFC in the current batch that introduces SCG as a dependency, as it also appears in AT-03 and AC-02. What’s the status of the SCG itself? If it’s still in draft or hasn’t been published, CSPs are being asked to comment on controls that reference a document they can’t yet read. Please confirm whether the SCG is published and where to find it, or clarify the timeline for its release relative to these control updates taking effect.
CM-08 (System Component Inventory): Exempting VDR and CCM BIR participants from monthly reporting is a meaningful burden reduction, but only if the alternative reporting cadence is clearly defined somewhere. The RFC says what VDR participants don’t have to do (monthly reports) without specifying what they do have to do instead. If the answer is “see the BIR guidance,” a cross reference would help.
CM-12(1): The RFC adds an undefined parameter referencing “CP-2(8) [essential].” This appears to be a copy and paste from a different control family (Contingency Planning). Is this intentional cross referencing or an error? If intentional, the relationship between information location tracking and essential contingency planning functions should be explained.

documents.title: Machine-readable intake of CISA BODs?
documents.text:
In the new [FedRAMP Vulnerability Detection and Response Standard](https://github.com/FedRAMP/docs/blob/main/markdown/FRMR.VDR.vulnerability-detection-and-response.md#frr-vdr-tf-02) it calls out remediating Known Exploited Vulnerabilities as required by CISA Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 22-01. I know CISA publishes KEV data in a machine-readable, easy to ingest format (JSON here: https://github.com/cisagov/kev-data and API available)

Is anyone aware of a similar place or process to ingest CISA BODs other than web scraping the HTML pages here: https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/directives ?

Curious if anyone has a way to automate bringing in BODs or if CISA is planning to publish their BODs in a similar machine-readable format to the KEVs and [CSAF advisories](https://github.com/cisagov/CSAF/tree/develop) they put out. 

While we are bringing in machine-readable evidence, vulnerability data, and FedRAMP 20x requirements it would be nice to bring in the CISA BODs as well. As far as I'm aware there isn't an explicit FedRAMP requirement for CSPs to meet all CISA BODs but they are mandatory for agencies... and a good idea for everyone else 

-- Isaac Teuscher (Paramify)

documents.text:
[VDR-TFR-NMV](https://www.fedramp.gov/2026/reference/vulnerability-detection-and-response/#non-machine-verification-and-validation) states "Providers MUST verify and validate the status of non-machine-based information resources at least once every 3 months" and once you break down the definitions, I'm interpreting the requirement as:

"CSPs must verify and validate documentation, personnel, and budgets every 3 months"
- Where verification effectively means: "collecting some sort of evidence that documentation, personnel records, and budgets are actually being followed" and
- Where validation effectively means: "checking that the collected evidence shows documentation personnel records and budgets are being followed correctly"

Is this an accurate interpretation of the requirements involved? And while the -1 controls in each control family in Rev5 would revert back to the ODPs, wouldn't this effectively create a new and different requirement for the policies and procedures (as well as various other documents)? Instead of reviewing them every 1/3 years, now they'd need to be verified and validated every 3 months. And then finally, if all of the above is true, would it make sense to notate this on the "Rev5 Control Guidance" page, given there's no direct mention that a VDR rule is impacting documentation?

documents.title: Balancing FedRAMP Rev5 against improvements to FedRAMP 20x
documents.text:
@pete-gov Appreciate the response, I think my original feedback wasn't as clear as it should have been. I wasn't focused on the export from the vulnerability tracking system; I was focused on the level of detail that has to be captured in the tracking system in the first place to satisfy these reporting requirements.

> There shouldn't be anything new created for this report if the VDR rules are being followed.

So my feedback is about the VDR rules themselves 

That's still too much per-vuln detail, particularly at container scale, which was the focus of my feedback. A medium to larger CSP can easily run 1000+ distinct containers. Even with minimal base images and aggressive stripping, you still take dependencies for things to function, and a robust container scanning process covering both OS-level and dependency vulns produces volume that grows quickly.

It also gets more complex when the same CVE shows up in different contexts. Just because one team has evaluated a CVE in one container doesn't mean the evaluation transfers to a different team's product in a different container. For base image vulns you can often get a "global answer," but that's not the case for most vulns, each context needs its own review.

So the suggestion isn't about reducing what gets exported; it's about simplifying the human-in-the-loop step so the resulting information is higher fidelity. Does the government really need each of these tracked as discrete structured fields, or would a single "justification" of why a vuln isn't yet remediated suffice for the narrative-judgment elements? In my experience, agencies primarily want to understand the "why", the justification for why remediation hasn't happened yet and what compensating factors are in place. The objective fields (tracking ID, detection time, reachability, etc.) absolutely should stay structured, that part of your response I fully agree with.

That said, this is just one CSP's perspective. I'd be genuinely curious to hear how other medium-to-large CSPs running most of their production workloads in containers have experienced the VDR BIR.

documents.title: Rev5 questions and discussion on the Consolidated Rules for 2026 (or Legacy)
documents.text:
FedRAMP team,

We believe there's a little ambiguity in how the VDR-TFR-PVR remediation clock is determined when a vulnerability is evaluated. 

The text in question under VDR-TFR-PVR:
"Providers with Class C Certifications SHOULD partially mitigate vulnerabilities, fully mitigate vulnerabilities, or remediate vulnerabilities to a lower Potential Agency Impact N-rating within the timeframes from evaluation shown below, factoring for the current Potential Agency Impact N-rating. . . ."

**Is the deadline for remediation or PAIN downgrades based on the initial evaluation date? Or is the deadline recalculated based on movement to a lower PAIN rating (or even LEV/IRV value)?**

As an example for Rev5 Class C providers:
- Let's say we have a PAIN-3, LEV+IRV vulnerability detected on 9/1 and evaluated on 9/2. 
- This deadline to act on this vulnerability is 16 days from evaluation, which is would 9/18.
- 16 days later on 9/18, we apply a mitigation that makes it PAIN-2, LEV+NIRV, which has a deadline of 128 days.
- Is the new deadline 9/18 + 128 days based on the movement to a lower PAIN rating? or always based on the original evaluation 9/2 + 128 days?

Appreciate any clarity you all could provide here.

Ah, my bad, I checked it briefly and focused on the copy/pastes from the VDR. The original doesn't say anything about containers either, so nothing about container requirements is changing here. This set of proposed changes might be overcome by events due to the changes planned in [NTC-0009](https://www.fedramp.gov/notices/0009/) either way, it's basically just bridging current requirements until July 2027.

documents.title: RFC-0027 FedRAMP Rev5 Security Controls Baseline Update for AC, AT, AU, CA, and CM Control Families
documents.text:
# RFC-0027 FedRAMP Rev5 Security Controls Baseline Update for AC, AT, AU, CA, and CM Control Families

❓   **Please note that FedRAMP will not answer questions in this thread as it is reserved for public comment. If you would like to ask a question or generally discuss this RFC informally, please use the [General discussion and Q&A for RFCs related to Rev5 Updates (RFCs 0026, 0027, 0028, 0029, & 0030) thread](https://github.com/FedRAMP/community/discussions/129). Thank you!**

**Status:** Closed
**Start Date:** March 19, 2026
**Closing Date:** April 22, 2026
---

## **Summary**

This is a technical RFC that proposes updates to the Additional FedRAMP Security Technical Controls Requirements and Guidance for FedRAMP Rev5 baselines.

To save space and to limit the breadth of a single RFC, this technical document shows only the proposed changes to the current baseline document and is restricted to a few control families. If verbiage is being updated, only the specific wording that is to be changed is identified in the old verbiage section. If the verbiage to be added is not replacing previous verbiage, but being added, it will be identified as “NEW” in the old verbiage section.  

Since this spreadsheet covers hundreds of controls across multiple tabs and sections, only those specific controls, sections, and tabs identified are being proposed for updates.  If it is not mentioned below, changes are NOT being proposed.  

**Commenters are advised to please mention specific controls in their comments\!**

This RFC addresses controls in the following families:

* Access Control (AC)  
* Awareness and Training (AT)  
* Audit and Accountability (AU)  
* Assessment, Authorization and Monitoring (CA)  
* Configuration Management (CM)

## **Motivation**

Many Rev5 FedRAMP Requirements and Guidance statements are based on outdated approaches that predated the release of the FedRAMP Authorization Act and M-24-15. This set of Requirements and Guidance needs a refresh to match FedRAMP’s current rules and approach.

The updates formalized after this RFC will be included in the FedRAMP Consolidated Rules for 2026\. That set of rules will be valid until December 31, 2028\. FedRAMP will provide a transition plan for adopting any new guidance that will enable cloud service providers to update their approach as part of their annual assessment as appropriate.

These changes are designed to lower the burden for cloud service providers and eliminate previous pain points.

Additionally, NIST released 800-53 Rev 5.2.0 in August of 2025\.  While this update was minor, control updates from NIST will require updates to FedRAMP Security Control Baseline in order to reflect this update. These changes will happen without public comment through FedRAMP since these are direct reflections of NIST changes. As subsequent iterations of the FedRAMP Security Control Baseline are published, it is FedRAMP’s intent only to carry over the following information from NIST 800-53; Control Family, Control Name, and Control ID. Following this will be FedRAMP-Defined Assignment / Selection Parameters and additional FedRAMP Requirements and Guidance.

## **Proposed Changes to Access Control Family**

This section contains proposed changes to the FedRAMP Requirements and Guidance section for each of these controls.

### **AC-02: Account Management**

**Tabs Affected:** High Baseline, Moderate Baseline, Low Baseline  
**Sections Affected:** Additional FedRAMP Requirements and Guidance  
**Current Verbiage:** NEW  
**Proposed Change**: a. Accounts types should align to those accounts identified within the FedRAMP Secure Configuration Guidance where applicable.  
**Rationale:** Alignment with the FedRAMP Secure Configuration Guidance (SCG).

### **AC-10: Concurrent Session Control**

**Tabs Affected:** High Baseline  
**Sections Affected:** FedRAMP-Defined Assignment / Selection Parameters  
**Current Verbiage:** AC-10-2 \[three (3) sessions for privileged access and two (2) sessions for non-privileged access\]  
**Proposed Change:** AC-10-2 \[one (1) session for Top-level administrative, three (3) sessions for privileged access, and two (2) sessions for non-privileged access\]  
**Rationale:** Alignment with the FedRAMP Secure Configuration Guidance (SCG).

## **Proposed Changes to Awareness and Training Family**

This section contains proposed changes to the FedRAMP Requirements and Guidance section for each of these controls.

### **AT-03 Role-based Training:**

**Tabs Affected:** High Baseline, Moderate Baseline, Low Baseline  
**Sections Affected:** Additional FedRAMP Requirements and Guidance  
**Current Verbiage:** NEW  
**Proposed Change:** a. Top-Level Administrative and Privileged Accounts Secure Configuration Guidance must be included as part of role based training where applicable.  
Rationale: Alignment with the FedRAMP Secure Configuration Guidance (SCG)**.**

## **Proposed Changes to Audit and Accountability Family**

No changes are being proposed

## **Proposed Changes to Assessment, Authorization, and Monitoring Family**

This section contains proposed changes to the FedRAMP Requirements and Guidance section for each of these controls.

### **CA-05: Plan of Action and Milestones**

**Tabs Affected:** Low Baseline, Moderate Baseline, High Baseline  
**Sections Affected:** FedRAMP-Defined Assignment / Selection Parameters  
**Current Verbiage:** CA-5 (b) \[at least monthly\]  
**Proposed Change:** CA-5 (b) \[at least monthly for traditional FedRAMP Processes\] \[every three months if opting into Collaborative Continuous Monitoring BIR\] \[Monthly Activity Report in lieu is due every month if opting into Vulnerability and Detection Response BIR\]  
**Rationale:** Updated based on BIRs

### **CA-05: Plan of Action and Milestones**

**Tabs Affected:** Low Baseline, Moderate Baseline, High Baseline  
**Sections Affected:** Additional FedRAMP Requirements and Guidance  
**Current Verbiage:** CA-5 Requirement: POA\&Ms must be provided at least monthly. CA-5 Guidance: Reference FedRAMP-POAM-Template  
**Proposed Change:** CA-5 Requirement: POA\&Ms must be provided at least monthly for traditional FedRAMP processes. For those opting into Collaborative Continuous Monitoring BIR, Ongoing Authorization Reports must be provided every three months. For those opting into Vulnerability Detection and Response BIR, a Monthly Activity Report is also required.  
CA-5 Guidance: Reference FedRAMP-POAM-Template \[traditional\], CCM-OAR-AVL for those opting into Collaborative Continuous Monitoring BIR, and VDR-TFR-MHR for those opting into Vulnerability Detection and Response BIR  
**Rationale:** Updated based on BIRs

### **CA-05: Plan of Action and Milestones**

**Tabs Affected:** Low Baseline, Moderate Baseline, High Baseline  
**Sections Affected:** Continuous Monitoring Periodicity  
**Current Verbiage:** CA-5 (b) \[at least monthly\]  
**Proposed Change:** CA-5 (b) \[at least monthly for traditional FedRAMP Processes\] \[Ongoing Activity Report in lieu is due every three months if opting into Collaborative Continuous Monitoring BIR\] \[Monthly Activity Report in lieu is due every month if opting into Vulnerability and Detection Response BIR\]  
**Rationale:** Updated based on BIRs

### **CA-06: Authorization**

**Tabs Affected:** Low Baseline, Moderate Baseline, High Baseline  
**Sections Affected:** FedRAMP-Defined Assignment / Selection Parameters  
**Current Verbiage:** CA-6 (e) \[in accordance with OMB A-130 requirements or when a significant change occurs\]  
**Proposed Change:** CA-6 (e) \[in accordance with OMB A-130 requirements or when a significant change occurs for those NOT participating in the SCN BIR\]   
**Rationale:** Updated based on BIRs

### **CA-07: Continuous Monitoring**

**Tabs Affected:** Low Baseline, Moderate Baseline, High Baseline  
**Sections Affected:** Additional FedRAMP Requirements and Guidance  
**Current Verbiage:** CA-7 Requirement: Operating System, Database, Web Application, Container, and Service Configuration Scans: at least monthly. All scans performed by Independent Assessor: at least annually.  
CA-7 Requirement: CSOs with more than one agency ATO must implement a collaborative Continuous Monitoring (ConMon) approach described in the FedRAMP Continuous Monitoring Playbook. This requirement applies to CSOs authorized via the Agency path as each agency customer is responsible for performing ConMon oversight.   
CA-7 Guidance: FedRAMP does not provide a template for the Continuous Monitoring Plan. CSPs should reference the continuous monitoring guidance provided in the FedRAMP Continuous Monitoring Playbook when developing the Continuous Monitoring Plan.  
**Proposed Change:** Changes to CA-7 are being proposed in RFC-0026 Clarifying CA-7 Continuous Monitoring Expectations for Rev5 Providers, under the “CA-7 Additional FedRAMP Requirements and Guidance” section.  Any comments associated with CA-7 should be submitted under RFC-0026.  
**Rationale:** Updated based on BIRs and implementation issues within agencies.

## **Proposed Changes to Configuration Management Family**

This section contains proposed changes to the FedRAMP Requirements and Guidance section for each of these controls.

### **CM-06: Configuration Settings**

**Tabs Affected:** Low Baseline, Moderate Baseline, High Baseline  
**Sections Affected:** Additional FedRAMP Requirements and Guidance  
**Current Verbiage:** CM-6 (a) Requirement 1: The service provider shall use the DoD STIGs or Center for Internet Security guidelines to establish configuration settings;  
CM-6 (a) Requirement 2: The service provider shall ensure that checklists for configuration settings are Security Content Automation Protocol (SCAP) validated or SCAP compatible (if validated checklists are not available).  
**Proposed Change:** CM-6 (a) Requirement 1:  The service provider shall use Security Configuration Guidelines (See CM-6) to establish instructions on how to securely access, configure, operate, and decommission top-level administrative accounts within the cloud service offering.  This MUST include explanations of security-related settings that can be operated only by top-level administrative accounts and their security implications. This SHOULD include explanations of security-related settings that can be operated only by privileged accounts and their security implications.  
CM-6 (a) Requirement 2:  The service provider shall use the DoD STIGs or Center for Internet Security guidelines to establish configuration settings;  
CM-6 (a) Requirement 3: The service provider shall ensure that checklists for configuration settings are Security Content Automation Protocol (SCAP) validated or SCAP compatible (if validated checklists are not available).  
**Rationale:** Updated based on SCG BIR

### **CM-07: Least Functionality**

**Tabs Affected:** Low Baseline, Moderate Baseline, High Baseline  
**Sections Affected:** Additional FedRAMP Requirements and Guidance  
**Current Verbiage:** CM-7 (b) Requirement: The service provider shall use Security guidelines (See CM-6) to establish list of prohibited or restricted functions, ports, protocols, and/or services or establishes its own list of prohibited or restricted functions, ports, protocols, and/or services if STIGs or CIS is not available.  
**Proposed Change:** CM-7 (b) Requirement: The service provider shall use Security Configuration Guidelines (See CM-6) to establish instructions on how to securely access, configure, operate, and decommission top-level administrative accounts within the cloud service offering as well as provide a list of prohibited or restricted functions, ports, protocols, and/or services or establishes its own list of prohibited or restricted functions, ports, protocols, and/or services if STIGs or CIS is not available.  
**Rationale:** Updated based on SCG BIR

### **CM-08: System Component Inventory**

**Tabs Affected:** Low Baseline, Moderate Baseline, High Baseline  
**Sections Affected:** FedRAMP-Defined Assignment / Selection Parameters   
**Current Verbiage:** CM-8 (b) \[at least monthly\]          
**Proposed Change:** CM-8 (b) \[at least monthly for those CSPs following traditional Rev 5 processes\]. Those CSPs participating in VDR and CCM BIRs are exempt from this formal reporting requirement.    
**Rationale:** Updated based on BIRs

### **CM-08: System Component Inventory**

**Tabs Affected:** Low Baseline, Moderate Baseline, High Baseline  
**Sections Affected:** Additional FedRAMP Requirements and Guidance  
**Current Verbiage:** CM-8 Requirement: must be provided at least monthly or when there is a change.  
**Proposed Change:** CM-8 Requirement: must be provided at least monthly or when there is a change for those CSPs following traditional Rev 5 processes.  Those CSPs participating in VDR and CCM BIRs are exempt from this formal reporting requirement.    
**Rationale:** Updated based on BIRs

### **CM-12: Information Location**

**Tabs Affected:** Moderate Baseline, High Baseline

You are correct, only rules with applicability for Rev5 would have to be met in a Rev5 Certification.

ALL 15 Rulesets (AFC, CDS, VDR, etc.) are applicable to both Rev5 & 20x. The big difference is Controls (Rev5) vs KSIs (20x).

documents.text:
1. **Define key terms that affect compliance**
   - “Persistently,” “representative samples,” “likely to drift,” and “evaluate” are high-impact terms. Consider concise definitions or pointers to the authoritative VDR sections so CSPs and 3PAOs don’t interpret them differently.
2. **Minimize ambiguity for 3PAO testing**
   - Where you introduce alternative constructs (e.g., “assessment scope” for MAS vs “established boundary” for traditional), add a short statement describing what evidence 3PAOs should use (e.g., inventory source of truth, sampling methodology, scan coverage proof, and evaluation SLA evidence).

documents.title: RFC-0014 Phase Two Security Indicators
documents.text:
Hi FedRAMP team, getting my comments in here. Overall, exceptional work. I have a comment specifically regarding KSI-PIY-01. The current wording of "Generate inventories of information resources from authoritative sources" is too vague. Normally I am a fan of open-ended standards that aren't overly prescriptive, but in this case I'd recommend tweaking the language to explicitly recommend the use of Package URL (PURL) format where applicable in order to ward off potential automation-breaking problems. The update looks like this:

KSI-PIY-01: Generate inventories of information resources from authoritative sources. For software components, SHOULD use Package URL (PURL) format to enable precise identification, version tracking, and supply chain risk management.

The VDR standard creates a dependency chain on inventory: KSI-PIY-01 (inventory) → SBOM generation → PURL identifiers → VDR compliance (i.e., KSI-MLA-03). Making inventory identifiers open ended would unravel this automation chain, making it virtually impossible to align on meaningful "apples to apples" metrics for many of the KSIs.

Similarly, for the SCN standard there is a dependency chain on inventory as well: KSI-PIY-01 (Inventory with PURL) → Change Detection & Categorization → SCN Compliance (FRR-SCN-03) → Automated Machine-Readable Reporting (FRR-SCN-08). Without a means of precisely identifying versioned components, it is virtually impossible to adequately scope changes at scale and validate their security comprehensively in an automated manner, undermining the SCN standard's core premise of agile deployment without advance government approval.

documents.title: Rev5 questions and discussion on the Consolidated Rules for 2026 (or Legacy)
documents.text:
Question on VER-EVA-EPA. The N4 and N5 definitions turn on how many agencies are affected, and FRD-PAI says the impact is cumulative across all agencies using the service. So does a vulnerability on a shared resource (say a core database that several agencies sit on) rate N4 or N5 because of breadth, even if the hit to any one agency would only be N3?

And is the expectation that we work that out from the inventory, which resources serve which agencies, rather than estimate it per vulnerability by hand? We build tooling and want to compute this the way you intend.

documents.title: RFC-0026 Clarifying CA-7 Continuous Monitoring Expectations for Rev5 Providers
documents.text:
Removing the JAB references is overdue and welcome. That language has been a source of confusion since M-24-15 dropped and the practical effect was CSPs explaining to agencies why their authorization letters referenced an entity that no longer existed in the same capacity.
The substantive question is about the enforcement structure. The tiered corrective action model, notification escalating through remediation plans to potential certification revocation after five failures in 12 months, sounds reasonable on paper. But the details matter.
What constitutes a “failure”? If a CSP conducts a collaborative monitoring meeting with 47 of 48 agency customers because one agency’s ISSO is unresponsive for three months, is that a gap? The requirement says CSPs must conduct recurring meetings with “all agency customers.” CSPs don’t control agency participation. If the obligation is to offer and document the attempt, that’s workable. If it’s to ensure meetings actually occur, that shifts agency accountability onto CSPs without giving them any enforcement mechanism of their own. Please clarify whether “conduct” means “facilitate and document good faith attempts” or “ensure completion.”
VDR vs. traditional pathway clarity. The RFC frames VDR and traditional monthly scanning as parallel options, but it’s unclear whether a CSP can choose one pathway globally or whether individual agency customers can demand one or the other. If Agency A wants VDR and Agency B insists on traditional monthly POA&M updates, the CSP is running both, which isn’t a reduction in burden but an increase. Is the pathway selection a CSP level decision, or does each agency customer relationship get its own pathway?
The grace period is well designed, effective immediately on publication with no corrective action through December 31, 2026, and enforcement starting January 2027. That’s the right structure. One ask: consider publishing example scenarios during the grace period that illustrate what FedRAMP considers compliant vs. noncompliant under CA-7, similar to how the IRS publishes revenue rulings. Real world examples calibrate expectations far better than control language alone, and the grace period is the natural window to do that before enforcement begins.
3PAO treatment of gaps as high impact findings. This is a significant change with cost implications. Annual assessments already run six figures for complex environments. If 3PAOs must now treat any CA-7 gap as high impact, that expands remediation timelines, potentially delays reauthorization, and increases assessment costs, all for a control that’s fundamentally about process cadence rather than technical vulnerability. Is the high impact classification mandatory regardless of context, or can 3PAOs exercise judgment about severity based on the nature and duration of the gap?

documents.text: I'd like to close this thread with the release of the Consolidated Rules for 2026, but I also acknowledge there are some very thoughtful posts that I still need to respond to that I simply haven't been able to dedicate appropriate time to over the past few weeks (@cpelote @mblanco474 @kcarr91). We're going to fold some of this feedback into FAQs on https://help.fedramp.gov so that this content is captured properly, and I'm going to try to carve out some time to address your VDR comments specifically this Friday prior to closing the thread. Thank you so much for the ongoing discussion!

documents.title: General discussion and Q&A for RFCs related to Rev5 Updates (RFCs 0026, 0027, 0028, 0029, & 0030)
documents.text:
Thanks, I must be context switching too much in the small amount of time I have to pop into GitHub and pulled up the wrong RFC. Thanks for your patience and providing that. 

Yes, this update to CA-7 would require sharing of scan data with all customers and FedRAMP; this is already expected, and folks upload this info to their shared folder. We've even audited it to monitor usage, but former JAB authorized services used to send that data just to FR for distribution and High impact services control access to their data in a way that FR doesn't audit it as effectively. The update isn't really intended to change requirements as much to clarify that things should work for former-JAB services the same way they work for everyone else, which is that agencies that want to see this should be able to. Even if they are never reviewed, they **can** be reviewed as needed. I'm aware of at least one instance where an OIG dinged an agency for not verifying integrity and accuracy of the raw scan logs on a monthly basis. Subject to change based on feedback of course.

Separately, the VDR is a more modern approach that resets the expectations for the exact reasons you've outlined and others - raw scan logs are not generally useful or used by agencies for the purpose of "double checking" or "verifying" the integrity and accuracy of decisions made by cloud service providers and they aren't necessarily of value to do that anyway. The additional transparency required by other areas of the VDR offsets the security blanket vibes of having access to raw scan data.

documents.title: Rev5 questions and discussion on the Consolidated Rules for 2026 (or Legacy)
documents.text:
> For long standing vulnerabilities with a previously agency-acknowledged POA&M remediation milestone, can a newly evaluated PAIN-based remediation deadline supersede those commitments, or must the CSP obtain agency concurrence before revising the existing milestones?

Most historical "long standing" POA&M milestones are simply an Accepted Vulnerability in the VDR, and can just be moved over and tracked as such. 

Edit to add: There's no FR requirement about a cloud service obtaining concurrence from an agency customer to accept vulnerabilities/etc. anymore as there's no JAB/sponsor after initial Certification. There may be existing contracts/agreements with particular customers about such things though!

documents.title: Rev5 questions and discussion on the Consolidated Rules for 2026 (or Legacy)
documents.text:
> Can the reported detection time be when the finding enters our evaluation process (the pull), provided the pull cadence is documented, instead of the scanner's first-seen date?

It does not seem accurate to track detection time as the time that detection data is transferred to or processed by a system later in the pipeline than the detection system. This would not make a lot of sense, and monitoring these timelines without factoring for the delay between detection and initial processing would give you an incomplete picture of your own vulnerability detection and response.

> If first-seen is expected, is it acceptable during the transition to report the gap between first-seen and evaluation and justify not meeting the 5-day VER-TFR-EVU SHOULD, while we work toward a shorter cadence?

The VDR-TFR-PVR (Mitigation and Remediation Expectations) timelines are from evaluation, not detection. You should still try to get timelines between detection and evaluation down to as close to zero as possible.

> Should these resources count as not likely to drift, with changes made through the IaC pipeline treated as updates to the intended state rather than drift?

Your engineering team can and should answer this question for you, based on your specific deployment and management process. In many situations like you describe it would be accurate to classify those resources as unlikely to drift, but that's not a guarantee - in other situations there may be lots of bespoke maintenance happening outside the control pipelines. 🤷 

> Some shared platforms that are core to our infrastructure are on vendor-supported versions, but a fix is only available in a new major version. Because many services depend on these platforms, a major upgrade needs extensive compatibility testing to avoid breaking dependent functionality, which typically can make it months of planned work. Is it appropriate to report these as accepted vulnerabilities with a reviewed category explanation (upgrade and compatibility risk, testing plan, planned upgrade date, compensating controls) plus a per-asset note? We would keep KEVs and internet-reachable likely exploitable findings outside this approach.

You should mitigate those vulnerabilities instead of just accepting them. It's highly irresponsible to leave likely exploitable vulnerabilities open to exploitation simply because a new vendor patch isn't available yet. You certainly can accept those vulnerabilities but that would definitely show a lack of intentional security approach to managing risk in the system. 

In the old vulnerability management process, FedRAMP did not consider mitigation as a viable path - that has changed entirely, and mitigation is now expected by default. If you choose not to mitigate vulnerabilities then at the very least you need to explain the risk and potential impact to the customer.

> If a KEV is fully mitigated and rated NO but not yet remediated by its CISA due date, should it be reported as overdue? Is a documented mitigation an acceptable justification for the SHOULD, or does BOD 26-04 expect remediation regardless?

CISA doesn't really play the mitigation game with KEVs. A fully mitigated KEV still needs to be remediated in 14 days.

documents.title: Q&A and casual open discussion on RFC-0012 (CVM)
documents.text:
Regarding FRR-CVM-03: "Providers MUST make vulnerability reports available to all necessary parties in similar human-readable and compatible machine-readable formats, including at least FedRAMP, CISA, and all agency customers." I'm curious to know what are the compatible machine-readable formats? STIX/TAXII v2.1 or are there other desired machine-readable formats beyond just XML, CSV, and JSON? I'm thinking about structured formats such as:

- Vulnerability Exploitability eXchange (VEX)
- Vulnerability Disclosure Reports (VDR)
- Open Vulnerability and Assessment Language (OVAL)
- Security Content Automation Protocol (SCAP)
- Common Weakness Enumeration (CWE)

Lastly, I'm curious to know where things sit with adding NIST OSCAL as a requirement versus nice-to-have.

documents.title: 20x questions and discussion on the Consolidated Rules for 2026
documents.text:
There does not have to be any interaction between N0 and Accepted Vulnerabilities. A cloud service provider may choose to accept the risk of a PAIN5 vulnerability. 

> If a vulnerability remains detectable but has been fully mitigated such that its likely agency impact is N0, does VER-TFR-MAV still require it to be categorized as an Accepted Vulnerability after 192 days, or does full mitigation satisfy the requirement regardless of continued detection?

Vulnerabilities should live on as a tracked vulnerability until they are remediated. Even a fully mitigated vulnerability that has been accepted needs to be tracked in case there's a future circumstance where it comes into play.

Remember that fully mitigated means it's still there, you can still see it. Remediated means it's gone. Remediation is the only true end state for tracking a vulnerability.

documents.title: Balancing FedRAMP Rev5 against improvements to FedRAMP 20x
documents.text:
I know I'm tardy to the party, but I have a question about the "Optional" BIRs with the phrase "Providers MUST plan to address all requirements and recommendations in this process by the end of the Open Beta on May 22, 2026."  

I worry I am being too pedantic, but does this mean that ADS, VDR, and CCM will be Mandatory for all Rev 5 Authorized Providers after the Open Beta closes, that CSPs will need to have plans in place, or that they remain truly optional after 22 May?

documents.title: RFC-0014 Phase Two Security Indicators
documents.text:
For public clarification, the proposed Key Security Indicators do not stand alone for FedRAMP 20x Authorization - providers must meet [all other relevant standards](https://www.fedramp.gov/20x/standards) including [those currently out for RFC](https://www.fedramp.gov/rfcs/) when they are finalized. FedRAMP deliberately removed KSIs or avoided adding KSIs that are part of other FedRAMP requirements.

Human-led penetration testing and red teaming is part of the definition of [Vulnerability Detection](https://github.com/FedRAMP/docs/blob/main/markdown/FRMR.FRD.fedramp-definitions.md#frd-all-21) as required by the Vulnerability Detection and Response standard, implemented in KSI-MLA-03 (though you may note there is a typo in the name of the VDR standard in the KSI). In short, penetration testing has moved to part of ongoing maintenance rather than one-time annual assessments.
