documents.title: Balancing FedRAMP Rev5 against improvements to FedRAMP 20x
documents.text:
> That's still too much per-vuln detail, particularly at container scale, which was the focus of my feedback. A medium to larger CSP can easily run 1000+ distinct containers. Even with minimal base images and aggressive stripping, you still take dependencies for things to function, and a robust container scanning process covering both OS-level and dependency vulns produces volume that grows quickly.

You're definitely tracking all of that on your side, so you'll have all that information available - but I totally agree that reporting all of this in detail is messy and undesirable. [VDR-EVA-GRV (Group Vulnerabilities)](https://preview.fedramp.gov/2026/providers/rev5/rules/vulnerability-detection-and-response/#group-vulnerabilities) is intended to provide that middle layer to reduce cruft in reporting and is designed expressly to allow flexibility by the CSP.

For containers in that situation, you would never need to scan all 1000 either - you presumably know every aspect of what is going into them on deployment based on a build setup and can establish guardrails to ensure they are not likely to drift during use. You can then entirely avoid the need to ever scan the containers by redeploying them within the monthly timeframe, or by using sampling to scan a limited number of containers. If you have 1000 unique containers then that's a design issue. ;)

End result is that in most situations, regular vulnerability detection and response reporting for a 1000 container environment is likely going to be whittled down to 1-5 rows of reporting data based on grouping, and those reports will generally be very simple.

> It also gets more complex when the same CVE shows up in different contexts. Just because one team has evaluated a CVE in one container doesn't mean the evaluation transfers to a different team's product in a different container. For base image vulns you can often get a "global answer," but that's not the case for most vulns, each context needs its own review.

Yes, that's certainly something we expect, within grouping/sampling. You can't just ignore evaluating something because you have a lot of different somethings. ;) There are lots of ways to establish technical guardrails to reduce the effort and impact here though, and the VDR encourages that.

Some re-architecture will be necessary to optimize the flexibility the VDR gives you, but we think that's going to be in your best interest in the long run. You can short-circuit a lot of evaluation via technical controls in advance, and would want to get to a place where "containers that have label X can never have an internet-reachable vulnerability" etc.

> So the suggestion isn't about reducing what gets exported; it's about simplifying the human-in-the-loop step so the resulting information is higher fidelity. Does the government really need each of these tracked as discrete structured fields, or would a single "justification" of why a vuln isn't yet remediated suffice for the narrative-judgment elements? 

We definitely want the information to be high-fidelity for humans, and hope that extensive grouping and sampling will address a lot of that. Reviewing a vulnerability report with 10-15 rows of detailed information will be a huge improvement for customers over the current situation of thousands and thousands of individual scan issues to parse through.

> In my experience, agencies primarily want to understand the "why", the justification for why remediation hasn't happened yet and what compensating factors are in place. 

Agreed! The reporting requirements serve two major purposes - the first is to provide this information to agencies as that's the most important critical stuff, which is why we want it condensed by group and sorted into simple fields.

The second reason we require detailed reporting, and all of the additional fields, is for the CSP to demonstrate that they are following a complete internal process to perform Vulnerability Detection and Response and showcase the effectiveness of that process. Most customers will not be concerned with this on a day-to-day basis, but it will play a significant role in both initial authorization and annual re-authorizations.

It also creates a competitive security marketplace that allows past performance metrics to be included in comparisons between vendors for the government. For example, given two similar offerings, an agency might be willing to pay more to adopt an offering that consistently demonstrates a clean, quick, and effective VDR process in their historical metrics over one that sneaks in consistently under the maximum timeframes.

In short, this is one of the areas we've adapted Rev5 to align more with the tenets of 20x - the government wants to see actual performance metrics of your security program, tracked over time, for effective decision making and awareness. Rev5 does not provide this in any meaningful way, and would quickly become unusable when compared to 20x if we did not require providers to adopt some additional metrics into their reporting.

documents.title: RFC-0026 Clarifying CA-7 Continuous Monitoring Expectations for Rev5 Providers
documents.text:
The following public comment was received via email from Salesforce on Wed April 22: I am copy/pasting into the public comment record on their behalf as required by the FedRAMP public comment process. This is not an endorsement of the commenter or the content within the comment. This was converted from a table to markdown, apologies for any formatting issues. Text should all be intact. --- | Requirement_ID | Title/Section | Salesforce Comment | |----------------|------------------------------|--------------------| | RV5-CA07-VLN | CA-07: Continuous Monitoring | _"Sharing Operating System, Database, Web Application, Container, and Service Configuration Scans, at least monthly; AND sharing updated Plans of Action and Milestones (POA&Ms), at least monthly; AND sharing all scans performed by an Independent Assessor, at least annually."_

**Concern:** Requiring monthly raw scans under RV5-CA07-VLN creates a security risk inconsistent with the VDR BIR, which prioritizes risk-contextualized reporting over sensitive data exposure (VDR-RPT-NID). Sharing of raw scan files has historically been limited to JAB authorized service offerings due to the PMO's ConMon support through monthly summary reports which was then disseminated to Agencies. Salesforce has major concerns over increasing the sharing radius of this data:

- Providing raw scan data on a broad scale is inefficient and perilous, as it lacks necessary context while simultaneously increasing the attack surface and risk of sensitive data exposure. Further do Agency customers have the tooling to process and accurately digest these files? Many agency customers struggle to accurately read and digest our monthly POA&M.
- Raw scans provide no actionable value to agency customers and require processing to accuratly understand risk and security status. Providing customers with context-rich summaries ensures that agencies receive actionable insights that they can actually act on.
- Lack of assurance that Agency customers will limit further sharing and adequately protect this sensitive scan data.

**Recommendation:** The sharing of raw scans should not be a default requirement, instead this should be an optional requirement. CSPs that feel comfortable in providing raw scans to agency customers should feel empowered and this should potentially be reflected on the FedRAMP Marketplace. |

documents.title: Rev5 questions and discussion on the Consolidated Rules for 2026 (or Legacy)
documents.text:
> On VER-EVA-AIA, is it fair to say that the user interaction metric from CVSS 3.x/4 could be used to say that a (CVE-type) vulnerability is not automatable? 

I don't think it's ever fair to just assume that relationship - but this could be used as evidence. If you know that the vulnerability requires a specific user action on a specific terminal but have walled off that terminal for the moment then it's probably not automatable, right? On the other hand, if the user interaction needed is for anyone in the company to open an email attachment and you can repeatedly automate sending that into people's inboxes past anti-spam then even with the user interaction limit it's still effectively automatable because _someone_ is gonna open that email.

But yes, in general, high user interactivity requirements are likely to reduce automatability.

documents.title: General discussion / Q&A on Rev5 improvements and changes in 2026
documents.text:
>  1. say that a CSP had a DFR when the JAB dissolved, and is now operating under Collab ConMon. To gain approval that the DFR had been remediated and close the finding, should one take it to their Collab ConMon now then inform [info@fedramp.gov](mailto:info@fedramp.gov) of the result? Asking for a friend. ;)

Yes! :D
 
> 2. The new VDR is mandated for CSP's to be adhered to by December 7 (or at least by March 7). Do CSPs need to run that through as an SCN given that we're just aligning to what we were mandated to do (i.e., it's not a "significant changes to their own products"), and if so, what type of change should we classify this as?

Definitely follow the process - this absolutely will vary from CSO to CSO, which is why the process adds that flexibility. I imagine that more likely for most folks it would end up being a combination of a few different security-impacting changes that happen over a period of time with different levels of changes. I think with the right approach for most providers would be to do this incrementally as adaptive or even routine recurring changes, without a big transformative change if at all possible.

In some cases it might be reasonable to declare an emergency in response to this urgent requirement and handle it like that if necessary as well. The important thing is the outcome here, which is ensuring agencies can meet the binding operational directive that requires them to have their information protected by risk-based vulnerability management.

> (Comment: Given that this deadline was abruptly moved up by six months, I expect that some CSPs will be coming in hot on this. If moving to the mandated VDR standard is deemed a transformative change that requires 30 **business** days' notice, the plans might really be "initial", with details not available until it's live.)

If CISA moves the deadline then we'll move the deadline. 🤷  I was a bit surprised by the 180 day deadline too but clearly they feel a sense of urgency on behalf of the entire federal government.

documents.title: General discussion and Q&A for RFC-0019 through RFC-0024!
documents.text:
> FedRAMP could help a lot of people by requiring a standard format machine readable product Vulnerability Disclosure Report (VDR) with up to date information on product vulnerabilities that consumers can download at anytime to check the status of a product, as of right now; think of a CARFAX report for digital products, including SaaS cloud offerings. [ossf/wg-vulnerability-disclosures#172](https://github.com/ossf/wg-vulnerability-disclosures/issues/172)

I think we've talked about this on other threads - this requirement exists in FedRAMP's updated Vulnerability Detection and Response, Continuous Collaborative Monitoring, and Authorization Data Sharing processes (minus the "standard format" - we're letting folks be a bit more flexible still). These are all still in pilot/beta but in a year or two from now I expect this information will be widely included.

We can't just flip a switch to require stuff like this but incentivized adoption should work.

documents.title: Q&A and Casual Discussion on Phase Two RFCs (14, 15, 16, 17, 18)
documents.text:
Yes, that's exactly right! We're starting to clarify in areas where the realistic expectation is that something will only apply to machine-based information resources versus all information resources. This started out in the [Vulnerability Detection and Response Standard](https://github.com/FedRAMP/docs/blob/main/markdown/FRMR.VDR.vulnerability-detection-and-response.md) when we realized there were times when specific requirements or recommendations should be focused or only applied to machines.

So, for example, with KSI-CNA-01 you don't need to limit inbound and outbound traffic of your personnel, and KSI-SVC-01 doesn't  require you to harden your office space, and KSI-SVC-04 doesn't expect you to automate your bill payment, KSI-SVC-05 doesn't require you to use cryptographic methods to verify that people at your office are the same people you hired, etc.

documents.title: Rev5 questions and discussion on the Consolidated Rules for 2026 (or Legacy)
documents.text:
> One thing I want to flag first. You mentioned "The first assessment starting after 2027-01-01 needs to match CPO, full stop.", but the CR26 Rev5 deadlines page shows CPO's maintain date as 2027-07-01 with a grace period ending on the first assessment started after 2027-07-01. Can you confirm which is correct?

Honestly we probably should've just set deadlines different than 07-01 - myself and many other folks struggle seeing the difference between 01-01 and 07-01. This was an especially egregious mistake considering I had originally messed up and put all of the +6mo grace periods for 01-01 maintain deadlines at 01-01 instead of 07-01 and it took many weeks for anyone to notice.

The deadlines in each ruleset are accurate. Always follow the rules as the source of truth, not something said elsewhere. :) I will edit my previous response to remove the incorrect dates.

> If these rulesets are not yet required in the above scenario, how can a CSP create a partial CR26 Certification Package without them (especially CPO and SDR)? I agree the cleanest path is to do a full scope, but is there a door for a partial package without key rulesets?

Yes, the expectation is that the cloud service provider finds a simple way to navigate this in a customer-experienced focused way. There is a bit of over-fixation on templates in the historical approach to FedRAMP, but we have deliberately moved away from that in the modern era. Providers are welcome to provide supplemental information about addressing FedRAMP Practices within the context of a legacy package or by simply producing standalone supplemental materials.

For example, VDR/VER does not have templates with how to report that information and there is no place for it in the traditional package, but that doesn't mean a provider can't easily figure out effective ways to share that information even if they haven't adopted the Certification Data Sharing rules.

> With no SDR then how is IVV met without verification and validation statements from both the IA and CSP? Where is IVV documented? Will the PMO allow discretion to the CSP with what supplementation looks like in the interim for all rulesets that have not yet hit their maintain dates? I hope you see where I am going and the source of confusion here.

Yes, this is intentional: [It's Not a Trap!](https://www.fedramp.gov/2026/rules/#its-not-a-trap)

This doesn't seem complicated to us. You can provide separate documents, add **Verification:** statements to the SSP control text, etc. You can progressively manage something like this with a machine-system and store it in a database/JSON/etc. while still manually doing the SSP in Word. 

>  I'd like to think it is one or the other until a certain date (Legacy Rev5 vs CR26 Rev5). After that, it is full CR26 then on and not partial frankenstein packages.

Oh no, we're definitely expecting frankenstein packages. We expect a lot of different approaches, some awesome, some incredibly poorly thought through. It's fine, it's all temporary. Our direction has been to prioritize incremental adoption among industry and government instead of setting an arbitrary cut-over date years in the future and to accept the risk of that mid-transition churn to prioritize earlier adoption of key bits. It needs to be clear that cloud service providers and assessors can't simply put everything off.

documents.title: RFC-0027 FedRAMP Rev5 Security Controls Baseline Update for AC, AT, AU, CA, and CM Control Families
documents.text:
Comment from Raj P.

Please find below my public comments on RFC-0027: FedRAMP Rev5 Security Controls Baseline Update for AC, AT, AU, CA, and CM Control Families.

Comment 1 
AC-02 — Account Management
No comment. Matching account types defined in account management to those referenced in FedRAMP Secure Configuration Guidance will increase consistency during assessments and minimize ambiguity during authorization review.
AC-10 — Concurrent Session Control
Limiting top level administrative accounts to single session is fair. FedRAMP needs to provide guidance if this control is meant to be enforced at the OS/network layer, application layer, or both. Additionally, FedRAMP should provide guidance as to how this control is implemented/enforced for IaaS, PaaS, and SaaS models.
AT-03 — Role-Based Training
FedRAMP should specify if this applies to all users with privileged account access or if this only applies to dedicated administrators. Along those lines, FedRAMP needs to provide a standard that better defines "where applicable" so that organizations can apply it consistently and in a manner that is proportionate.

Comment 2
AU — Audit and Accountability
No change suggested. No comment. Future Recommendation: Provide guidance around acceptable automated audit analysis capabilities and their effects on ConMon reporting requirements.
CA-05 — Plan of Action and Milestones
Separate tracks for traditional, CCM BIR, and VDR BIR reporting is greatly appreciated. FedRAMP should specify the mapping of traditional POA&M components to the newly developed reporting standards for adequate oversight.
CM-06 — Configuration Settings
Requirement 1 is required and supported. FedRAMP needs to specify what SHOULD be included in Security Configuration Guidance. Is the Security Configuration Guidance a standalone document, or is it part of the SSP? Does the language of SHOULD allow assessors to elevate findings if guidance is not present?

Comment 3
CM-07 — Least Functionality
Clear, concise. No additional comment. Matches CM-06.
CM-08 — System Component Inventory
Allows vendors to opt-out of inventory for VDR/BIR which lessens burden. Need FedRAMP to define minimum acceptable automated inventory standards to meet this requirement. This would include minimum discovery cycles, ephemeral/container components, and tie into CM workflow.
CM-12 — Information Location
Revision ties CM-12 control to MAS BIR boundary framework. No additional comment.
CM-12(1) — Automated Tools to Support Information Location
This special parameter has already been defined in CP-2(8). Consider revising the language to "CM-12(1) — [essential]"
IA-8 — Identification and Authentication Through Mobile Devices
Requiring an OTP is in-line with industry best practices. FedRAMP needs to allow for compliance of legacy applications that do not support OTP without major rewrites.

documents.title: RFC-0014 Phase Two Security Indicators
documents.text:
Appreciate the ongoing engagement from @pete-gov and the FedRAMP team - wanted to share a quick perspective as a CSP not selling penetration testing services.

The FedRAMP 20x standard should not go backwards by imposing a separate, one-size-fits-all “red-team” mandate. Human-led penetration testing and red teaming are already embedded within the VDR requirement (KSI-MLA-03), which is designed for ongoing detection, not a fixed annual checkbox.

Instead, CSPs should focus on automation and continuous controls validation - automating vulnerability detection, misconfiguration checks, and attack-path simulations - so that human-led testing can be triggered when risk indicators justify it. This enables real-time detection of configuration drift and rapid response to emerging threats, while reducing the cost, scheduling overhead, and redundancy of fixed-schedule red-team exercises.

By contrast, a blanket red-team mandate can drive higher costs, rigid scheduling, and lower signal-to-noise when conducted annually without regard to actual risk.

Automation combined with risk-triggered human testing produces stronger assurance, aligns with 20x’s modernization goals, and ensures we’re investing resources where the real risk lies.

documents.title: Proposal for v1.0 of FedRAMP Machine-Readable Docs (w/ significant changes)
documents.text:
# Changes for `v1.0`

To address a lot of these lessons learned we're going to make a bunch of changes that will affect the underlying structure of the machine-readable requirements and recommendations files and the way they are displayed in human-readable versions; **but no actual requirements or recommendations will be materially changed.**

### 1. Everything will be combined into three JSON datafiles - KSIs, definitions, and others others.

KSIs will get their own JSON file because it's a whole thing and they have a wildly different structure in many cases - and that will probably expand a lot more. Same for Definitions.

Otherwise all of the other requirements and recommendations and definitions will be folded into a single file for combined maintenance because they should all consistently follow the same structure and be part of the same whole.

- Updates to each specific requirement or recommendation will tracked individually
- Only combined releases of the entire document set will be given formal versions
- Many other aspects of each specific requirement or recommendation will be tracked individually, such as applicability (including 20x vs Rev5), corrective actions, etc. as appropriate

### 2. Each requirement and recommendation will use a unique 3 stage identifier comprised of 3 letters each

No more than 3 stages will ever be used and nothing will start with FRR/FRD/FRA/etc.

- The first stage will use the existing process initialism such as `KSI`, `VDR`, etc.
- The second stage will use an initialism for a specific theme or subset of the process; this will vary by process. You're familiar with this for Key Security Indicators, such as `KSI-CNA` or `KSI-IAM` and it will be applied to other processes like changing `FRR-ADS-TC` to `ADS-TRC`. In general there will be some recurring themes, such as `ABC-GEN` to refer to general requirements.
- The third stage will use a unique initialism _that matches the human-readable short name_ instead of a number. For example, `KSI-AFR-07 Recommended Secure Configuration` will become `KSI-AFR-RSC Recommended Secure Configuration` or `FRR-MAS-04 Metadata Inclusion` might become `MAS-GEN-MDI`.
  - If 3 words really don't make sense then we'll use 3 letters that do or an X, for example `Independent Assessment` might become `IAS` or `Feedback Mechanism` might become `FMX` (or something like that)  

### 3. No more built-in human-readable formatting.

This mostly means removing italics - we'll address highlighting defined terms programmatically.

### 4. Simplify maintenance with JSON5

I'm going to experiment with using [JSON5](https://json5.org/) to make the underlying JSON file easier to maintain. This lets us add comments, quote things in different ways, not worry about trailing commas, carry text across newlines, etc. We'll make a final determination on this before we go live.

### 5. Fix earlier processes that have Application or other similar sections that aren't requirements or recommendations.

These will get integrated as either notes, technical assistance, or rephrased into something that makes more sense in context.

### 6. Maintain some backward compatibility.

We'll keep the old id's referenced where applicable to help people change over.

# Overall

This will create a pretty big change but it will let us consistently do more cool stuff, like:

1. Not worrying about "ordering" anything when we write new requirements and recommendations
2. Easily generate separate materials for things like providers, assessors, impact level, etc. without human-readable "gaps" appearing in materials
3. Separate the maintenance of terms in requirements to something that is entirely programmatic
4. Simplify referring to specific requirements or recommendations because they'll make sense ("MAS-GEN-SOF" is obviously separate from "MAS-GEN-SFT" and easier to context align than "FRR-MAS-AY-01" and "FRR-MAS-AY-02")

## Feedback/etc.

Any thoughts, feedback, etc. from folks that have been working with these materials in their JSON form would be appreciated. 

I recognize this is a large shift but it's one we need to do **before** the current requirements and recommendations are formally standardized into a non-pilot/beta state.

documents.title: RFC-0026 Clarifying CA-7 Continuous Monitoring Expectations for Rev5 Providers
documents.text:
Strong support for this RFC. The existing CA-7 guidance has carried the JAB reference for the twenty months since M-24-15, and the ambiguity has produced real operational drift across CSPs with multiple agency customers. Clarifying that all agency customers must have access to the same ConMon data is correct in principle and aligns with what the FedRAMP model promises agencies that leverage authorizations.

Agency-side perspective on the all-agency access requirement. I directed Agency Authorization lifecycle work for 60+ enterprise cloud deployments across the VA, representing $3.8B in federal contracts. In practice, the JAB-path vs. Agency-path distinction in the old CA-7 language produced visibility tiers where lead agencies received richer ConMon feeds than downstream agencies leveraging the same service. Downstream agencies making ongoing authorization decisions were doing so with materially less current information than the FedRAMP model promised. This RFC corrects that. Please keep the all-agency access baseline.

On the raw scan sharing pathway. The community discussion in the general thread surfaced a legitimate operational concern: most downstream agencies lack the capability or staffing to parse raw scan outputs at cadence. That observation is accurate and worth acknowledging **without walking the requirement back**. Making scan data available is a data-provisioning requirement, not a customer-enablement requirement. Consider adding an explicit clarification that CSPs meet the requirement by making the data accessible through their standard ConMon channels, and that agency capacity to consume that data is an agency responsibility. The distinction matters because it prevents CSPs from over-investing in customer education and correctly scopes the cost.

On the corrective action schedule. The graduated five-failure structure is well-designed, with predictable off-ramps and proportional consequences. One clarification worth building in: how does the process handle documented good faith disruptions during BIR transition activity, partial VDR adoption, or coordination-driven meeting slips where no agency customer attends a scheduled meeting? I would suggest either explicit exception language or clear confirmation that the initial Corrective Action Plan submission at first failure is the correct venue to document and resolve those conditions. Either answer works; removing ambiguity is what matters.

On the effective date. The alignment with CR26 publication, Q3–Q4 2026 grace period, and January 1, 2027 enforcement is sensible and gives CSPs a real implementation window. The BIR incentive structure is correctly oriented: CSPs that adopt VDR and CCM BIRs inherit cleaner ConMon alignment and exit the traditional corrective action schedule. That is the right direction of travel. 

Thank you to the PMO for closing a guidance gap that has been structurally out of sync with M-24-15 for almost two years. This is meaningful cleanup.

Michael Schroeder
