documents.title: Rev5 questions and discussion on the Consolidated Rules for 2026 (or Legacy)
documents.text:
CISA BOD 26-04 proposed a staged implementation where rules were put in place and then implemented, but the key point is that at the beginning of Phase III, within 180 days of issuance, agencies are expected to remediate each vulnerability as quickly as possible and no later than the timelines/etc. You can't just leave a bunch of old stuff lying around and not get to it, everything needs to be getting handled.

Note that the VDR does not calculate deadlines from detection time, it calculates them from evaluation time. It simply expects you to report on the time between detection and evaluation and expects you to begin evaluation **promptly.** It is certain fair for the deltas between those dates to be longer than normal during a transition from one approach to another approach.

The best approach is to begin implementing the new rules now: start performing the required steps with older stuff lying around to determine if you even need it lying anymore (CISA indicated that likely 90% or more of current vulnerabilities are not likely exploitable and have a likely PAIN of 1 or 0, so you just saved a lot of work). Then prioritize the stuff that you look at and realize it's an actual serious problem that you should've fixed 2 weeks ago but ignored because you had 30 days. Then start reporting on all of that stuff. And then bringing in new vulnerabilities, repeat.

documents.title: Rev5 questions and discussion on the Consolidated Rules for 2026 (or Legacy)
documents.text:
> We believe there's a little ambiguity in how the VDR-TFR-PVR remediation clock is determined when a vulnerability is evaluated.

If you stick to the wording it should be fine, I think there's just a habit that's formed from previous guidance that the counter never reset if you mitigated vulnerabilities (which was bad). The wording in the rule is deliberate and intended to eliminate that ambiguity - the goal is to reduce the PAIN.

The outcome of a successful mitigation of PAIN should be a new evaluation which determines there is a different set of risks and the clock resets based on that evaluation. The deadlines take this into account.

> Is the deadline for remediation or PAIN downgrades based on the initial evaluation date? Or is the deadline recalculated based on movement to a lower PAIN rating (or even LEV/IRV value)?

The clock is intended to reset when mitigations have meaningfully reframed the vulnerability, because all of the risks/etc. have changed. The goal is to encourage mitigation as the highest priority - you should never wait for a remediation to be available when you can apply mitigations to reduce the potential of a vulnerability to be exploited or the potential damage. 

As a reminder, these "deadlines" are intended to be absolute worst-case and will be exceeded consistently by providers with good security programs. :)

> Is the new deadline 9/18 + 128 days based on the movement to a lower PAIN rating?

Yes.

documents.title: RFC-0026 Clarifying CA-7 Continuous Monitoring Expectations for Rev5 Providers
documents.text:
- RV5-CA07-VLN states that providers must follow either the VDR standard or traditional Rev 5 processes including scan file and POA&M uploads. This contracts with Notice 0009, which states “Mandatory adoption of the Vulnerability Detection and Response process for all Rev5 cloud services” with an anticipated deadline of 6/1/2027. Which is the correct guidance?
- Likewise, RV5-CA07-CCM states that providers have options for meeting ConMon, either the Collaborative BIR approach, or the traditional approach. However, Notice 0009 states “Mandatory adoption of the Collaborative Continuous Monitoring process for all Rev5 cloud services” with an anticipated deadline of 4/2/2027. Which is the correct guidance?
- RV5-CA07-VLN uses the term “Service Configuration Scans” without defining what these should be run on. The scope of this term has been loosely defined in FedRAMP and causes unnecessary confusion during assessments and ConMon. Some CSPs will only run such scans against Hosts, others will include Databases, and others still will also include Container Images, but it’s left up to 3PAOs to attempt to enforce a consistent approach and different 3PAOs think differently on this subject. CM-6 does not explicitly state asset types either, so referencing CM-6 language does not help here. FedRAMP’s vulnerability scanning requirements for containers does reference CM-6, but this language is often ignored by 3PAOs, causing inconsistent enforcement of service configuration scans. Please provide clear guidance directly in this or another control on what types of assets these scans should be run on to ensure a level playing field and consistent assessments across 3PAOs.

documents.title: RFC-0017 Persistent Validation and Assessment Standard
documents.text:
> FRR-PVA-01
Providers MUST maintain simple high-level summaries of at least the following for each Key Security Indicator:
> 1. Goals for how it will be implemented and validated, including clear pass/fail criteria and traceability

> FRR-PVA-03
Providers MUST treat failures detected during persistent validation or failures of the persistent validation process as vulnerabilities and follow the requirements and recommendations in the FedRAMP Vulnerability Detection and Response Standard for such findings.

We support the intent of FRR-PVA-01 and FRR-PVA-03 in ensuring that failures in persistent validation are treated as vulnerabilities and managed under the FedRAMP Vulnerability Detection and Response (VDR) Standard. However, as currently written, these requirements risk creating gaps in how agencies understand and act on risk.

1. Pass/Fail Criteria May Not Capture Risk:
The current model emphasizes binary pass/fail results for KSIs. While efficient, this approach may obscure meaningful risk. For example, a CSP could define a KSI implementation as “all data flows are encrypted except for X flow.” The validation logic would pass because it aligns with the CSP’s stated implementation, but the exception (X flow unencrypted) represents a real residual risk. Agencies would not see this context unless they performed additional follow-up, which undermines the purpose of persistent validation.
2.	Oversight in Risk Classification:
CSPs are currently able to classify and assign risk ratings under VDR with minimal oversight. Given the subjectivity involved in contextualizing vulnerability risk, there is a need for structured, ongoing oversight. 3PAOs are already embedded in the assessment of KSIs and are well-positioned to provide authoritative input on the severity of KSI failures and their corresponding risk to federal data.

> FRR-PVA-AA-01
> Assessors MUST evaluate the underlying processes (both machine-based and human-based) that providers use to validate Key Security Indicators; this evaluation should include at least:
> 3. The coverage of these processes within the cloud service offering, including if all of the consolidated information resources listed are being validated

This requirement (# 3) is ambiguous in how CSPs are expected to demonstrate compliance. Specifically, there is no clear requirement for a CSP to present a centralized, structured artifact (e.g., a system-level diagram) that shows which information resources (systems, subsystems, data flows, roles) are in scope and how they will be validated.

Without such a requirement, 3PAOs must rely on unstructured, conversational descriptions and ad hoc artifacts from CSPs. This becomes highly problematic (or even unworkable) for large or complex CSPs, where multiple teams contribute to system architecture, data flows, identity management, configuration, and monitoring.

FedRAMP should require CSPs to produce a **FedRAMP system architecture diagram** to (a) reduce assessor dependence on loosely defined descriptions, (b) improve consistency and transparency across CSPs, and (c) make assessments more scalable and reliable even in complex environments.

> FRR-PVA-AA-02
> Assessors` MUST evaluate the accuracy of the Key Security Indicator goals against actual implementation of the process to determine whether or not the provider has accurately documented their process.

This phrasing creates uncertainty about the intended object of evaluation. Specifically:
- It first directs 3PAOs to evaluate KSI goals against **_actual implementation_** (suggesting a process effectiveness / implementation audit).
- It then instructs 3PAOs to determine whether the CSP has **_accurately documented_** the process (suggesting a documentation / alignment check).

It is unclear whether the KSI requires validation of (a) the CSP’s documentation against its stated goals, or (b) the CSP’s actual operational implementation against those goals. Both are important, but they require different evidence and evaluation methods. Without clarity, 3PAOs may apply different interpretations - some focusing on document accuracy, others on process execution - leading to inconsistent assessments across CSPs.

> FRR-PVA-AA-09
Assessors MUST deliver a high-level summary of their assessment process and resulting findings for each Key Security Indicator that is intended for inclusion in the provider’s authorization data.

The current requirement directs assessors to provide a high-level summary of their assessment process and findings for each KSI, but does not specify a consistent format. This lack of standardization will likely result in varied reporting styles across 3PAOs.

FedRAMP should provide a standardized summary template for 3PAOs to use. A common format would reduce variability, decrease agency confusion, and limit repetitive follow-up questions –  improving both efficiency and clarity in the authorization process.

> FRR-PVA-AA-10
Assessors MUST NOT deliver an overall recommendation on whether or not the cloud service offering meets the requirements for FedRAMP authorization; this will be determined by FedRAMP based on the assessment findings for each Key Security Indicator.

FedRAMP should publish clear expectations on which assessment outcomes or deficiencies are considered unacceptable for authorization. This would give 3PAOs consistent direction, prevent confusion during assessments, and ensure CSPs understand the potential impact of significant findings.

documents.title: Consolidated 20x Phase 2 pilot Q&A / discussion
documents.text:
> I’ve been following along with 20x discussions and have heard things about pentesting in 20x but was unable to find guidance specifying the requirement for pentesting and red team in 20x assessments. Will pentests and red team be required for 20x? If so, do will they match the currently posted guidance based on rev.5?

Under 20x, penetration testing and red-teaming is part of [Vulnerability Detection and Response](https://www.fedramp.gov/docs/vulnerability-detection-and-response/#frr-vdr-rp-02-high-level-overviews). Cloud service providers are not **required** to perform these activities but are instead expected to determine if those activities will have positive security outcomes and leverage them as appropriate for their specific situation.

In general, cloud service offerings that regularly run penetration testing and perform red-team style exercises are more likely to have better security and will receive better scoring on FedRAMP assessments if they can prove the beneficial security outcomes from those activities.

> Also, I noticed that the latest draft version of the penetration testing guidance which included a red team section was removed from public access. Is there another version we should use or look out for other than the version on the website dated 2022-06-30?

Nope, that's the only current official guidance for Rev5 penetration testing. If FedRAMP produces updated materials for this it will [go through our RFC process](https://fedramp.gov/rfcs) but we do not currently plan to provide updated guidance for Rev5 on this. Draft guidance shouldn't be used as if it is formal guidance - we switched to the RFC process to avoid that confusion in the future.

documents.title: Balancing FedRAMP Rev5 against improvements to FedRAMP 20x
documents.text:
> Where an auditor's expectations and an AO's expectations diverge, there is currently no clear mechanism to resolve that conflict, potentially resulting in duplicative or inconsistent documentation.

FedRAMP's direction is to create rules that encourage innovative private-sector driven solutions.

FedRAMP is deliberately moving away from standardizing artifacts in a way that limits innovation and discourages cloud service providers from competing on customer experience. In the short term this may cause some issues because many agencies do not have access to automated GRC platforms or other capabilities that can easily translate machine-readable information into their preferred format, but all agencies are required by policy to implement such tooling. And this type of capability is simpler than ever in 2026.

On the human-readable side, we strongly encourage folks to think outside the template box. You can engage design experts to work with customers and build something that provides value to everyone, factoring for your unique environment and complexity. This flexibility allows you to compete on the quality of your vulnerability detection and response presentation, instead of flattening everything and everyone into a single janky spreadsheet.

Independent assessors should only be verifying and validating that you're meeting the requirements, not demanding a specific format. And while an AO's expectations may diverge, that is a simple fact of business and it gives you an opportunity to work with them to craft something better for both of you (hint: don't confuse contractors working for an AO with an AO - you should be working directly with an AO on something like this).

> Additional guidance on partial remediation would reduce ambiguity. The current framework does not clearly define what constitutes a valid partial remediation. 

I think this might be a term issue that I can do a pass through for clarity. We don't use remediation and mitigation interchangeably, and don't allow for partial remediation. We consider a Fully Mitigated Vulnerability to be different from a Remediated Vulnerability. Hence statements like "Providers SHOULD partially mitigate, fully mitigate, or remediate vulnerabilities..." don't include "partial remediation" because that's actually partial mitigation. Semantics, but is intended to avoid confusion through precise language.

- **Mitigation:** Take steps to make something bad less severe. [Partially Mitigated Vulnerability](https://preview.fedramp.gov/2026/definitions/#partially-mitigated-vulnerability), [Fully Mitigated Vulnerability](https://preview.fedramp.gov/2026/definitions/#fully-mitigated-vulnerability)
- **Remediation:** Remove the bad thing. [Remediated Vulnerability](https://preview.fedramp.gov/2026/definitions/#remediated-vulnerability)

Our guidance should be consistent in mitigation being a step-by-step process that can have an outcome of full mitigation or remediation. Either way, partial mitigation is defined as linked above, so please let me know if that definition needs more clarity!

_edit: oh, I noticed that "partially mitigate" and "fully mitigate" aren't configured as alternate variants of the Partially Mitigated Vulnerability and Fully Mitigated Vulnerability definitions so they don't hit the **terms** array so it's not obvious these are defined while looking at the rules - will fix!_

> Further clarify SHOULD versus MUST requirements. The distinction between SHOULD and MUST requirements in the VDR framework deserves greater emphasis.

We've added a slightly more detailed [Force of the Rule](https://preview.fedramp.gov/2026/rules/#force-of-the-rule) section in the Consolidated Rules, but have generally avoided adding too much complexity here. The intent here is to allow normal reasonable people the flexibility to make decisions that make sense in the context of their service.

Vulnerability Detection and Response is a bit of an art. The limitation on MUST requirements and focus on SHOULD recommendations in the VDR is designed to ensure that cloud service providers do the **right thing, the responsible and secure thing** when making decisions, instead of doing the **compliant thing.**

The timelines are a great example of that - partially mitigating something just under the wire of a timeframe might be the **compliant** thing, but it shows a focus on compliance over security. 

The **right thing** usually is to partially mitigate something as quickly as possible and not care what the maximum timeframe is in most cases... but there are (rare) valid situations where the **right thing** is to let something slide past the timeframe (active investigation, partial mitigation carries higher risk, etc.). In those cases we want to ignore the timeframes and do the right thing.

Less compliance, more responsible decision making for everyone. :)

documents.title: RFC-0025 Retrospective on the Public Comment Process
documents.text:
The following public comment was received via email from Raj Prahast Maheswarapu on Tues April 21:

I am copy/pasting into the public comment record on their behalf as required by the FedRAMP public comment process. This is not an endorsement of the commenter or the content within the comment.

---

Hi Pete,

Please find my public comments below on RFC-0025 Retrospective on the Public Comment Process.

Comment 1:  Discoverability

I find out about RFCs via GovDelivery alerts. Any practitioner who isn't subscribed to that list has essentially no way of knowing that a new RFC has been published. Sending out a digest email at the beginning of each comment period with links to all active RFCs would help increase visibility without any additional infrastructure.

Comment 2:  Comment Period

For RFCs that impact only one control family, 30 days is sufficient. For heavily technical RFCs that impact multiple families (RFC-0030 impacted four, with mostly dual-track VDR changes) it can be a bit rushed. Allowing 45-days where an RFC impacts multiple control families would increase the usefulness of the responses received.

Comment 3:  Outcome Summaries

I like seeing Initial Outcomes published. However, they tend to summarize feedback thematically rather than address specific technical comments. If a practitioner makes a detailed comment on a specific change and it doesn't seem to be accounted for in the outcome, there is no way for them to know if it was considered and rejected or just overlooked. Adding a small section to outcome documents that list technical notes would increase trust in the process.

Thank you for the opportunity to comment on this RFC.

Best regards,
Raj Prahast Maheswarapu
Data Governance Lead - State of Florida

documents.title: Consolidated 20x Phase 2 pilot Q&A / discussion
documents.text:
Some of this will adjust during the pilot, and I'd caution against approaching this thinking there are firm acceptance criteria in place that be banked on in advance - that wouldn't be much of a pilot. ;)

>  * What would the definition of done be during the collaborative workshop/process?

We want the cloud service provider, their assessor, and FedRAMP to all be confident that the provider is ready to finalize a package and submit it. This will take as long as it takes, and if we can't get there then the cloud service provider will be asked to step back.

>  * If we are accepted into cohort 1, the ultimate deliverable is submitting the package on Jan 27, but are there other milestones or expectations of completeness throughout that timeframe?

Cohort 1 collaborative workshops will take place during December - we'll expect them to have been finished before we start Cohort 2. 
 
>  * Are there any specific technical pieces that need to be ready by time of application? Specific standards have to already be defined in the submission, percentages or coverage of KSIs already in place, etc?

At time of application?  Providers should have enough in place that we can be confident completion is achievable within two months. If you come into a pilot proposal without anything done (no trust center, no authorization data sharing prototype, no VDR proof of concept, etc.) then you've got quite an uphill battle convincing us you can do that in two months. :) 

The overall number of requirements and recommendations to address between Phase 1 and Phase 2 went from like ~80 to ~400. I really don't expect many folks to be crazy enough to try to build all of that in two months.

documents.title: Rev5 questions and discussion on the Consolidated Rules for 2026 (or Legacy)
documents.text:
> Does the service-base approach mean that a vulnerability capable of causing a complete outage across multiple federal agency customers must receive PAIN-5, even when the service performs only non-mission-critical functions?

Nope! We recommend checking into the [Using the Consolidated Rules](https://www.fedramp.gov/2026/rules/#definitions) section of the site to read about how we use defined terms to clarify stuff like this in the rules. In the human-readable version of the site, each rule links to all of the defined terms that it uses for quick reference.

There are a bunch of specifically defined terms used in [VER-EVA-EPA (Estimate Potential Agency Impact)](https://www.fedramp.gov/2026/reference/vulnerability-evaluation-and-reporting/#estimate-potential-agency-impact) that should address this question in the context of the rules:

- N5 specifically is " could be expected to have a **debilitating customer effect** on more than one agency that uses the cloud service offering."
- [Debilitating customer effect](https://www.fedramp.gov/2026/definitions/#debilitating-customer-effect) is defined as "An unwanted customer effect that interrupts use of the cloud service for most users or compromises the integrity or confidentiality of most federal customer data. If the adverse customer effect is unknown then it should be treated as if it is debilitating until proven otherwise."

If you know a service isn't performing mission-critical functions such that it isn't likely to affect most users / most customer data, then you would not evaluate it as a likely debilitating customer effect at PAIN5. More likely it would be something like a [narrow customer effect ](https://www.fedramp.gov/2026/definitions/#narrow-customer-effect)on one or more agencies that use the cloud service offering at PAIN2.

documents.title: General discussion and Q&A for RFCs related to Rev5 Updates (RFCs 0026, 0027, 0028, 0029, & 0030)
documents.text:
Sorry I missed this Q in my stack - there is no such thing as a "non-vulnerability finding" - a vulnerability by definition includes assessment findings:

> [FedRAMP Definition of **Vulnerability**](https://www.fedramp.gov/docs/rev5/balance/fedramp-definitions/#vulnerability): Has the meaning given to "security vulnerability" in [6 USC § 650 (25)](https://www.govinfo.gov/app/details/USCODE-2024-title6/USCODE-2024-title6-chap1-subchapXVIII-sec650), which is "any attribute of hardware, software, process, or procedure that could enable or facilitate the defeat of [...] management, operational, and technical controls used to protect against an unauthorized effort to adversely affect the confidentiality, integrity, and availability of an information system or its information." This includes gaps in Rev5 controls and 20x Key Security Indicators, software vulnerabilities, misconfigurations, exposures, weak credentials, insecure services, and all other such potential weaknesses in protection (intentional or unintentional).

The VDR has specific instructions for reporting on [Vulnerability Details](https://www.fedramp.gov/docs/rev5/balance/vulnerability-detection-and-response/#vulnerability-details). These are similar in scope to what used to be a POA&M, however it also allows the cloud service provider to just straight up accept a vulnerability (definition: [accepted vulnerability](https://www.fedramp.gov/docs/rev5/balance/fedramp-definitions/#accepted-vulnerability)) and provides instructions on how to [Mark Accepted Vulnerabilities](https://www.fedramp.gov/docs/rev5/balance/vulnerability-detection-and-response/#mark-accepted-vulnerabilities).

So if there is a traditional finding where the result is that the cloud service just doesn't intend to address it for whatever reason, they would document it as an Accepted Vulnerability and it would live in their vulnerability reports forever or until they have a reason to revisit and fix it.

documents.title: RFC-0025 Retrospective on the Public Comment Process
documents.text:
I appreciate FedRAMP taking a step back to evaluate the process itself. A few observations from someone who’s participated across multiple cycles.
The 30-day window is workable for a single RFC. What’s harder is when FedRAMP drops four or five RFCs simultaneously, each covering different control families with materially different implications. The effort to read, cross reference, and draft substantive comments across a batch scales nonlinearly. When RFC-0027 through RFC-0030 all land at once with overlapping concepts (VDR pathways, BIRs, SCG references), a CSP compliance team is effectively running a small project just to comment. Consider staggering batches or extending windows when multiple related RFCs publish together.
On visibility concerns: the real barrier isn’t anonymity. It’s that commenting publicly signals your compliance posture. If a CSP raises a concern about a specific control, agencies reading that thread may infer the CSP struggles with it. That’s not paranoia; it’s how procurement risk assessments work. Anonymous submission helps, but the deeper fix is FedRAMP actively normalizing that commenting is participation, not an admission of weakness. The framing of this RFC does that well. More of that.
On outcome transparency: the gap isn’t whether FedRAMP publishes a summary of what changed. It’s whether commenters can trace their specific input to a disposition. “We received feedback on X and decided Y because Z” is far more useful than “we updated the language based on public input.” Without that traceability, the process feels consultative rather than collaborative, and rational participants discount the value of investing time in detailed comments.
One concrete suggestion: publish a comment disposition matrix alongside the final rule, similar to what NIST does with SP 800-53 public drafts. Map each substantive comment to an accept/reject/modify decision with a one line rationale. That would do more for participation rates than any notification mechanism change.
Finally, the distinction between GitHub discussion comments and formal comments is genuinely unclear. I’ve seen substantive technical feedback buried in discussion threads that may or may not have been treated as formal input. If both channels feed the same review process, say so explicitly. If they don’t, make the boundary obvious so people don’t waste effort in the wrong venue.

documents.title: Consolidated 20x Phase 2 pilot Q&A / discussion
documents.text:
## Big Key Security Indicators Update!!

For everyone's awareness, we just released version 25.12A for the Key Security Indicators:

- [Machine Readable Version](https://github.com/FedRAMP/docs/blob/main/FRMR.KSI.key-security-indicators.json) (which I'm sure you're already using if you're in the pilot)
- [Human Readable Version](https://www.fedramp.gov/docs/20x/key-security-indicators/)

From the changelog:

> This release updates a significant number of KSIs to improve clarity and expectations; in general the measures required to meet each KSI remain unchanged but these updates should make it easier to address them. In additional, some KSIs have been retired. 

After these retirements, there are now **56** low and **61** moderate KSIs.

# Detailed changes

You can likely generate the delta quite easily from the machine readable versions but here are the notes I worked off when making these changes for reference.

KSI-CED-01 General Education
Require and monitor the effectiveness of training given to all employees on policies, procedures, and security-related topics.
New: Persistently review the effectiveness of training given to all employees on policies, procedures, and security-related topics.

KSI-CED-02 Role-Specific Education[¶](https://www.fedramp.gov/docs/20x/key-security-indicators/#ksi-ced-02-role-specific-education)
Require and monitor the effectiveness of role-specific training for high risk roles, including at least roles with privileged access.
New: Persistently review the effectiveness of role-specific training given to employees in high risk roles, including at least roles with privileged access.

KSI-CED-03 Development and Engineering Education[¶](https://www.fedramp.gov/docs/20x/key-security-indicators/#ksi-ced-03-development-and-engineering-education)
Require and monitor the effectiveness of role-specific training provided to development and engineering staff that covers best practices for delivering secure software.
New: Persistently review the effectiveness of role-specific training given to development and engineering staff that covers best practices for delivering secure software.

KSI-CED-04 Incident Response and Disaster Recovery Education[¶](https://www.fedramp.gov/docs/20x/key-security-indicators/#ksi-ced-04-incident-response-and-disaster-recovery-education)
Require and monitor the effectiveness of role-specific training to staff involved with incident response or disaster recovery.
New: Persistently review the effectiveness of role-specific training given to staff involved with incident response or disaster recovery.

KSI-CMT-02 Redeployment[¶](https://www.fedramp.gov/docs/20x/key-security-indicators/#ksi-cmt-02-redeployment)
Execute changes though redeployment of version controlled immutable resources rather than direct modification wherever possible
New: Execute changes to machine-based information resources through redeployment of version controlled immutable resources rather than direct modification wherever possible.

KSI-CMT-04 Change Management Procedure[¶](https://www.fedramp.gov/docs/20x/key-security-indicators/#ksi-cmt-04-change-management-procedure)
Always follow a documented change management procedure.
New: Persistently review the effectiveness of documented change management procedures.

KSI-CNA-01 Restrict Network Traffic[¶](https://www.fedramp.gov/docs/20x/key-security-indicators/#ksi-cna-01-restrict-network-traffic)
Configure all machine-based information resources to limit inbound and outbound network traffic.
New: Persistently ensure all machine-based information resources are configured to limit inbound and outbound network traffic.

KSI-CNA-02 Minimize the Attack Surface[¶](https://www.fedramp.gov/docs/20x/key-security-indicators/#ksi-cna-02-minimize-the-attack-surface)
Design systems to minimize the attack surface and minimize lateral movement if compromised.
New: Persistently ensure machine-based information resources have a minimal attack surface and that lateral movement is minimized if compromised.

KSI-CNA-05 Unwanted Activity[¶](https://www.fedramp.gov/docs/20x/key-security-indicators/#ksi-cna-05-unwanted-activity)
Protect against denial of service attacks and other unwanted activity.
New: Persistently review the effectiveness of protection against denial of service attacks and other unwanted activity.

KSI-CNA-06 High Availability[¶](https://www.fedramp.gov/docs/20x/key-security-indicators/#ksi-cna-06-high-availability)
Design systems for high availability and rapid recovery.
New: Appropriately optimize machine-based information resources for high availability and rapid recovery.

KSI-CNA-07 Best Practices[¶](https://www.fedramp.gov/docs/20x/key-security-indicators/#ksi-cna-07-best-practices)
Ensure cloud-native information resources are implemented based on host provider's best practices and documented guidance.
New: Persistently ensure cloud-native machine-based information resources are implemented based on the host provider's best practices and documented guidance.

KSI-IAM-05 Least Privilege[¶](https://www.fedramp.gov/docs/20x/key-security-indicators/#ksi-iam-05-least-privilege)
Configure identity and access management with measures that always verify each user or device can only access the resources they need.
New: Persistently ensure that identity and access management employs measures to ensure each user or device can only access the resources they need.

KSI-INR-01 Incident Response Procedure[¶](https://fedramp.github.io/docs/20x/key-security-indicators/#ksi-inr-01-incident-response-procedure)
Always follow a documented incident response procedure.
New: Persistently review of the effectiveness of documented incident response procedures.
KSI-INR-02 Incident Logging[¶](https://www.fedramp.gov/docs/20x/key-security-indicators/#ksi-inr-02-incident-logging)
Maintain a log of incidents and periodically review past incidents for patterns or vulnerabilities.
New: Persistently review past incidents for patterns or vulnerabilities.

KSI-INR-03 Incident After Action Reports[¶](https://www.fedramp.gov/docs/20x/key-security-indicators/#ksi-inr-03-incident-after-action-reports)
Generate after action reports and regularly incorporate lessons learned into operations.
New: Generate incident after action reports and persistently incorporate lessons learned.

KSI-MLA-02 Audit Logging[¶](https://www.fedramp.gov/docs/20x/key-security-indicators/#ksi-mla-02-audit-logging)
Regularly review and audit logs.
New: Persistently review and audit logs.

KSI-MLA-05 Infrastructure as Code[¶](https://www.fedramp.gov/docs/20x/key-security-indicators/#ksi-mla-05-infrastructure-as-code)
Perform Infrastructure as Code and configuration evaluation and testing.
New: Persistently evaluate and test the configuration of machine-based information resources, especially infrastructure as code.

KSI-PIY-01 Automated Inventory[¶](https://www.fedramp.gov/docs/20x/key-security-indicators/#ksi-piy-01-automated-inventory)
Use authoritative sources to automatically maintain real-time inventories of all information resources.
New: Use authoritative sources to automatically generate real-time inventories of all information resources when needed.

KSI-PIY-02 Security Objectives and Requirements[¶](https://www.fedramp.gov/docs/20x/key-security-indicators/#ksi-piy-02-security-objectives-and-requirements)
Document the security objectives and requirements for each information resource or set of information resources.
New: Retired / Superseded by KSI-AFR-01 MAS

KSI-PIY-03 Vulnerability Disclosure Program[¶](https://www.fedramp.gov/docs/20x/key-security-indicators/#ksi-piy-03-vulnerability-disclosure-program)
Maintain a vulnerability disclosure program.
New: Persistently review the effectiveness of the provider’s vulnerability disclosure program.

KSI-PIY-04 CISA Secure By Design[¶](https://www.fedramp.gov/docs/20x/key-security-indicators/#ksi-piy-04-cisa-secure-by-design)
Monitor the effectiveness of building security and privacy considerations into the Software Development Lifecycle and aligning with CISA Secure By Design principles.
New: Persistently review the effectiveness of building security and privacy considerations into the Software Development Lifecycle and aligning with CISA Secure By Design principles.

KSI-PIY-05 Evaluate Implementations[¶](https://www.fedramp.gov/docs/20x/key-security-indicators/#ksi-piy-05-evaluate-implementations)
Document methods used to evaluate information resource implementations.
New: Retired / Superseded by KSI-AFR-04 VDR

KSI-PIY-06 Security Investment Effectiveness[¶](https://www.fedramp.gov/docs/20x/key-security-indicators/#ksi-piy-06-security-investment-effectiveness)
Monitor the effectiveness of the organization's investments in achieving security objectives.
New: Persistently review the effectiveness of the organization's investments in achieving security objectives.

KSI-PIY-07 Supply Chain Risk Management[¶](https://www.fedramp.gov/docs/20x/key-security-indicators/#ksi-piy-07-supply-chain-risk-management)
Document risk management decisions for software supply chain security.
New: Retired / Superseded by KSI-TPR-03

KSI-PIY-08 Executive Support[¶](https://www.fedramp.gov/docs/20x/key-security-indicators/#ksi-piy-08-executive-support)
Regularly measure executive support for achieving the organization’s security objectives.
New: Persistently review executive support for achieving the organization’s security objectives.

KSI-RPL-01 Recovery Objectives[¶](https://www.fedramp.gov/docs/20x/key-security-indicators/#ksi-rpl-01-recovery-objectives)
Define Recovery Time Objectives (RTO) and Recovery Point Objectives (RPO).
New: Persistently review desired Recovery Time Objectives (RTO) and Recovery Point Objectives (RPO).

KSI-RPL-02 Recovery Plan[¶](https://www.fedramp.gov/docs/20x/key-security-indicators/#ksi-rpl-02-recovery-plan)
Develop and maintain a recovery plan that aligns with the defined recovery objectives.
New: Persistently review the alignment of recovery plans with defined recovery objectives.

KSI-RPL-03 System Backups[¶](https://www.fedramp.gov/docs/20x/key-security-indicators/#ksi-rpl-03-system-backups)
Perform system backups aligned with recovery objectives.
New: Persistently review the alignment of machine-based information resource backups with defined recovery objectives.

KSI-RPL-04 Recovery Testing[¶](https://www.fedramp.gov/docs/20x/key-security-indicators/#ksi-rpl-04-recovery-testing)
Regularly test the capability to recover from incidents and contingencies.
New: Persistently test the capability to recover from incidents and contingencies, including alignment with defined recovery objectives.

KSI-SVC-07 Patching[¶](https://www.fedramp.gov/docs/20x/key-security-indicators/#ksi-svc-07-patching)
Use a consistent, risk-informed approach for applying security patches.
New: Retired  / Superseded by KSI-AFR-04 VDR

KSI-SVC-08 Shared Resources[¶](https://www.fedramp.gov/docs/20x/key-security-indicators/#ksi-svc-08-shared-resources)
Do not introduce or leave behind residual elements that could negatively affect confidentiality, integrity, or availability of federal customer data during operations.
New: Persistently review plans, procedures, and the state of information resources after making changes to limit and remove unwanted residual elements that would likely negatively affect the confidentiality, integrity, or availability of federal customer data.

KSI-TPR-03 Supply Chain Risk Management[¶](https://www.fedramp.gov/docs/20x/key-security-indicators/#ksi-tpr-03-supply-chain-risk-management)
Identify and prioritize mitigation of potential supply chain risks.
New: Persistently identify, review, and mitigate potential supply chain risks.

documents.title: Evidence collection and Inventory creation for AWS
documents.text:
This is a great summary of the 20x mindset:

> A large part of the reasoning for NOT providing more prescriptive guidance is to allow providers to present security information in a way that makes sense for the specific system. We presume that the service provider has already put a lot of thought into how to monitor risk for themselves and we want the agency to have access to that experience rather than trying to force fit data into specific templates or formats. And of course the independent validation and FedRAMP review process ensures that providers are transparent and comprehensive in providing this information.

I shared this with someone last week just starting to implement 20x and their response was relief that they won't have to redesign everything for FR. 

To the question in this thread of 
>what constitutes a "unique" inventory component

They understood that if multiple compute instances have the same image and config they can treat that as a single component. But at the same time they understood that they will need to provide evidence to support their claim of consistent inventory if they are going to show 1 that represents many components. Meaning if you say 1000 EC2s are accurately represented as 1 "unique" inventory component you should back that up with some evidence to verify how you know they are the same and there isn't drift between them. 

I think the VDR standard sets a good approach of asking for more frequency [on information resources that are likely to drift ](https://www.fedramp.gov/docs/20x/vulnerability-detection-and-response/#persistent-sample-detection:~:text=information%20resources%20that%20are%20likely%20to%20drift) vs [information resources that are NOT likely to drift ](https://www.fedramp.gov/docs/20x/vulnerability-detection-and-response/#persistent-drift-detection:~:text=information%20resources%20that%20are%20NOT%20likely%20to%20drift) and making it clear that sampling (a bit of a scary word in automation-based audit/assessment) can work on "[identical information resources](https://www.fedramp.gov/docs/20x/vulnerability-detection-and-response/#avoid-kevs:~:text=Providers%20MAY%20sample%20effectively%20identical%20information%20resources)". I think the key part is giving some evidence to back up the claim of identical resources so there is assurance that all resources are being accurately assessed. To Dan's point above, that type of evidence and what each CSP counts as 1 unique component will vary based on system architecture. Thankfully it won't always have to be IP addresses anymore 🙌 

-- Isaac (Paramify)

documents.title: RFC-0027 FedRAMP Rev5 Security Controls Baseline Update for AC, AT, AU, CA, and CM Control Families
documents.text:
Strong support for this cleanup work. The SCG alignment across AC, AT, and CM is overdue, and the BIR integration into CA-05 reporting cadence and CM-08 inventory requirements correctly reflects where the program is moving. A few specific comments follow.

On CM-12(1) Information Location – Automated Tools to Support Information Location. The proposed change body reads "CP-2 (8) - [essential]" which appears to be an incorrect copy from the adjacent CP-2(8) change in RFC-0028. The control being updated is CM-12(1), not CP-2(8). The parameter value for CM-12(1) should reference the CM-12(1) control family, and the FedRAMP-defined assignment should be specified **explicitly**. Recommend rewriting this change block so that the control ID and the parameter value align, and confirming the intended parameter value for CM-12(1) is established clearly in the published baseline.

On CM-06 Configuration Settings. The proposed introduction of a new Requirement 1 specifying Security Configuration Guideline instructions for top-level administrative account access, configuration, operation, and decommissioning is a meaningful substantive addition, not a simple SCG alignment. Suggest the Initial Outcome make this visibility explicit, and that the published materials flag this as a net-new CM-06 requirement for CSPs to scope in their implementation updates. Proactive CSPs will scope it correctly regardless. Making the addition visible up front prevents surprise during assessment.

On CA-05 Plan of Action and Milestones. The three-cadence structure tied to BIR adoption (monthly traditional, Ongoing Authorization Reports every three months for CCM BIR, Monthly Activity Report for VDR BIR) is a reasonable reflection of the pathway options. Recommend that CSPs be expected to document their pathway selection explicitly in the SSP so that the reporting cadence for any given service is unambiguous to assessors and agency customers at any point in time.

On AT-03 Role-based Training. Adding SCG content to role-based training is appropriate. The practical question is implementation timing. Suggest confirming that CSPs have until their next annual assessment cycle after CR26 publication to incorporate the updated content into their role-based training materials. Training content updates are a slow-cycle change, and the grace period should reflect that reality.

General posture. These changes are consistent with the direction of travel in RFC-0024, RFC-0026, and the BIR structure. The complexity introduced through pathway dependence is real, but manageable if the pathway selection is documented clearly at the SSP level - which will remain critical to agency customers. Thank you to the PMO for taking the time to sweep through these control families with a consistent lens.

Michael Schroeder

documents.title: RFC-0017 Persistent Validation and Assessment Standard
documents.text:
Please consider below gaps and recommendation:

FRR‑PVA‑01 (“Providers MUST maintain … summaries … for each KSI”)
Gap: The clause requires both “machine‑based processes …” and “human‑based processes …” for each KSI. It is ambiguous when either/or might suffice. Some KSIs may only realistically have one type of validation.
Recommendation: Clarify whether both machine‑based and human‑based validation must always apply, or allow “one or the other” if appropriate. Add “or” option where valid.

FRR‑PVA‑02 (“Providers MUST persistently run automated and non‑automated validation processes …”)
Gap: The dual requirement of “automated and non‑automated” may be burdensome or impractical for certain KSIs that naturally lend to one type only. Also lacks guidance on how to define the cycle, or tool maturity.
Recommendation: Permit flex‑model: “automated or non‑automated validation (or both) depending on KSI nature, with justification included”. Provide tool‑maturity guidance or criteria when automation is required.

FRR‑PVA‑03/04 (treat failures as vulnerabilities; include activity in VDR reports)
Gap: No remediation timeframe specified for validation failures, and no escalation path defined for recurring or systemic failures.
Recommendation: Add requirement: define maximum time to remediate persistent‑validation failures (e.g., within X days/hours by severity), and require escalation to senior management or external assessors if repeated failures occur.

FRR‑PVA‑T F‑LO / T F‑MO (timeframes)
Gap: Timeframes are defined for Low and Moderate impact systems—no timeframes are defined for High impact systems (if/when applicable).
Recommendation: If High impact (or “High” baseline) is in scope, define appropriate shorter validation cycles and assessment intervals for High impact systems. If High not in scope, clarify explicitly.

FRR‑PVA‑PA‑02 (assessment must allow full access to code/pipelines/etc)
Gap: Does not clearly define scope of “underlying code, pipelines, configurations, automation tools” in outsourced/hybrid arrangements—i.e., how to handle third‑party components or managed services.
Recommendation: Add requirement: providers must identify outsourced/hybrid service components, and ensure contractual/access arrangements permit assessors to verify underlying validation tooling/processes even in managed or third‑party contexts.

FRR‑PVA‑AA‑04 (assessors must use combination of quantitative and expert qualitative assessment)
Gap: Lack of defined quantitative metrics, benchmarks, or methodology; without guidance, quantitative component may be inconsistent or subjective across assessors.
Recommendation: Provide a reference or appendix with suggested quantitative metrics (e.g., % validated assets, time to detection/remediation, coverage %, false‑positive/false‑negative rates) and require providers to capture and report these metrics, with assessors evaluating them.

FRR‑PVA‑AA‑06 (assessors must not rely on screenshots/config dumps except when evaluating process that generates them)
Gap: Some KSIs (especially non‑technical ones, human/process ones) may inherently rely on point‑in‑time artifacts. The blanket prohibition could limit feasible assessment of non‑automated processes.
Recommendation: Clarify that for non‑technical/human KSIs, assessors may rely on structured evidence (logs, reports, process execution records) rather than only avoiding “point‑in‑time” screenshots; define acceptable formats for human‑process evidence.

documents.title: RFC-0028 FedRAMP Rev5 Security Controls Baseline Update for CP, IA, IR, MA, and MP Control Families
documents.text:
IA (Identification and Authentication), Phishing Resistant MFA:
This is the most consequential change in the batch. Explicitly stating that OTP, mobile push with number matching, and token based OTP are not phishing resistant provides clarity that the field has needed. CSPs have been interpreting “phishing resistant” differently for years, and this draws a clear line.
The operational concern is timeline. Many CSPs, particularly those serving agencies that haven’t adopted FIDO2/WebAuthn, are running authentication stacks built on exactly the methods this RFC now excludes. The RFC doesn’t specify a transition period for IA controls specifically. Will CSPs currently using number matching push (which many adopted because it was considered an upgrade from basic push) have until their next annual assessment to migrate? Or is this effective on publication? The answer determines whether this is an orderly transition or a fire drill.
Also: the requirement to document authentication factors in SSPs and Architecture Boundary Diagrams is good practice, but the Architecture Boundary Diagram is already one of the most labor intensive artifacts in a FedRAMP package. Adding per factor documentation for every authentication flow, including those inherited from IaaS/PaaS providers, could significantly expand the diagram. Is the expectation that CSPs document their own authentication factors only, or also the factors implemented by underlying service providers within the authorization boundary?
IR-06 (Incident Reporting), FedRAMP Secure Inbox:
Adding the FSI as the centralized point of contact for incident reporting and VDR related communications is a sensible consolidation. The question is about response rate expectations. The RFC references “appropriate response rates” per FSI Guidance, but from the CSP side, the FSI has historically been unidirectional. CSPs submit; responses come when they come. If FedRAMP is now establishing response rate expectations for CSPs, reciprocal SLAs for FedRAMP acknowledgment and triage would build confidence that the inbox is actively monitored and not a queue that grows faster than it drains.
MA (Maintenance), Nationality Documentation:
This mirrors the same requirement in RFC-0029 for personnel security. The policy question is the same in both places: what does “where applicable” mean? Some CSPs operate globally and use maintenance contractors across multiple countries. Others are US only. “Where applicable” without criteria leaves CSPs guessing whether they need to document nationality for every contractor or only when a specific condition triggers. Even a short list of conditions (clearance requirements, physical access to federal data, access to FedRAMP boundary systems) would make this actionable.
CP-2(8), Essential Parameter:
Adding “[essential]” as the parameter value for CP-2(8) is fine, but this same parameter reference appears in CM-12(1) in RFC-0027 without explanation. These should be cross referenced so reviewers understand the relationship between contingency planning essentiality designations and information location tracking.

documents.title: Balancing FedRAMP Rev5 against improvements to FedRAMP 20x
documents.text:
Posting our VDR beta feedback here at the request of the PMO:

- **Developing a new reporting methodology was significant.** I basically have had to build this from scratch. I started with a manual approach to understand the data model and build evaluation logic during the beta period. This was a necessary first step, not a target state. Automation via cloud-native tooling APIs is planned for subsequent cycles, using the schema and decision logic developed during the beta as the specification.
- **The terminology is hard to get used to.** There is something intuitive about Critical, High, Medium... vs N5, N4, N3... (aka N-rating) I'm sure that will become muscle memory with time.
- Despite more awkward terminology, **the LEV/NLEV + N-rating approach is far better than CVSS** - especially in light of NIST's recent announcement about CVEs in NVD. Also, with the LEV/NEV approach we can now actually use all the good exploitability data from our scans that the current process basically ignores. 
- **Vendor dependencies have no explicit treatment in the framework.** A finding where a fix exists in an upstream library but has not been incorporated by the image maintainer is somewhere in the middle ground between Remediating and Accepted. 
  - I like the current requirement to check in every 30 days. A hard decision may be needed at some point. For example, if the vendor is unlikely to do certain patching or is simply not maintaining the project at all, the current process is a good way to monitor this. We may ultimately select a more secure vendor. I created "Disposition categories" in my reports - and noted these as "Monitoring - fix deferred". 
- **The IRV definition is conceptually correct but practically difficult to apply in containerized environments.** IIn GKE, EKS, and AKS deployments — now the dominant architecture for FedRAMP Moderate systems — all containers sit behind an ingress layer. Automated network exposure tooling does not resolve this ambiguity — container-level exposure flags typically show no direct internet exposure for all containers including the ingress controller itself. Recommend FedRAMP publish IRV evaluation guidance specific to containerized architectures, including how to treat the ingress layer as an IRV boundary. (written by Claude)
- **The machine-readable reporting requirement remains ambiguous**.  My reports are based on an assumed schema with output to JSON and CSV. Will this be acceptable? FedRAMP should publish a reference schema so CSPs building automated pipelines have a consistent target.
- **The RFC defines "Accepted" and "False Positive" but does not consider other response states.** Without defined categories for findings that are actively remediating, monitoring for a vendor fix, or blocked on a third-party image maintainer, machine-readable reporting will be inconsistent across CSPs. In my beta reports, I created disposition categories.
- **Our agency is aware of this change**, but doesn't fully understand it yet. They are receptive to it, but will need to overcome the learning curve (noting also terminology). Plus, I've introduced some of my own disposition categories to add more terminology.
  - however, if the agency has multiple CSP, how does a standard emerge if I'm introducing my own disposition categories for example.

documents.title: RFC-0036 FedRAMP 20x Class D Cloud-Hosted Pilot Requirements
documents.text:
I am in agreement with almost all of these requirements. Some might believe these are difficult, but if you are using enough automation and AI assistance then it is actually simpler and more secure to achieve than legacy rev 5. Especially, if you consider the time when class D will be fully released there will be even better tools available to assist in achieving the certification. 

VER-EVA-IOC - I have seen this in practice and definitely useful exercise when discovering a past vulnerability existed in a codebase. Allowing flexibility on level of effort to search for IOCs is good too as long as CSPs document how they searched, as reviewing a years' worth of logs with a script is easier than hiring a forensics team to search for IOCs. All organizations have vulnerabilities at one point or another even if they don't admit it openly so to me this is a valuable check.

FRC-FRA-FOD - The FOCI ones are useful and important going forward as it provides better visibility into the overall setup of an organization. I agree with the setup too where it puts the details in the hands of the agency due to sensitivity of some information. It is clear adversaries have been using FOCI as a way in for a long time as seen in DOW posture to this problem, so it makes sense FedRAMP aligns. FOCI documentation is a positive step in transparency and a powerful security signal when used properly. 

FRC-CLD-PCD - Agree on the progressive steps to achieve class D. Gating the process is useful as we have seen spun up fake startups especially with AI attempt to map out the class D ecosystem. Any company that jumps right into class D without the proper experience should require more review. This allows a vetting period and ensures companies are actually ready and saves everyone time and money. 

FRC-CLD-CCH - Agree with this change, though it opens up an inheritance gap if CSPs don't architect around it properly. If a Class D CSP uses standard Class C serverless or managed PaaS options, an underlying platform support engineer (who may not meet Class D suitability expectations) could potentially access sensitive data or source code.
 
KSI-IAM-MPI and KSI-IAM-MST should block this threat since a CSP typically cannot verify 3rd-party cloud support engineers persistently, the CSP should be forced to use technical controls like Confidential VMs, CMEK, and gated support access. 

FRC-CLD-CTP - Agree with this requirement too since it creates a cohesive secure system when the data can be tracked through vetted providers. It is scoped well to actual risk of federal data which makes it achievable for CSPs.

Overall, these requirements are clear and reasonable for class D.

documents.title: Policies needed for 20x
documents.text:
I'll just add up front to be super clear that **none** of the Rev5 SSP Appendices are required by 20x - all of the expected materials are addressed in Key Security Indicators (especially in the KSI-AFR family). 

I also want to point out that when KSIs say "document X" it doesn't necessary require a human memo written in prose. For [KSI-AFR-04 Vulnerability Detection and Response](https://www.fedramp.gov/docs/key-security-indicators/#ksi-afr-04-vulnerability-detection-and-response) for example one could theoretically document everything necessary in the configuration of a tool/platform that can do all of those things then present the configuration itself as documentation.

Generally this type of approach would be preferred; don't much care what you think you should be doing but we really do care what you're actually doing.

Final related point - a lot of the underlying FRR's point towards a need for documentation or similar in a way that can be mapped to some KSI's. For example, [KSI-CMT-04 Change Management Procedure](https://www.fedramp.gov/docs/key-security-indicators/#ksi-cmt-04-change-management-procedure) requires you to always follow a documented change management procedure while the SCN, PVA, and VDR all require you to do a bunch of things with changes in various places - so all of those need to be mapped to KSI-CMT-04. (Note: the updated KSI here is "always follow" not just "have" a change management procedure ;)

Other things that might benefit from a policy, even if it's informal for just grounding before implementing and formalizing:

- Any time something is done [_persistently_](https://www.fedramp.gov/docs/fedramp-definitions/#persistently) there must be a documented set of activities (though this can and should be documented in code whenever possible, sometimes it will make sense to have written goals too)
- [FRR-MAS-01 Cloud Service Offering Identification](https://www.fedramp.gov/docs/minimum-assessment-scope/#frr-mas-01-cloud-service-offering-identification) certainly would benefit from a plan for how the MAS will be maintained
- [FRR-ADS-01 Public Information](https://www.fedramp.gov/docs/authorization-data-sharing/#frr-ads-01-public-information) plus the following ADS requirements would probably benefit from a plan about how this will be maintained 
- [FRR-ADS-03 Detailed Service List](https://www.fedramp.gov/docs/authorization-data-sharing/#frr-ads-03-detailed-service-list) **definitely** would benefit from a plan, especially since it seems like no cloud service provider does a good job of maintaining such lists already.
- [FRR-CCM-01 Ongoing Authorization Reports](https://www.fedramp.gov/docs/collaborative-continuous-monitoring/#frr-ccm-01-ongoing-authorization-reports) et al - folks definitely should have policies on how they're going to handle all the CCM stuff
- [FRR-RSC-01 Top-Level Administrative Accounts Guidance](https://www.fedramp.gov/docs/recommended-secure-configuration/#frr-rsc-01-top-level-administrative-accounts-guidance) et al probably needs a plan

etc.

Basically we didn't eliminate prose with 20x (far from it), but we've tried to limit it to be used for specific goals that are validated by automation. Whenever possible these plans or policies should be as simple as heck and align with whatever is in the best interest of the provider.

**Random fun fact:** In the phase 1 pilot a BUNCH of folks had an RPO/RTO policy written out that said things like "our RPO is within 6 hours" then had their systems configured to do snapshots every 24 hours or similar. It was kinda mind blowing and shows why the written policy isn't that important.

documents.title: RFC-0030 FedRAMP Rev5 Security Controls Baseline Update for RA, SA, SC, SI, and SR Control Families
documents.text:
Overall, we welcome the updates proposed in this RFC. The alignment of RA-5 parameters with the VDR BIR, the cleanup of outdated references, and the clarifications around configuration baselines and operational directives represent meaningful progress in modernizing FedRAMP's Rev5 requirements. We appreciate FedRAMP's continued effort to reduce burden on CSPs while maintaining rigorous security expectations.

**RA-5 -** The proposed language for the traditional Rev5 path under RA-5(a) reads:

> [monthly operating system/infrastructure; monthly web applications (including APIs) and databases for traditional Rev5 processes]

This same scan type enumeration appears repeatedly throughout this RFC — across the FedRAMP-Defined Assignment/Selection Parameters, Additional FedRAMP Requirements and Guidance, and Continuous Monitoring Periodicity sections — and the concern below applies to all instances.
Container scanning is absent from this language. This is not new — the original Rev5 baseline predated FedRAMP's separate container scanning guidance and was never updated to explicitly include containers alongside OS/infrastructure, web application, and database scans. This RFC represents an opportunity to correct that gap, and we strongly urge FedRAMP to do so.
FedRAMP should explicitly confirm in this RFC whether container scans are required for CSPs on the traditional Rev5 path. If they are — which we believe they should be given the prevalence of containerized workloads in modern cloud architectures and the existence of FedRAMP container scanning guidance — every instance of the traditional Rev5 scan type enumeration in this RFC must be updated to include containers explicitly. Implicit coverage under "infrastructure" is insufficient; OS/infrastructure, web applications, and databases are each called out as distinct scan types, and containers warrant the same explicit treatment.
Proposed language wherever this enumeration appears for the traditional Rev5 path:

> [monthly operating system/infrastructure; monthly web applications (including APIs) and databases; monthly containers for traditional Rev5 processes]

Leaving containers unaddressed in this update would perpetuate an existing gap at exactly the moment FedRAMP has the opportunity to close it.

**SI-8 -** The SI-8 guidance — both current and proposed — addresses DMARC only in the context of outbound email sent on behalf of the government, but leaves several common CSO email scenarios unaddressed. We request FedRAMP explicitly clarify the following:

Spam protection (SI-8): Is spam protection required only when the CSO sends email, only when it receives email, or both? Is there any SI-8 obligation for CSOs that neither send nor receive email as part of their offering?
DMARC (outbound): Does the policy=reject requirement apply only when sending on behalf of the government, or also when the CSO sends email from CSP-owned domains for any purpose?
DMARC (inbound): If a CSO accepts inbound email and controls its own spam filtering — without delegating that control to customers — is the CSO expected to enforce DMARC rejection on inbound mail failures?

The existing guidance is explicit for the government-email-sending scenario but silent on these adjacent cases, creating inconsistency in how CSPs implement SI-8 and how 3PAOs assess it.

**SC-13 -** We applaud the addition of explicit guidance directing CSPs to follow FedRAMP instructions for cryptographic modules listed as "historical" in the CMVP database. This has been a recurring source of confusion during the authorization process, and surfacing it directly in the baseline makes compliance expectations more evident to both CSPs and assessors.

documents.title: RFC-0014 Phase Two Security Indicators
documents.text:
**Main Comment**
Human-led penetration testing is critical for validating that these security controls actually work in the real world. While automated tools and continuous monitoring are fantastic for baseline security, there's simply no substitute for skilled penetration testers actively trying to break things. They catch vulnerabilities that control assessments and automated scans miss entirely, things like complex privilege escalation chains, business logic flaws, cross-site scripting in dynamic content, SQL injection in custom code, insecure direct object references, and authentication bypass scenarios. These are the kinds of issues that only surface when someone is actively thinking like an attacker and chaining together multiple minor issues into major compromises.

Human-led penetration testing is particularly valuable for validating the effectiveness of multiple KSIs working together as a defensive system. For example, while KSI-CNA indicators can show you have network segmentation in place and KSI-IAM can validate your access controls exist, only a penetration test will reveal if an attacker can bypass these through credential stuffing, session hijacking, or exploiting trust relationships between systems. I (and I’m sure agency customers) would strongly encourage explicitly incorporating at least annual human-led penetration testing (and where appropriate, red team exercises) as a validation mechanism for 20x. This is especially important for Moderate authorizations where sophisticated threat actors are a real concern.  At the end of the day these controls need to stand up to actual attack attempts and penetration testing should be part of the 20x moderate baseline. 

_Edit based on Pete clarification that Human-led penetration testing and red teaming is part of the VDR standard_ 
This should be made clear that these are requirements, Pen Test report is the thing agencies ask to review more than any other document.  it would make sense to make this a stand alone KSI to clear up any confusion and allow agencies to automatically pull pen test reports through their GRC tool. 

**Minor comments.** 
> KSI-CED-01:
> -  Updated: Ensure all employees receive security and privacy awareness training, incident response training, and are familiar with all relevant policies and procedures.
 
Including IR training in KSI-CED-01 could create confusion about training requirements. While all employees need basic incident response awareness, dedicated IR teams require specialized training that belongs in KSI-CED-03.

By calling out IR training here, CSPs might think they've satisfied all IR training requirements and miss the need for role-based advanced training. I'd suggest either clarifying that KSI-CED-01 only covers basic company-wide IR awareness within general security training, or preferably, removing IR training from KSI-CED-01 entirely and consolidating IR training requirements under KSI-CED-03. This would provide clearer delineation between basic awareness for all staff versus specialized training for IR teams

> KSI-PIY-06:
> -  Updated: Have staff and budget for security commensurate with the size, complexity, scope, executive priorities, and risk of the service offering that demonstrates commitment to delivering a secure service.

This control is too vague to provide meaningful validation. Any CSP could likely pass without proving their security program is adequately resourced. For public companies, this information already exists in SEC filings (10-K, 10-Q), consider allowing them to reference those directly.

While FedRAMP wants to showcase automation, this is a poor candidate for it. Automated pulls of budget numbers and security headcount don't demonstrate whether a CSP's security program is appropriately funded for their risk profile. The metrics would be superficial and wouldn't show if resources are sufficient or effectively allocated. Consider removing this KSI. 
 
   
> KSI-SVC-01:
> -   Updated: Continuously evaluate machine-based information resources for opportunities to improve security

This control is too high-level and needs clearer scope definition through an accompanying FedRAMP standard or requirements document. Without proper scoping, CSPs could pass validation while missing critical areas. For example, a CSP might demonstrate IaaS security using a CSPM tool like Wiz but neglect OS-level hardening or Kubernetes infrastructure security. This creates gaps where automated validation passes for one layer while vulnerabilities exist in others. Please specify which infrastructure layers and components must be included in security posture monitoring to ensure comprehensive coverage.

> KSI-CED-03:
> - Require role-specific training for development and engineering staff covering best practices for delivering secure software.
 
Building on my KSI-CED-01 comment, this control should explicitly include incident response staff alongside development and engineering staff. IR teams require specialized role-based training that goes beyond general security awareness and should be specifically called out here.

> KSI-SVC-10
> -  Remove unwanted information promptly, including from backups if appropriate.

While this maps to data retention controls (SI-12/18), I feel this should be more scoped to data spill cleanup and moved to the INR family. If we want to keep this more of like just a data retention control, then change the word “unwanted”.   Unwanted to me more reads as IR-9 information spillage response.

documents.title: RFC-0012 FedRAMP Continuous Vulnerability Management Standard
documents.text:
First of all, thank you for providing the opportunity to deliver feedback on FedRAMP’s direction. Overall, FedRAMP is moving in a direction that aligns with how GitHub thinks about risk management, namely the prioritization of `credibly exploitable` vulnerabilities and their actual impact to our organization. This alignment does enable a few positive things to happen:

- We can properly prioritize actual risk to our organization over and above other vulnerabilities that are mitigated or not impactful.  
- Hygiene patching remains important, but we gain a great deal of flexibility with the longer timelines afforded for `All detected vulnerabilities`.  
- Alignment (or enablement) of logical grouping of vulnerabilities. This is already how we operate as an organization, but we have to instead group by asset & CVE for our current con-mon reporting.

The move away from previously difficult to parse language is also greatly appreciated.

That said, we do have some specific feedback that would be useful to drive further clarification within the standard.

## Definitions

### `Credibly Exploitable Vulnerability`

We believe the intent behind `Credibly Exploitable Vulnerability (CEV)` is good. Our concerns stem from a lack of clarity on what constitutes a `CEV`. The way the standard is written, a good deal is left up to the organization and security program to determine. This *is* a good thing, we worry however that this will devolve into requiring large justifications for many vulnerabilities.

A sample criteria or recommendation in an appendix could be a useful tool to guide the conversation between organizations and their sponsoring agencies. While it’s obvious that anything on the CISA KEV list likely belongs as a `CEV`, and likewise if we have another intelligence source giving us reason to believe there is an exploit available then it qualifies. On the less clear side of things, EPSS is a useful tool for triaging and ranking priorities. Is there an EPSS (Exploit Prediction Scoring System) score that should escalate a finding to `CEV`? Probably, but the methodology here is likely to vary highly between organizations.

How does physical access play into this? Do we consider physical exploits as `CEV`? Should we include notes about the security of our datacenters? What about when utilizing cloud vendors?

### Remediation & Mitigation

We think directly referencing the definition in `NIST SP 800-216` makes more sense than re-defining it in this standard.

### False Positives

We often see scanning vendors detect all possible CVEs against a kernel, even when the exploitable kernel module is not present. For example, bluetooth vulnerabilities on Ubuntu kernels. This code is not loaded or present, but due to the way scanning vendors detect CVEs, often they are just included in as a result of basic version matching. Would these be considered `Fully Mitigated` or `False Positives`? We currently consider these `False Positives`.

### Risk Adjustment

Something not covered in the document is the ability to risk adjust vulnerabilities. Currently, we are only allowed to adjust the risk score of a vulnerability by one level (High \-\> Moderate for example). Clarifying that we have greater control to make risk based decisions here would be helpful.

documents.title: General discussion / Q&A on Rev5 improvements and changes in 2026
documents.text:
I say the following in my personal professional capacity and do not represent the opinion of my employer in any way.

As a FedRAMP Audit SME and a private citizen I am raising a Conscientious Objection to both this decision and the way it was made.  

In summary, the removal of minimum requirements in the form of FedRAMP-specific Parameters and Requirements without a dedicated Request-For-Comment period is a sharp decline in the quality of the FedRAMP Certification as well as a direct violation of the requirement for dedicated public feedback.

1. The FedRAMP-specific Parameters and Requirements represent a significant portion of the absolute minimum-security standard that any Cloud Service must adhere to when selling to the Federal Government.  Summarily removing those Parameters and Requirements means that you are removing that minimum.  Removing the minimum means that Federal Agencies can no longer expect any solid security requirements associated with FedRAMP.
2. A market-driven approach to regulation is a misunderstanding of the market and regulation.  Regulations exist to protect the consumer, in this case Federal Agencies and the data of US citizens that they hold.  The market exists to make money.  The two can be aligned, but frankly often are not.  A company can choose to sacrifice security and privacy for cost savings if there is no regulation.  The customers may not even know about this until their information has been compromised.  By the time the market corrects, the data is already exposed and damage has already been done.  The customers are USA Federal Agencies and the data at risk is from USA Federal Agencies and the taxpayers that support them.  Regulation exists to prevent that from even being an option to companies serving the Federal Government.
3. Humans are lazy and not all companies are security-centric.  I still have to have conversations with employees about why multi-factor authentication is necessary.  I still have to explain why STIGs are better than CIS Level 2 in most cases.  I still have to use FedRAMP requirements as justifications for the business to choose the more expensive, but more secure and private route.  Removing the FedRAMP Parameters and Requirements is hamstringing those discussions.
4. FedRAMP exists to make a uniform approach for Federal Agencies to select Cloud Service Providers with a minimum set of security and privacy requirements.  The uniformity of parameters and requirements is a large part of the uniformity of the overall security and privacy that was the goal of FedRAMP.
5. The Notice that includes this massive change to the program is referencing a tangentially related topic.  The original RFC was about specific verbiage changes to the FedRAMP Parameters and Guidance, not their total removal.  The public was not given the opportunity to directly comment on this change.  Isolated comments that suggest this change may be desirable is analogous to the situation with putting pricing information on the marketplace.  Assorted commentary from interested parties made it seem like that would be the best way forward, but a dedicated forum on the subject showed the outright rejection of the premise.  In this case we were not even given that opportunity.

I am very supportive of VDR, CCM, SCG, and most other changes represented in CR26 because they will be an improvement to the security and privacy of the Cloud Service Offerings.  Careful risk-based assessments of a broader definition of vulnerabilities, and a focus on mitigating that risk is a big step forward for securing the software, configurations, and supply-chain.  Bringing together all USA Federal agencies with a stake in the Cloud Service Offering to understand the security and compliance of the offering is a big step forward in relationships with Federal agencies and transparency on security and compliance.  However, the removal of FedRAMP-specific parameters and requirements can only result in a sharp decline in the security and privacy of those Cloud Service Offerings to the detriment of the FedRAMP program, the USA Federal Agencies, and the taxpayers that both serve.  I am sorry, but I must object to this decision.

documents.title: Rev5 questions and discussion on the Consolidated Rules for 2026 (or Legacy)
documents.text:
The schemas aren't designed to enforce any rules, so the requirements in there are based around the minimum structure necessary. It doesn't matter if something is optional or required in the schema itself when it comes to determining if providing that information is optional or required.

There may be situations where a provider wants to supply information about a vulnerability that doesn't have a PAIN rating - for example, the PAIN rating isn't applicable for false positives.
