documents.title: RFC-0012 FedRAMP Continuous Vulnerability Management Standard
documents.text:
On behalf of Confluent, we appreciate the updated Continuous Vulnerability Management Standard proposed in RFC-0012 and the opportunity to comment on it. 

Overall, we think the intent of the proposed Standard goes in the right direction of modernizing the vulnerability scanning and management requirements for CSPs. We’d like to especially highlight the move towards contextual prioritization of vulnerabilities that goes beyond just using CVSS scores. Having said that, we have some concerns regarding aspects of the proposal we’d like to see addressed by the FedRAMP 20x program, in order to avoid ambiguities and set up CSPs for success. 

### 1. Applicability and Timelines of Standard to 20x Authorizations Post-RFC 

The most pressing question is whether the final version of the RFC will immediately apply to all 20x Moderate Authorizations on Day One, or if we can initially use existing Rev5-compatible artifacts for the sponsor-less 20x Moderate process. As a reminder, Confluent is currently going through the FedRAMP 20x Phase One for Low Authorization and we were planning to continue to Moderate Authorization in the FedRAMP 20x Phase Two immediately afterwards.

The RFC does state that the standard will apply to all FedRAMP 20x authorizations upon formalization. However, if this is the case, it would effectively prevent any CSP including ourselves from proceeding with FedRAMP 20x Phase Two when it opens, as implementing these new requirements would take several months at best. 

While some timelines have been shared with participants of the “FedRAMP Vulnerability Management Special Event” that took place on July 30th, 2025 (i.e. closed beta, public beta, 6-9 months for full release etc), it’s unclear how these will affect Phase Two and the requirements for participation. 

**Recommendation**: Provide clear written timeline instructions and which (if any) requirements of the new post-RFC ConMon Standard will be applicable specifically to CSPs waiting to join the upcoming 20x Phase Two for Moderate Authorization – is it going to apply as a whole on Day One, or can CSPs join Phase Two with their existing Rev5-related processes and gradually switch to the new Standard over time.

### 2. Interpretation of Credibly Exploitable Vulnerabilities 

The RFC introduces new vulnerability attributes and terms without providing guidance or instructions to help us translate them into practical business logic for how a CSP should determine applicability. A critical element, as highlighted in the SLA table, is whether a CVE finding is considered "Credibly Exploitable.": _A vulnerability where a likely threat actor with knowledge of the vulnerability would likely be able to gain unauthorized access, cause harm, disrupt operations, or otherwise have an undesired adverse impact; vulnerabilities must be reachable and not fully mitigated to be credibly exploitable._

We understand the intent, but this definition in our view is open to interpretation. It's unclear if this refers to CISA KEVs or a CVE with an EPSS score above a certain threshold or a combination of other factors. Relatedly, currently the FedRAMP PMO under Rev5 does not accept Temporal Metrics like EPSS. The RFC's impact on this EPSS acceptance policy is ambiguous, requiring clarification from the FedRAMP 20x office. 

**Recommendation**: Provide clearer guidance on how CSPs should interpret this definition as different CSPs will treat this in various ways. Or, if the CSPs actually have the agency of interpreting it depending on their environment (which seems to be strongly implied by **FRR-CVM-04**), add a specific written mention for that so that there is no misunderstanding. Additionally, provide written clarity on whether EPSS scores and/or other threat intelligence can be leveraged by CSPs to determine Credibly Exploitable Vulnerabilities (and also the Potential Adverse Impact). 

### 3. Burden of Required Contextual Analysis for Vulnerabilities 

If the answer to the above described concern is that CSPs have the agency to determine Credibly Exploitable, then while **FRR-CVM-04** is posed as a positive, it has the potential to turn into a big negative based on the current language of _MUST adjust the risk [...] factoring for at least criticality, reachability, exploitability, detectability, prevalence, and mitigation, to determine if vulnerabilities are credibly exploitable and the potential adverse impact of exploitation._

In the interest of keeping this comment submission manageable length-wise, consider that we have a similar concern as point `1` in this previously submitted comment: https://github.com/FedRAMP/community/discussions/59#discussioncomment-14011556. Our concern is not so much with the establishment of a new definition, but the requirement to force CSPs to take into account all the contextual factors mentioned. Implementing all these can become a burdensome process engineering-wise that will eventually spill into manual effort and will go against the spirit of 20x’s focus on automating vulnerability management for ConMon.

**Recommendation**: Adjust the language in **FRR-CVM-04** to give CSPs the agency to leverage a selection among the factors mentioned (what makes more sense in their environment) versus being forced to rigorously perform all of these types of analysis for each and every vulnerability found by a scanner which won’t have this information in the first place.

### 4. NVD CVSS vs Other CVSS Sources 

There is no explicit mention about this in the RFC, although we assume the prior Rev5 guidance applies. There, NVD is explicitly mentioned as the source of CVSS scores CSPs must use (CVSSv3 first, then CVSSv2, then scanner severity if the aforementioned don’t exist). Our experience has been that there are many cases where NVD provides inflated scores compared to other CVSS sources closer to the vulnerability being identified, e.g. a host OS package vulnerability could be rated as a Critical or High by NVD, but Medium by RedHat/Amazon who are closer to the problem and understand the impact better. Forcing CSPs to use NVD has been a source of frustration in these cases. 

**Recommendation**: There is an opportunity as this new RFC gets defined to add language regarding CSPs being able to select the base CVSS score (e.g. in **FRR-CVM-04**) from the source (e.g. Redhat, Ubuntu, Amazon, etc) that makes the most sense for their environment (and fallback to NVD if such alternative doesn’t exist), versus a blanket requirement to always utilize NVD CVSS scores. 

### 5. Potential Adverse Impact vs CVSS-based Severities (Rev5) 

The three current Rev5 Severities (High, Moderate, Low) have been replaced by the "Potential Adverse Impact," another NIST term with five levels. We have a similar concern as the other newly introduced terms in the ConMon process around proper interpretation of this by CSPs. This is another area where spillover into manual evaluation of CVEs will likely take place, contradicting the spirit of automating the ConMon process. Ironically the RFC itself labels this new attribute as qualitative rather than quantitative, showcasing the problem. 

Apart from the issue above – that Engineering rigor or manual effort will be required by a CSP to perform this new analysis versus a CVSS-based translation into a Severity rating – the end result is questionable. This is because the current Remediation SLA matrix (shown under "Quick Reference - Vulnerability Response Time Frames") follows a bit of an all-or-nothing approach whereby it “doesn’t matter” what the Potential Adverse Impact is, if the CVE is deemed Credibly Exploitable. Putting the doesn't matter in quotes as there is a difference of course if the Impact is Low, but in practice it seems a futile effort to try to accurately determine this new Potential Adverse Impact level with great rigor only for the CSP to fall into the 3 or 7 day window in most cases anyway. 

**Recommendation**: Provide guidance for how CVSS scores (adjusted per **FRR-CVM-04**) can be mapped to the new Potential Adverse Impact. Interestingly NIST SP 800-30 actually tries to do this with some numerical values (range of 1-10 and 1-100) which theoretically could be mapped to equivalent CVSS score ranges. 

### 6. New Aggressive Remediation SLAs

In the interest of keeping this comment submission manageable length-wise, consider that we have a similar concern as point `2` in this previously submitted comment: https://github.com/FedRAMP/community/discussions/59#discussioncomment-14023844 

**Recommendation**: Tighten the definitions of various terms as asked above, and in addition and as a follow up to concern `5` above (`Potential Adverse Impact vs CVSS-based Severities (Rev5)`), break down the SLA table into less aggressive timelines depending on the Potential Adverse Impact, for example moving lower Adverse Impact levels from the first two rows downwards in the table. 

### 7. Network Reachability Requirements 

In the interest of keeping this comment submission manageable length-wise, consider that we have a similar concern as point `1` in this previously submitted comment: https://github.com/FedRAMP/community/discussions/59#discussioncomment-14072158 

**Recommendation**: Tighten the definitions of this term, and in addition and as a follow up to concern `6` above (`New Aggressive Remediation SLAs`), consider the suggestion posted in this previously submitted comment: https://github.com/FedRAMP/community/discussions/59#discussioncomment-14156740 for **FRR-CVM-TM-09** (last 2 paragraphs at the bottom of the comment) regarding SLA and acceptable risk level for non-internet reachable vulnerabilities (although we don’t necessarily endorse the updated definition the commenter suggested for **FRD-CVM-07**). 

### 8. Unauthenticated Scanning Requirements 

The introduction of an unauthenticated scanning requirement introduces confusion to CSPs running heavily containerized environments and in our opinion is a step backwards. Opening up network access where it doesn't exist, or even container ports just for the CSP to be able to say that they performed an unauthenticated scan, will introduce risk in the environment for no benefit compared to the existing Rev5 mandated authenticated requirements (which for containers could be satisfied by image scanning). 

Furthermore, CSPs could have selected network topologies and architectures that are ephemeral based (e.g. creation of new networks on the fly for a server workload that goes away after some time), where network access to and from a "scanning network" for network-based unauthenticated scans to be performed wasn't taken into account - but host OS agents are used instead for authenticated scans on compute assets. This new requirement changes that and these complicated topologies will require engineering-heavy programmatic network access to be setup to and from a "scanning network" only to adhere to this unauthenticated scanning requirement while at the same time authenticated scans can take place (e.g. via host OS agents). 

**Recommendation**: Explicitly make it so that if authenticated scanning takes place on the asset (e.g. via a host OS agent, or image scanning), it supersedes the need for (network based) unauthenticated scanning. If you don’t agree with the recommendation, explicitly mention what should CSPs do in the case of containers where we think any sort of "unauthenticated" scanning doesn't make sense.

### 9. CISA KEVs Remediation Timelines

In the interest of keeping this comment submission manageable length-wise, consider that we have a similar concern as point `5` in this previously submitted comment: https://github.com/FedRAMP/community/discussions/59#discussioncomment-14011556 

**Recommendation**: Define more concrete and realistic remediation timelines for CISA KEVs, rather than relying on the published due dates in the KEV database as stated in **FRR-CVM-TM-03**, as most of the time when KEVs appear in the environment they are immediately overdue.

documents.title: RFC-0017 Persistent Validation and Assessment Standard
documents.text:
```
FRR-PVA-01
Providers MUST maintain simple high-level summaries of at least the following for each Key Security Indicator:
Goals for how it will be implemented and validated, including clear pass/fail criteria and traceability
The consolidated information resources that will be validated (this should be a high-level consolidated summary such as “all employees with privileged access that are members of the Admin group”)
The machine-based processes for validation and the persistent cycle on which they will be run
The human-based processes for validation and the persistent cycle on which they will be run
Current implementation status
Any clarifications or responses to the assessment summary
```
Why are CSPs going to determine which KSI's are needed, what criteria constitutes a pass/fail? Fox guarding the hen house. KSIs need to be defined by a central authority like the PMO at a minimum. 

```
FRR-PVA-02
Providers MUST persistently run automated and non-automated validation processes on the cycle documented in their Key Security Indicators, following the requirements and recommendations outlined in FRR-PVA-TF regarding timeframes for persistent validation and reporting; this process is called persistent validation and is part of vulnerability detection.
```
What is a non-automated validation process? How is that any different than the current Rev5 structure of control-defined interval monitoring of the control objective? Who performs the non-automated validation? When does the non-automated validation get validated by a third party?
```
FRR-PVA-04
Providers MUST include persistent validation activity in the reports on vulnerability detection and response activity required by the FedRAMP Vulnerability Detection and Response Standard.
```
So based on this, the Key Security Indicator is being treated in the same way as a Rev5 vulnerability. It receives a risk rating that will be, automated? How is that risk rating determined, will it be based on the nature of the KSI? Since the CSP defines the KSIs, that also means that the CSP will have unilateral and unchecked authority to rate KSI severities without any oversight. With the transition to 20x, all the existing institutional knowledge about Rev5 risk rating severities will be tossed out the window. 
Repeating previous feedback in this same comment, KSIs should not be determined in a vacuum by the CSP. 
```
FRR-PVA-05
Providers MUST track significant changes that impact their Key Security Indicator goals and validation processes while following the requirements and recommendations in the FedRAMP Significant Change Notification Standard; if such significant changes are not properly tracked and supplied to all necessary assessors then a full Initial FedRAMP Assessment may be required in place of the expected Persistent FedRAMP Assessment.
```
What is the threshold for a full initial assessment? Would this be a 20x or a Rev5 assessment? 
```
FRR-PVA-TF-LO-01
Providers MUST complete the validation processes for Key Security Indicators of non-machine-based information resources at least once every 3 months.
```
How is this an improvement from Rev5? The control-defined processes exist to validate most KSIs at an equal or greater frequency than quarterly.
```
FRR-PVA-TF-LO-02
Providers MUST complete the validation processes for Key Security Indicators of machine-based information resources at least once every 7 days.
```
Since the CSP defines the KSI, do they also define what is machine-based information or not? PMO should define what KSIs are machine based. 
```
FRR-PVA-TF-MO-01
Providers MUST complete the validation processes for Key Security Indicators of non-machine-based information resources at least once every 3 months.
```
How is this an improvement from Rev5? The control-defined processes exist to validate most KSIs at an equal or greater frequency than quarterly.
```
FRR-PVA-TF-MO-02
Providers MUST complete the validation processes for Key Security Indicators of machine-based information resources at least once every 3 days.
```
Since the CSP defines the KSI, do they also define what is machine-based information or not? PMO should define what KSIs are machine based. 
```
FRR-PVA-TF-MO-03
Providers MUST complete a Persistent FedRAMP Assessment at least once every 9 months.
```
Nine months is just awkward. It should stay at an interval that can be easily planned out, year to year. Either 3, 6, or 12 month intervals. 
```
FRR-PVA-PA-02
Providers MUST allow a complete assessment of validation procedures (including underlying code, pipelines, configurations, automation tools, etc.) by all necessary assessors.
```
A majority of assessors are not able to read code. This will end up being solved by ChatGPT or Gemini, which will generate AI slop that does not enhance the security posture of any CSP. 
```
FRR-PVA-PA-03
Providers SHOULD be prepared and willing to provide technical explanations, demonstrations, and proof to all necessary assessors regarding their assertions of the technical capabilities they employ to meet Key Security Indicators and to provide validations.
```
So instead of defending the system configuration, the CSP will be defending their KSI methodology and how they are technically validated at each defined interval? This would be like asking a CSP how Nessus identified vulnerabilities instead of what vulnerabilities are on the sytem. 
```
FRR-PVA-PA-04
Providers MUST be responsive to recommendations and requests from FedRAMP during initial assessment and authorization; otherwise they will be removed from authorization review and barred from submitting an updated authorization request for at least six months.
```
This required is vague and not well defined. 
```
FRR-PVA-PA-05
Providers MAY ask for and accept advice from their third-party assessor during assessment regarding techniques and procedures that will improve the effectiveness, clarity, and accuracy of their validation and reporting procedures for Key Security Indicators, UNLESS doing so might compromise the objectivity and integrity of the assessment (see also FRR-PVA-AA-07).
```
This implies that the 3PAO will be dropping a tool into the environment to perform a task. Is this going to be subject to SCR requirements? How do we know that the 3PAO's tool is fit and proper for the environment? Can the tool be a cloud interconnection, containerized, installed on a compute instance, or a script written out in AWS SSM? What if the assessment tool introduces a flaw into the system, e.g. tool is not using FIPS crypto module? Does that count against the CSP during the validation process? 
```
FRR-PVA-PA-06
Providers MUST include in their authorization data a high-level summary of any advice from their third-party assessor that was received and acted upon during assessment.
```
Does this mean the A2LA requirements for 3PAO will also be changing to allow for the **Third Party** Assessment Organization to give advice? Or is this a requirement on the CSP to report unethical 3PAOs (this I completely support)? Would unethical behavior be held against the individual or would it be held against the company? Can the company remediate a deficiency here by terminating the unethical employee? This requirement is so vague that I need a Sage Stick to see through the smoke. 
```
FRR-PVA-AA-02
Assessors MUST evaluate the accuracy of the Key Security Indicator goals against actual implementation of the process to determine whether or not the provider has accurately documented their process.
```
This reads like a security control audit with extra steps and added unnecessary discretion for the CSP, with a sprinkling of SOC "define the process and then show me that you do the process." This is security theater. 
```
FRR-PVA-AA-03
Assessors MUST evaluate whether or not the underlying processes are consistently creating the desired security outcome documented by the provider.
```
So 3PAOs will be auditing the audit methodology? This doesn't seem consistent with a standardized security approach or "one audit, many uses." This is too vague and defined to be useful. 
```
FRR-PVA-AA-06
Assessors MUST NOT rely on screenshots, configuration dumps, or other point-in-time output as evidence EXCEPT when evaluating the accuracy and reliability of a process that generates such point-in-time output.
```
Can this just be made explicitly clear instead of being vague? PMO defines KSIs and what to monitor, plus which KSI is a monitor-over-time versus point-in-time? This seems to be the largest issue with 20x, nobody can plan ahead because we do not know what a FedRAMP audit will actually look like. We cannot forecast staffing, resources, or project schedules with this so undefined. 
```
FRR-PVA-AA-07
Assessors MUST assess whether or not procedures are consistently followed, including the processes in place to assure this occurs; assessors MUST NOT rely solely on the existence of a procedure document for assessing if appropriate processes and procedures are in place
```
How do we audit a procedure that does not or has not occurred, e.g. user termination/onboarding? 
```
FRR-PVA-AA-08
Assessors MAY share advice with providers they are assessing about techniques and procedures that will improve the effectiveness, clarity, and accuracy of their validation and reporting procedures for Key Security Indicators, UNLESS doing so might compromise the objectivity and integrity of the assessment (see also FRR-PVA-AA-05).
NOTE: This is intended to provide some leeway that allows an assessor to explain when and why something doesn’t make sense or is hard to understand, or to share pro-tips or similar based on previous experience; it does not allow assessors to consult on the security of a system in general during an assessment.
```
This provision is going to be misused by every 3PAO and auditor. The current standard of "no advice" should be retained. 
```
FRR-PVA-AA-09
Assessors MUST deliver a high-level summary of their assessment process and resulting findings for each Key Security Indicator that is intended for inclusion in the provider’s authorization data.
```
So.... the 3PAO writes up a summary of how the KSI was assessment and the results. Maybe we call it "Assessment Test Procedure." Instead of having a standardized KSI matrix, we are going to have a customized KSI defined by the CSP that the 3PAO then has to write to. How are we going to forecast LOE for an assessment when every client is going to have a different standard? How are assessors going to be expected to learn a new KSI matrix every few weeks? 
```
FRR-PVA-AA-10
Assessors MUST NOT deliver an overall recommendation on whether or not the cloud service offering meets the requirements for FedRAMP authorization; this will be determined by FedRAMP based on the assessment findings for each Key Security Indicator.
```
Good. Keep this in here. 
```
FRR-PVA-AA-11
Assessors MUST limit the assessment during a Persistent FedRAMP Assessment to significant changes made by the cloud service offering since the most recently completed FedRAMP assessment UNLESS the provider is unable to supply the necessary information to do so.
```
So the annual audit is only going to include significant changes. How would we know that the KSIs are actually being monitored and that their magic KSI tool isn't just spitting out garbage data? Do we check the KSI tool for valid output? Who makes sure that all 475+ FedRAMP systems have valid KSI tool outputs? How do we figure out LOE for an assessment every year when the scope constantly changes? 
```
FRR-PVA-AA-12
Assessors MUST consult with FedRAMP, in collaboration with the provider, if they determine a provider has not maintained sufficient information about significant changes to properly scope a Persistent FedRAMP Assessment.
```
This was undefined in FRR-PVA-05, should probably be defined there too.

documents.text:
> I'm sure we see different universes - maybe small/med CSPs vs larger hyperscalers, etc.

Even within the context of a very large organization (e.g., a "hyperscaler") you naturally find variation in capabilities and investments. In my past I've worked on some of the most security-critical parts of a large provider (lowest level virtualization technologies, firmware management, mitigation of novel CPU-level microarchitectural side channel and transient execution vectors, etc.). We went down to the CPU and hardware system design to build robust protections so that other teams don't have to be concerned about them.

> And so I'll still put a steak dinner against any DR sheet and I guarantee I find some false FPs

This is almost certainly true. Today's software systems are complex, and even experts will make mistakes when analyzing. There are also varying opinions among experts about what qualifies as a "false positive."

The volume of "findings" produced my most scanners often makes it impractical for many organizations to analyze each and every one, therefore the most commonly accepted remediation strategy for findings is to make a change to the software system, even when a finding is almost certainly a false positive. 

See [CVE-2023-45853 (9.8 CRITICAL)](https://github.com/madler/zlib/issues/868#issuecomment-2807804350) as a case study. Due to limitations in the software management systems commonly used today, if I have the `zlib` package from Amazon Linux 2 that is older than `1.2.7-19.amzn2.0.3.aarch64`, most scanners will identify a "vulnerability." This is merely because Amazon Linux packages the `minizip` sample library as a sub-package of the `zlib` source rpm, and [an update](https://alas.aws.amazon.com/AL2/ALAS-2023-2320.html) was produced to incorporate the fix. Note that _nothing included in the Amazon Linux 2 distribution_ uses the `minizip` sample library.

Because FedRAMP scanner requirements require CVSSv3 base scores present in the NVD to be reported as the "risk score", you end up with a "critical" finding that you have to remediate one way or another. What would the perfect deviation request look like for this particular finding, and how many times should it have to be independently produced by a CSP during the authorization or ConMon process?

documents.text:
> For Ready Conversion applicants with a penetration test performed by an independent third party that is not a FedRAMP-recognized independent assessor, may the designated independent assessor conducting the Ready Conversion assessment review, validate, and incorporate those results into the CSP's initial certification assessment, or must the independent assessor independently execute another penetration test?

FedRAMP does not _require_ a penetration test from a FR Recognized independent assessor under the Consolidated Rules for 2026. The results of your penetration test from another assessor can definitely be included in your Vulnerability Detection and Response activity reports et al. 

If you're planning on submitting under the legacy rules and then converting to CR26 by February, then we'll let you take a POA&M/finding on not having a FR Recognized penetration test and you can document what you did instead and why you don't think there's a significant resulting risk. Then once you switch over to CR26 it would go poof.

documents.title: RFC-0016 Collaborative Continuous Monitoring Standard
documents.text:
# RFC-0016 Collaborative Continuous Monitoring Standard

---

# **RFC Front Matter**

* **Status:** Closed  
* **Created By:** FedRAMP  
* **Start Date:** 2025-09-15  
* **Closing Date:** 2025-11-17
* **Short Name:** rfc-0016-collaborative-continuous-monitoring

In addition to this markdown, this RFC is available in the following formats:

- **PDF file:** [0016-collaborative-continuous-monitoring.pdf](https://github.com/FedRAMP/rfcs/raw/main/rfc/assets/0016-collaborative-continuous-monitoring.pdf)
- **Word file:** [0016-collaborative-continuous-monitoring.docx](https://github.com/FedRAMP/rfcs/raw/main/rfc/assets/0016-collaborative-continuous-monitoring.docx)

## Where to Comment

Members of the public may submit multiple different comments on different issues during the public comment period. The public is asked to please refrain from including documents or spreadsheets (especially those with in-line comments or suggested changes) in public comment as this creates a significant additional review burden.

Formal public comment for official consideration by FedRAMP can be made via the following mechanisms in order of preference:

1. GitHub Post: [https://github.com/FedRAMP/community/discussions/87](https://github.com/FedRAMP/community/discussions/87)   
2. Public Comment Form: [https://forms.gle/eMHRbk7TnDBzQsWh7](https://forms.gle/eMHRbk7TnDBzQsWh7)   
3. Email: [pete@fedramp.gov](mailto:pete@fedramp.gov) with the subject "**RFC-0016 Feedback**"

Note: FedRAMP will review and publicly post all public comments received via email, but will not otherwise respond. Email submissions from federal agencies will only be made public when requested by the agency.

## Summary & Motivation

Fifteen years ago it was common for a single agency to be the only user of a cloud service for years, leading to the concept of a “sponsor” for FedRAMP \- a single agency that would commit to performing expensive and burdensome oversight of a cloud service on behalf of the entire federal government.   
   
Many different agencies with varying missions and use cases now operate the same shared commercial cloud services. Historically, relying on a single agency to oversee a cloud service on behalf of every agency user has created conflict and confusion between agencies, delayed access to new capabilities, and led to unexpected and undesirable security outcomes in some cases.

This proposed Collaborative Continuous Monitoring Standard continues implementing the vision of OMB Memorandum M-24-15 to redesign the government-wide continuous monitoring of cloud services to better align with the requirements of OMB A-130 and the NIST Risk Management Framework. This standard supplements the Significant Change Notification Standard, Vulnerability Detection and Response Standard, and Authorization Data Sharing Standard by adding the following additional requirements and recommendations:

1. Providers are expected to host meetings every 3 months that are open to all agency customers for high-level briefings of changes to the offering.  
2. Providers are expected to establish clear lines of support for agency security personnel.  
3. Agencies will be able to consume *authorization data* using automation and make ongoing authorization decisions based on *persistently* supplied information filtered for criticality based on their agency use case in accordance with their Information Security Continuous Monitoring plans.

This standard will apply firmly to FedRAMP 20x authorizations when formalized, however application to Rev5 will be optional and may require negotiation between cloud service providers and agencies based on existing customer agreements and expectations.

## Effective Date(s) & Overall Applicability

This is a draft standard released for public comment; it does not apply to any FedRAMP authorization and MUST NOT be used in draft form.

* FedRAMP **20x**:  
  * This standard will initially apply to all FedRAMP 20x authorizations when formalized.  
  * Phase One Pilot participants have one year from authorization to fully implement this standard but must demonstrate continuous quarterly progress.  
  * Phase Two Pilot participants must demonstrate significant progress towards implementing this standard prior to authorization.  
* FedRAMP **Rev5**:  
  * See [Balancing FedRAMP Rev5 against improvements to FedRAMP 20x](https://github.com/fedRAMP/community/discussions/38) for general information how improved FedRAMP standards will be applied carefully and deliberately to Rev5 authorizations.  
  * Rev5 providers should expect to adopt at least the Significant Change Notification Standard and Vulnerability Detection and Response Standard prior to adopting this Balance Improvement Release.

## Documentation Guidelines

The following FedRAMP documentation guidelines apply to this document:

* The capitalized key words "MUST", "MUST NOT", "REQUIRED", "SHALL", "SHALL NOT", "SHOULD", "SHOULD NOT", "RECOMMENDED", "MAY", and "OPTIONAL" in this document are to be interpreted as described in [IETF RFC 2119](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc2119).  
* FedRAMP-specific terms defined in [FRD-ALL (FedRAMP Definitions)](https://github.com/FedRAMP/docs/blob/main/markdown/FRMR.FRD.fedramp-definitions.md) are italicized throughout this document for reference.

---

**Background & Authority**  
[OMB Circular A-130: Managing Information as a Strategic Resource](https://whitehouse.gov/wp-content/uploads/legacy_drupal_files/omb/circulars/A130/a130revised.pdf) section 4 (c) states that agencies SHALL *“conduct and document security and privacy control assessments prior to the operation of an information system, and periodically thereafter, consistent with the frequency defined in the agency information security continuous monitoring (ISCM) and privacy continuous monitoring (PCM) strategies and the agency risk tolerance”*

[The FedRAMP Authorization Act (44 USC § 3609 (a)(1))](https://www.govinfo.gov/app/details/USCODE-2023-title44/USCODE-2023-title44-chap36-sec3609) directs the Administrator of the General Services Administration to *“develop, coordinate, and implement a process … including, as appropriate, oversight of continuous monitoring of cloud computing products and services”* 

## Purpose

Agencies are required to continuously monitor all of their information systems following a documented process integrated into their Information Security Continuous Monitoring (ISCM) strategy. These strategies are specific to each agency and may even vary at the bureau, component, or information system levels. 

The concept behind collaborative continuous monitoring is unique to government customers and creates a burden for commercial cloud service providers. This standard attempts to minimize this burden by encouraging the use of automated monitoring and review of *authorization data* required by other FedRAMP standards and limiting the expected human interaction costs for cloud service providers and agencies. Agencies are expected to use information from the cloud service provider collaboratively in accordance with their agency ISCM strategy without blocking other agencies from making their own risk-based decisions about ongoing authorization.

## Expected Outcomes

* Cloud service providers will operate their services and share additional information with agency customers to ensure they can meet their responsibilities and obligations for safely and securely operating the service  
* Federal agencies will have streamlined access to the information they actually need to make ongoing security and authorization decisions while having support from government-wide policies that demonstrate the different responsibilities and obligations for operating cloud services

---

# **Definitions**

**FRD-CCM-01**

**Ongoing Authorization Report:** A *regular* report that is supplied by FedRAMP Authorized cloud service providers to agency customers, aligned to the requirements and recommendations in the FedRAMP Collaborative Continuous Monitoring Standard.

**FRD-CCM-02**

**Quarterly Review:** A *regular* synchronous meeting hosted by a FedRAMP Authorized cloud service provider for agency customers, aligned to the requirements and recommendations in the FedRAMP Collaborative Continuous Monitoring Standard.

# **Requirements**

## FRR-CCM

These requirements and recommendations apply ALWAYS to ALL FedRAMP Authorized cloud services based on the current Effective Date(s) and Overall Applicability of this standard.

**FRR-CCM-01**

Providers MUST make an *Ongoing Authorization Report* available to *all necessary parties* every 3 months, in a consistent format that is human readable, covering the entire period since the previous summary; this report MUST include high-level summaries of at least the following information:

1. Changes to *authorization data*  
2. Planned changes to *authorization data* during at least the next 3 months  
3. *Accepted weaknesses*  
4. *Transformative changes*  
5. Updated recommendations or best practices for security, configuration, usage, or similar aspects of the *cloud service offering*  
   

**FRR-CCM-02**

Providers SHOULD establish a *regular* 3 month cycle for *Ongoing Authorization Reports* that does not align with calendar quarters so that reports are spread out during the calendar quarter for agencies.

**FRR-CCM-03**

Providers MUST publicly include the target date for their next *Ongoing Authorization Report* with the *authorization data* required by FRR-ADS-01.

**FRR-CCM-04**

Providers MUST establish and share an asynchronous mechanism for *all necessary parties* to provide feedback or ask questions related to each *Ongoing Authorization Report*; all such feedback and questions from agencies, along with responses from the provider, MUST be available to FedRAMP.

**FRR-CCM-05**

Providers MUST NOT share feedback or questions from agencies publicly or with other parties than FedRAMP UNLESS the agency that submitted the feedback or question approves.

**FRR-CCM-06**

Providers MUST NOT irresponsibly disclose sensitive information in an *Ongoing Authorization Report* that would *likely* have an adverse effect on the *cloud service offering*.

**FRR-CCM-07**

Providers MAY responsibly share some or all of the information an *Ongoing Authorization Report* publicly or with other parties if the provider determines doing so will NOT *likely* have an adverse effect on the *cloud service offering.* 

## FRR-CCM-QR

This section includes requirements and recommendations for providers hosting synchronous *Quarterly Reviews* with all agencies.

**FRR-CCM-QR-01**

Providers SHOULD host a synchronous *Quarterly Review* every 3 months, open to all necessary parties, to review aspects of the most recent *Ongoing Authorization Report* that the provider determines are of the most relevance to agencies.

**FRR-CCM-QR-02**

Providers SHOULD regularly schedule *Quarterly Reviews* to occur at least 3 business days after releasing an *Ongoing Authorization Report* AND within 2 weeks of such release.

**FRR-CCM-QR-03**

Providers MUST NOT irresponsibly disclose sensitive information in a *Quarterly Review* that would *likely* have an adverse effect on the *cloud service offering.*

**FRR-CCM-QR-04**

Providers MUST include either a registration link or a downloadable calendar file with meeting information for *Quarterly Reviews* in the *authorization data* available to *all necessary parties* required by FRR-ADS-06 and FRR-ADS-07; providers who do not host *Quarterly Reviews* MUST clearly state this and explain this decision in the same *authorization data.*

**FRR-CCM-QR-05**

Providers hosting *Quarterly Reviews* MUST publicly include the target date for their next *Quarterly Review* with the *authorization data* required by FRR-ADS-01.

**FRR-CCM-QR-06**

Providers SHOULD include additional information in *Quarterly Reviews* that the provider determines are of interest, use, or otherwise relevant to agencies.

**FRR-CCM-QR-07**

Providers SHOULD NOT invite third parties to attend *Quarterly Reviews* intended for agencies unless it is of specific relevance; this is because agencies are less likely to actively participate in meetings with third parties.

**FRR-CCM-QR-08**

Providers MUST NOT disclose feedback or questions from agencies during a *Quarterly Review* with the public or third parties UNLESS the agency that submitted the feedback or question approves.

**FRR-CCM-QR-09**

Providers SHOULD record or transcribe *Quarterly Reviews* and make such available to *all necessary parties* with other *authorization data* as required by FRR-ADS-06 and FRR-ADS07.

**FRR-CCM-QR-10**

Providers MAY responsibly share recordings or transcriptions of *Quarterly Reviews* with the public or other parties ONLY if the provider removes all agency information (comments, questions, names, etc.) AND determines sharing will NOT *likely* have an adverse effect on the *cloud service offering.*

**FRR-CCM-QR-11**

Providers MAY share content prepared for a *Quarterly Review* with the public or other parties if the provider determines doing so will NOT *likely* have an adverse effect on the *cloud service offering.*

## Agencies

This section includes requirements and recommendations for agencies who are using FedRAMP Authorized cloud services.

**FRR-CCM-AG-01**

Agencies MUST review each *Ongoing Authorization Report* to understand how changes to the *cloud service offering* may impact the previously agreed-upon risk tolerance documented in the agency’s Authorization to Operate of a federal information system that includes the *cloud service offering* in its boundary.

Note: This is required by 44 USC § 35, OMB A-130, FIPS-200, and M-24-15.

**FRR-CCM-AG-02**

Agencies SHOULD consider the Security Category noted in their Authorization to Operate of the federal information system that includes the *cloud service offering* in its boundary and assign appropriate information security resources for reviewing *Ongoing Authorization Reports*, attending *Quarterly Reviews*, and other ongoing *authorization data.*

**FRR-CCM-AG-03**

Agencies SHOULD designate a senior information security official to review *Ongoing Authorization Reports* and represent the agency at *Quarterly Reviews* for *cloud service offerings* included in agency information systems with a Security Category of High.

**FRR-CCM-AG-04**

Agencies SHOULD formally notify the provider if the information presented in an *Ongoing Authorization Report*, *Quarterly Review*, or other ongoing *authorization data* causes significant concerns that may lead the agency to remove the *cloud service offering* from operation.

**FRR-CCM-AG-05**

Agencies MUST notify FedRAMP by sending a notification to [info@fedramp.gov](mailto:info@fedramp.gov) if the information presented in an *Ongoing Authorization Report*, *Quarterly Review*, or other ongoing *authorization data* causes significant concerns that may lead the agency to stop operation of the *cloud service offering*.

*Note: This is an OMB policy; agencies are required to notify FedRAMP in OMB Memorandum M-24-15 section IV (a).*

**FRR-CCM-AG-06**

Agencies SHOULD NOT request additional information from cloud service providers that is not required by this FedRAMP standard UNLESS the head of the agency or an authorized delegate makes a determination that there is a demonstrable need for such.

*Note: This is related to the Presumption of Adequacy directed by 44 USC § 3613 (e).*

**FRR-CCM-AG-07**

Agencies MUST inform FedRAMP after requesting any additional information or materials from a cloud service provider beyond those required in this policy by sending a notification to info@fedramp.gov.

*Note: This is an OMB policy; agencies are required to notify FedRAMP in OMB Memorandum M-24-15 section IV (a).*

documents.title: RFC-0031 Updated Incident Communications Procedures
documents.text:
Quzara LLC — Public Comment on RFC-0031
Updated Incident Communications Procedures
Submitted by: Quzara LLC
Date: May 2026
GitHub Discussion: #138

Quzara LLC operates Cybertorch™, a FedRAMP High Authorized Managed Detection and Response (MDR) and SOC-as-a-Service platform built on Azure Government. We provide 24/7 security monitoring, incident detection, triage, and response for federal agencies, Defense Industrial Base contractors, and cloud service providers maintaining FedRAMP authorizations. We support this RFC's goals and the shift to a tiered reporting model.
These comments are grounded in our operational experience running a Class D (High) SOC and managing the full incident lifecycle — from detection through recovery — on behalf of federal customers.

Comment 1: The reporting clock has no defined starting point
Rules: ICP-CSO-EFR, ICP-CSO-EFI, ICP-CSO-IRT
Problem: The reporting timelines begin after "evaluation," but the RFC does not define when evaluation is complete. In a SOC environment, an incident passes through multiple measurable phases before anyone can determine federal reportability or assign a PAIN rating:

MTTD (Mean Time to Detect) — elapsed time from incident occurrence to detection by monitoring systems
MTTA (Mean Time to Acknowledge) — elapsed time from alert firing to analyst acknowledgment
MTTI (Mean Time to Investigate/Triage) — elapsed time from acknowledgment to initial classification, which is where reportability and impact rating determination actually happen

The reporting timelines sit downstream of all three phases but don't acknowledge any of them. Without a defined trigger, the boundary between "still triaging" and "evaluation complete" is subjective. This creates an unintentional incentive to delay formal classification to extend the reporting window — the opposite of what this RFC intends.
Recommendation: Define the reporting trigger as completion of initial triage — the point at which the incident response team has sufficient information to make a preliminary reportability determination and assign an initial impact rating. Clarify that this determination need not be definitive and that impact ratings may be revised in subsequent reports as the investigation matures.

Comment 2: Managed security providers are invisible in the notification chain
Rules: ICP-CSO-EFR, ICP-CSO-AAP, ICP-CSO-IIR, ICP-CSO-IRT
Problem: The RFC assumes incident communications are a direct provider-to-FedRAMP/agency relationship. In practice, many FedRAMP-authorized providers rely on FedRAMP-authorized managed security providers for detection, triage, and escalation. The MDR provider is often the first entity to detect an incident, complete triage, and determine reportability — sometimes before the provider itself is aware.
This creates a timing problem. The coordination handoff from MDR provider to the CSP — alert, escalate, brief, confirm — introduces latency that could consume a significant portion of a 15- or 30-minute Class D reporting window. The RFC doesn't account for this handoff.
Recommendation: Acknowledge that providers may designate a FedRAMP-authorized managed security provider as a reporting agent for notification and reporting purposes. The provider retains compliance responsibility, but the MDR provider may initiate notifications and submit initial and ongoing reports on the provider's behalf under a documented arrangement. This reflects existing operational practice and directly supports faster reporting.

Comment 3: Multi-tenant notification doesn't scale within Class D timelines
Rule: ICP-CSO-AAP
Problem: A Class D provider serving 20+ federal agency customers cannot realistically notify each agency individually — using potentially different channels and contact arrangements — within 15 minutes (N5) or 30 minutes (N4) while simultaneously conducting containment and response. The notification logistics alone (composing per-agency communications, following each agency's specified contact procedures, confirming receipt) can exceed the reporting window.
Recommendation: Allow centralized notification mechanisms as compliant alternatives: a secure broadcast to a pre-established distribution list, an authenticated machine-readable incident notification feed that agencies subscribe to, or a structured push through the provider's Trust Center. Agencies requiring non-standard channels could document those in their customer agreements. This scales operationally while preserving agency-specific flexibility — and is consistent with the machine-readable status page approach already established for availability reporting.

Comment 4: Ongoing reporting cadence competes with active response
Rules: ICP-CSO-IRT, ICP-CSO-OIR
Problem: At Class D N5, ongoing reports are required every 3 hours. During active containment and forensics, the team managing the incident is simultaneously expected to produce structured narrative reports on a fixed cadence. Every report cycle diverts analyst attention from containment and recovery — the work that actually reduces federal customer risk.
The RFC already states that providers should prioritize prompt notification with potentially incomplete information above delayed reporting. That principle should apply to ongoing reporting as well.
Recommendation: Allow structured machine-readable status updates (via API endpoint, Trust Center feed, or standardized JSON/OSCAL schema) to satisfy ongoing report requirements. Reserve human-authored narrative content for initial and final reports, where completeness and context are most valuable. This keeps agencies informed in near-real-time without pulling responders off the actual response.

Comment 5: "Responsibly" needs sharper guidance at Class D
Rules: FRD-RSP, ICP-CSO-IIR
Problem: The definition of "responsibly" is intentionally flexible, which works at Class B/C. At Class D — supporting DoD and high-impact federal workloads — the 15-minute N5 reporting window creates tension with responsible disclosure. Within 15 minutes of completing triage, the response team may have confirmed an active compromise but not yet identified the full attack vector or completed containment. Sharing indicators of compromise at that stage could alert the adversary or expose technical details before the environment is secured.
Recommendation: Add Class D-specific guidance clarifying that initial reports at N4/N5 should prioritize the fact of the incident, the impact rating, functional impact to federal customers, and contact information. Detailed indicators of compromise, attack vectors, and root cause analysis may be appropriately deferred to ongoing or final reports once the response team determines that disclosure will not compromise active containment.

Comment 6: CISA notification requirements will create duplicative reporting
Rule: ICP-CSO-CSA
Problem: The RFC requires FedRAMP notification plus separate CISA notification. Many providers already report to CISA under existing authorities. When CIRCIA reporting requirements take effect, there will be three or more overlapping notification obligations with different timelines, formats, and thresholds — all triggered by the same incident.
Recommendation: Clarify that a single CISA notification satisfies the RFC's CISA reporting requirement regardless of which authority triggers it. FedRAMP should coordinate with CISA on a shared reporting format or intake mechanism so that one submission satisfies both requirements.

Comment 7: The most aggressive Class D timelines should be validated before enforcement
Rule: ICP-CSO-IRT
Problem: The Class D N5 initial report window is 15 minutes. Even for a mature 24/7 SOC, when you account for the full detection-to-notification chain — detection, analyst acknowledgment, triage, report composition, delivery — 15 minutes from completed triage to delivered report is extremely tight. Industry benchmarks for mean time to detect alone frequently exceed 15 minutes for sophisticated attacks. The combined chain, even at a well-staffed SOC, is realistically measured in hours, not minutes.
FedRAMP's own Phase 2 lessons learned demonstrated that pilot-based validation produces better outcomes than untested mandates.
Recommendation: Implement Class D N5 and N4 initial report timelines in two phases. Phase 1 (January 1, 2027): set both at 1 hour — already more demanding than today's uniform standard because the new timelines are scoped to confidentiality/integrity incidents only, eliminating noise. Phase 2 (July 1, 2027): tighten to the proposed 15- and 30-minute targets after reviewing 6 months of reporting data. This validates feasibility before enforcement, consistent with FedRAMP's broader iterative approach to modernization.

Comment 8: SOC performance metrics should be part of Ongoing Authorization Reports
Rule: CCM-OAR-AVL
Problem: The RFC introduces reporting timelines but provides no framework for measuring or improving the operational capabilities that determine whether those timelines can be met. A provider can file reports on time while running a SOC with poor detection and triage performance. The timelines only measure the last mile of a much longer chain.
The updates in this RFC add incident summaries and lessons learned to Ongoing Authorization Reports, which is a step forward. But they don't capture the operational health of the provider's detection and response capability.
Recommendation: Require or strongly encourage Class C and Class D providers to include SOC performance metrics in their Ongoing Authorization Reports:

MTTD (Mean Time to Detect) — measures detection capability
MTTA (Mean Time to Acknowledge) — measures SOC staffing and responsiveness
MTTI (Mean Time to Investigate) — measures triage efficiency and directly determines how quickly the reporting clock starts
MTTC (Mean Time to Contain) — measures active response capability
MTTR (Mean Time to Recover) — measures recovery speed and directly determines when the final report deadline begins
MTTN (Mean Time to Notify) — measures notification execution against the timelines in this RFC

Trending these metrics over time gives FedRAMP and agency customers visibility into the provider's actual operational posture — not just whether they filed reports on time, but whether the entire detection-to-response pipeline is improving. This turns incident communications from a reactive compliance exercise into a measurable continuous improvement program, consistent with the Phase 2 finding that trending validation data promotes confidence in a provider's security program.

We appreciate FedRAMP's commitment to transparent rulemaking and the opportunity to contribute operationally grounded feedback.

documents.title: RFC-0012 FedRAMP Continuous Vulnerability Management Standard
documents.text:
Just writing to provide the way I'm viewing these items in hopes that it helps manage these standards if/when released. Assuming they don't change much. I believe that this RFC is overall positive; and in my opinion, gives the industry a chance to implement actual security, rather than focusing on compliance for compliance sake, when its not actually benefiting security.

1 I believe this is already written into this RFC that CVSS base score must be used in the rating. I don't read this RFC as we are "changing the base score" - but instead deriving a new one leveraging it.

3 The way this RFC reads to me, CSPs can perform unauthenticated scans of those assets. That has always been the case, and this just allows nuance to be a part of the discussion, rather than being overly specific and making this a "check-box."

4 Given the definition of internet-reachable here, I interpret that there are different definitions for Zero-Trust than are being used for vulnerability management. I don't disagree that everything _*could*_ be internet exploitable under the right scenarios like compromising VPNs/networks, but the fact is that is less likely than stuff that is freely accessible on the internet without other comrpomises. ZT is focusing on something that isn't vulnerability management.


5 Does it need to? If that is a factor that can be put in automatically (or manually for hopefully only a few vulnerabilities), then it can be included if a CSP included that in the assessment. But a security assessment being automated is said many times to be encouraged and the desired outcome, so by definition, this is a security assessment.

7 This RFC doesn't propose excusing those. Like all standards/requirements in FedRAMP, I read this as an "in addition to all other controls that apply."

10 I think allowing CSPs to define this based on how and when their scanners do this, and ensuring it makes "sense" is best here. Allowing a government agency to specify exactly how those situations should be treated lacks context especially as technology changes.

11 - 24 - I disagree with the intention of the comments with these. These all should be "Should's." They allow for situations where thats not possible to be raised and discussed with nuance and context without punitive actions being taken by default just because you didn't check a box.

documents.title: RFC-0012 FedRAMP Continuous Vulnerability Management Standard
documents.text:
Just writing to provide the way I'm viewing these items in hopes that it helps manage these standards if/when released. Assuming they don't change much. I agree that this RFC is overall positive and in my opinion, gives the industry a chance to implement actual security, rather than focusing on compliance for compliance sake, when its not actually benefiting security.
1. I think this "gap" can be easily covered by CSP discretion for what makes "sense". Personally I don't see it is as a gap. Some products (appliances etc) *can't* be scanned with authentication, and vice versa. Realistically, if we do unauthenticated network scans of all the resources/networks that containers run on, thats the unauthenticated scan, and then the authenticated one is the container scanning and/or the authenticated scanning of the node itself (if thats available to you, as the CSP, as its not with some providers using serverless). Personally, I think the discretion here allows the program to grow as new technologies emerge and aligns with the programs intent to allow CSPs to "create" better and provide federal agencies with the latest and greatest in the most efficient way. As new technologies emerge, having strict standards often means we are all *only* focused on the square peg & round hole, rather than focusing on what makes actual sense for true security.
2. Agree, I love the move away from CVSS Scores. So ➕ on that.
3. In looking at the intent of these timelines these don't scare me. Credibly exploitable vulnerabilities in our CSP environments are rare, and the focus of this standard is clear that the first action considered should be to mitigate. Remediation is always a preference, but not always practical (patches don't always exist etc). So the way we are looking at things, these vulnerabilities will basically trigger alarms that get on-call support when in off hours. The FIRST thing that should be done is evaluate its true exploitability, even with internal knowledge. If that proves that this is actually not exploitable with current information, then this is no longer credible exploitable, and adjust the vulnerability appropriately, and can all go home to resume "normal" vulnerability operations. Assuming we do find that it is credible exploitable through manual methods as well, the second actions we will be looking at are the quick wins to mitigate the likelihood of exploitability. That COULD be full remediation, but could also be a specific WAF rule, a relatively quick/safe application change etc. As I mentioned, this may not remediation, but it mitigates to, again, no longer being credibly exploitable and no longer requires the 3/7/21 days. We have every intention of full remediation "quickly" - but to align with safe release practices and such, that may be 2-4 weeks, which is fine if the issue is not credibly exploitable anymore.
4. Personally, I don't think there should be specific machine-readable requirements coming from FedRAMP right now. The program has made clear that centralized systems to recieve/review vulnerabilities are on the way out. Until something is centralized and mandated, I think its more flexible with CSP engineering teams to be able to get the data "however" their systems produce it now, so we can all start collaborating on whats specifically working and not working.
5. Personally, I prefer not to have specificity here. Rather than retaining 2 years worth of "continuous reports" in an actual versioned format, some of us would prefer to just have a realtime changelog on each item. And some may prefer the former. Either way, the same information is retained. But the former, on a true "continuous" reporting mechanism is unreasonable and more difficult to parse, but might be more possible for some CSPs than others.
6. As repeated previously, I think not having so many "specifics" from FedRAMP is a good thing. It enables us to have more thoughtful conversations about actual security risk, rather than just checking boxes. Private VPC endpoints are sometimes exposed directly to the internet, but not always. Allowing CSPs to put their true context into their systems is best. I read the intent of FedRAMP 20x to encourage more thoughtful conversations about risk between agencies and CSPs, rather than check-box compliance. Asking FedRAMP to provide edge cases and decision criteria removes a CSPs ability to provide their own context that the program might not be able to conceive today.
7. Agreed, though admittedly, many CSPs are already doing this as endorsed by several agencies and the PMO for Rev5 practices.

documents.title: Consolidated 20x Phase 2 pilot Q&A / discussion
documents.text:
> I may have written the question poorly so perhaps an example will help.

Ah, that's probably my bad, I misread your question on my phone as asking if someone had to have a 20x authorization to follow the SCN process.
 
> Let's say in the future a CSP has achieved a FedRAMP 20x Moderate authorization for its new CSO but has no agency users of it yet. (The CSO has no rev5 FedRAMP status or ATO.) The CSP makes a "transformative change" to the offering and desires to invoke the significant change notification (SCN) process (whatever that turns out to be for FedRAMP 20x) to maintain its existing 20x authorization. Can the SCN be invoked with no agency users of the offering (i.e., no agency ATOs have been issued)?

The [Significant Change Notification](https://www.fedramp.gov/docs/significant-change-notifications/) process is intended to allow cloud service providers to make changes to their services **without explicit government approval.** There is no requirement in the SCN process for an agency AO to approve any part of the process. 

Under 20x, cloud service providers simply need to follow the process and address all requirements and recommendations in the process - this is how they earn and maintain their FedRAMP authorization. It doesn't matter if there is an agency ATO of the system or not. FedRAMP will validate that providers are following the process and take corrective action against those who don't.

It's worth noting that 20x requirements are designed to allow a prospective agency customer to see how well a cloud service has done at meeting 20x requirements historically (such as Significant Change Notifications, Vulnerability Detection and Response, etc.) so that this can factor into the authorization decision.
